pools.title: Recognizing by Pattern: Telling Apart and Treating Alike
pools.covers: reading §7.0 (the unnumbered Opening), §7.1.1, §7.1.2 · lecture 7.1 slides title, no_detector_for_an_eel, recognizing_by_pattern, telling_apart_treating_alike, two_demands_one_mapping

items.stem: A small fish smells the same eel twice in one afternoon, an hour apart. Why are the two smells not the same?

options.text: The eel’s mixture of chemicals changes from moment to moment, and it mixes with whatever else is in the water, such as leaves, other fish, and mud.
options.why: Correct. The mixture differs from eel to eel, and even for one eel from moment to moment, and it is always mixed with everything else in the stream.

options.text: The fish’s smell receptors are replaced between the two encounters, so that the same chemicals now produce a new pattern of activity in its nostrils.
options.why: Replacing receptors is not what makes the two smells differ. The smells differ because the eel’s mixture varies from moment to moment and mixes with everything else in the water.

options.text: The eel gives off one chemical whose strength alone rises and falls, so that only the size of the fish’s response differs from one encounter to the next.
options.why: An eel gives off a complex constellation of chemicals, not one. That is why no receptor can stand for an eel, and why the mixture is never twice the same.

options.text: The two smells are in fact the same, since one eel always gives off one fixed mixture, and only different eels give off different mixtures of chemicals.
options.why: The mixture does differ from eel to eel, but it also differs for the same eel from one moment to the next. That is what “never twice the same” means.

items.stem: Suppose a fish has eight kinds of smell receptor, and every one of the eight responds both to an eel and to a harmless fish, each at its own strength. What can identify the eel?

options.text: The pattern of activity across the eight kinds together, since no one kind of receptor is an eel receptor.
options.why: Correct. Each kind of receptor responds to some chemicals and not to others, and an eel gives off a mixture of many. What identifies an eel is the pattern across many receptors, and much of that pattern also turns up for harmless fish.

options.text: Whichever one of the eight kinds responds most strongly, since the strongest response is the one that marks the eel.
options.why: The strongest receptor also responds to the harmless fish, so it cannot stand for an eel on its own. Nothing in the fish’s nostrils stands for an eel.

options.text: A ninth kind of receptor the fish must also have, since each smell that matters has a receptor that responds to it alone.
options.why: There is no eel receptor, just as there is no coffee receptor. The eel is identified by a pattern across receptors that respond to other things as well.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a receptor that responds to harmless fish as well can carry no information about eels.
options.why: Each receptor does carry some information; it just does not identify the eel alone. The combination of activity across all of them is what does.

items.stem: What did a single unit of Module 4 do with its inputs, and what did that amount to?

options.text: It added up its weighted inputs and fired when the sum crossed a threshold, which amounts to drawing one straight line or plane through the space of its inputs.
options.why: Correct. Firing on one side of one line and not on the other is all a single threshold unit can do.

options.text: It stored each input it received and fired whenever a new input matched a stored one, which amounts to keeping a list of everything it had encountered.
options.why: Storing examples is a different procedure altogether. A unit of Module 4 kept no list; it summed its weighted inputs against a threshold.

options.text: It multiplied all of its inputs together and fired only when every one of them was present, which amounts to a separate labeled line for each input.
options.why: A unit of Module 4 added its weighted inputs rather than multiplying them. And a labeled line is a single sensory neuron routed to a response, not a unit of this kind.

options.text: It passed its strongest input on unchanged and dropped all the rest, which amounts to relaying a single receptor’s signal at each moment.
options.why: A threshold unit combines all of its weighted inputs into one sum. It does not pass on one input and drop the others.

items.stem: A single unit draws one line, and learning can move that line. For which of these animals would one such line be enough?

options.text: A worm for which one chemical, or one simple combination of chemicals, reliably means food wherever it turns up.
options.why: Correct. Where one input, or one simple combination of inputs, reliably meant food or copper, one line was enough.

options.text: A fish for which an eel arrives as a pattern across many receptors, much of that pattern shared with harmless fish.
options.why: An eel has no detector of its own. Its pattern is shared in large part with harmless fish and changes between encounters, which one line cannot handle.

options.text: A bird for which its mate arrives as a different pattern of sights and sounds at every encounter with that mate.
options.why: A mate is one of the things that has no detector of its own and arrives as a changing pattern, which is what one line was not enough for.

options.text: A mouse for which the way home arrives as a pattern across many senses that changes from one trip to the next.
options.why: The way home is one of the cases of a pattern with no detector of its own. One line was enough only where a single input reliably signaled something.

items.stem: One line was enough for a worm and copper. Why is one line not enough for most of what matters to an animal?

options.text: Prey, predators, mates, and the way home have no detector of their own, and arrive as patterns across many inputs that change from one encounter to the next.
options.why: Correct. Copper had a neuron that responded to it. Most of what matters does not, and the pattern it arrives as is never quite the same twice.

options.text: A single unit cannot learn, so its line stays wherever it started, however much the animal’s world changes around it over the course of a lifetime.
options.why: Learning can move a unit’s line, as described in Module 5. The trouble is not that the line is stuck, but that one line cannot handle a pattern with no detector that keeps changing.

options.text: Most of what matters reaches the animal through only one sense, and so overloads a single unit with far more inputs than it can add up at once.
options.why: The number of inputs is not the problem, and things that matter often arrive through several senses. What matters is that no input identifies them alone.

options.text: Most of what matters gives off signals too faint to cross a threshold, so a single unit would never fire to it at all, however its weights were set.
options.why: Faintness is not the point. Things that matter can produce strong signals; what they lack is a detector of their own, and their patterns keep changing.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a single threshold unit, whose line learning can move, was enough for a worm and copper but is not enough for a fish and an eel.
items.answer: A single threshold unit adds up its weighted inputs and fires when the sum crosses a threshold, which amounts to drawing one straight line through the space of its inputs, and learning can move that line. That was enough where one input, or one simple combination of inputs, reliably meant food or copper. An eel is different. Nothing in the fish’s nostrils stands for an eel: each kind of receptor responds to some chemicals and not to others, and an eel gives off a mixture of many. What identifies an eel is a pattern of activity across many receptors, much of it shared with harmless fish, and that pattern changes from one encounter to the next. Most of what matters to an animal, its prey, predators, mates, and the way home, is like the eel rather than like copper.
rubric: Describes the unit as a weighted sum against a threshold, drawing one line that learning can move.
Says one line was enough where one input, or one simple combination, reliably meant food or copper.
Says no receptor stands for an eel, so the eel is identified by a pattern across many receptors.
Notes that much of the eel’s pattern is shared with harmless fish, or that the pattern changes between encounters.

items.stem: How does the small fish’s forebrain compare with a mammal’s?

options.text: The fish has a pallium, the roof of the vertebrate forebrain, which in mammals grew into the neocortex; the fish itself has no neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The pallium is the part the two share. In mammals it grew into the neocortex, and the fish has the pallium without the neocortex.

options.text: The fish has a small neocortex with the same six layers, which in mammals grew much larger without any change to its plan at all.
options.why: The fish has no neocortex at all. What it shares with mammals is the pallium, the structure that grew in mammals into the neocortex.

options.text: The fish has neither a pallium nor a neocortex, so whatever it recognizes has to be handled by its receptors and its muscles alone.
options.why: The fish does have a pallium, and it faces the same problem any neocortex faces. Pattern recognition needs something between the receptors and the muscles.

options.text: The fish has a neocortex but no pallium, since the pallium is the part of the forebrain that first arose in the mammals.
options.why: That reverses the history. The pallium is the roof of the vertebrate forebrain, and in mammals it grew into the neocortex.

items.stem: The question left open about the neocortex is what it computes, yet the module follows a fish that has no neocortex. Why is the fish a reasonable place to begin?

options.text: It faces the problem any neocortex faces, recognizing a thing from inputs never twice the same, and that problem should be made exact first.
options.why: Correct. The fish has a pallium rather than a neocortex, but the problem is the same, and being exact about the problem comes first.

options.text: The fish has a small neocortex of its own, so its circuits can be studied as a simpler version of the mammal’s six-layered sheet, one layer at a time, from the bottom up.
options.why: The fish has no neocortex. What makes it useful is that it faces the same problem, not that it carries a small copy of the structure.

options.text: The fish recognizes everything by labeled lines, so it shows by contrast what a neocortex adds to recognition that no labeled line could ever provide on its own.
options.why: The fish recognizes an eel by pattern, not by a labeled line. It is useful because its problem is the very one a neocortex faces.

options.text: The fish has no forebrain at all, so whatever it manages to recognize shows what can be done with no structure resembling the neocortex anywhere in its brain.
options.why: The fish has a pallium, the roof of the vertebrate forebrain. Its usefulness is that it faces the same problem as a neocortex, without having one.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, state the question that a nearly uniform neocortex raises, and explain why a fish with no neocortex is a reasonable place to start on it.
items.answer: In mammals the pallium, the roof of the vertebrate forebrain, grew into the neocortex, a large, nearly uniform sheet with one kind of circuit and the same six layers whether its signals come from the eyes, the skin, or the ears. A structure that does the same thing to every kind of input raises a question with two possible answers. Either its one operation is general enough to be useful to every sense, or the circuit adds nothing of its own, and what each area does comes entirely from what is connected to it. The small fish has no neocortex, but it has a pallium, and it faces the same problem any neocortex faces: it must recognize a thing from inputs that are never twice the same. So before asking what the neocortex computes, we can be exact about what recognizing an eel requires.
rubric: Describes the neocortex as nearly uniform, with one kind of circuit and the same six layers whatever the sense.
States both possibilities: one operation general enough for every sense, or a circuit that adds nothing of its own.
Presents the question as open, without treating either possibility as settled.
Says the fish has a pallium but no neocortex, and faces the same problem of recognizing a thing from inputs never twice the same.
Says the problem has to be made exact before asking what the neocortex computes.

items.stem: How does the worm of Module 4 recognize copper?

options.text: A sensory neuron responds to copper and its output is routed to the machinery that turns the worm away, so the neuron firing is, in effect, the recognizing.
options.why: Correct. Nothing else has to happen. In the worm, that neuron firing and the worm recognizing copper come to the same thing.

options.text: Activity across many receptors is combined downstream into a state that means copper, and that state then drives the machinery that turns the worm away.
options.why: That is how the fish has to recognize an eel. The worm needs no downstream state, because one neuron responds to copper and is routed straight to turning away.

options.text: Several copper-sensing neurons respond at once, and the worm turns away only when most of them are active together, so that no single neuron is enough on its own.
options.why: One neuron routed to turning away is enough for the worm. Nothing has to tally the responses of several neurons.

options.text: The worm compares the chemicals around it with a stored memory of copper, and turns away whenever the chemicals around it match that stored memory.
options.why: No stored memory is consulted. A single sensory neuron responds to copper, and its output alone turns the worm away.

items.stem: How does the way the worm recognizes copper differ from the way the small fish recognizes an eel?

options.text: The worm relies on one neuron that responds to copper; the fish relies on a combination across many receptors, no one of which identifies the eel alone.
options.why: Correct. These are the two quite different ways an animal can recognize something: a labeled line, and pattern recognition.

options.text: The worm relies on a combination across many copper receptors; the fish relies on one receptor that responds to eels and to nothing else in the whole stream.
options.why: That reverses the two. The worm has one neuron routed to turning away, and nothing in the fish’s nostrils responds to eels and only to eels.

options.text: The worm recognizes copper only after learning about it; the fish recognizes an eel without ever needing to learn anything at all about eels.
options.why: Learning is not what separates the two ways. The difference is one responding neuron against a combination across many receptors.

options.text: The worm and the fish recognize in the same way, by a single neuron each, and differ only in which of the senses that single neuron belongs to.
options.why: They recognize in two quite different ways. A single neuron serves the worm, but an eel can only be identified from a pattern across many receptors.

items.stem: Which of these animals is recognizing something by pattern recognition?

options.text: A dog identifying its owner from activity across many smell receptors, no one of which responds to that owner alone.
options.why: Correct. The owner is identified by a combination of activity across many receptors, and no single receptor identifies the owner on its own.

options.text: A frog snapping whenever any one of its many motion-sensing cells fires, since each of those cells is enough on its own.
options.why: Many cells are involved, but each one alone triggers the response, so each works as its own labeled line. Pattern recognition needs a combination, no one part of which suffices.

options.text: A worm turning away whenever its single copper-sensing neuron fires, routed directly to the machinery of turning.
options.why: That is a labeled line. The neuron firing is, in effect, the recognizing, and nothing else has to happen.

options.text: A fly cleaning one leg whenever a single bristle on that leg is touched, by a cell that responds to that touch alone.
options.why: One cell routed to one response is a labeled line, the other way of recognizing. Pattern recognition depends on a combination across many inputs.

items.stem: What is pattern recognition?

options.text: Identifying something from a combination of activity across many inputs, no one of which identifies it alone.
options.why: Correct. The small fish recognizing an eel is the central case: no receptor responds to eels alone, so the eel is identified from the combination.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a faint or partial input produces the response the whole would.
options.why: That is pattern completion, something a circuit can do with a stored pattern. Pattern recognition is identifying a thing from a combination across many inputs.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage of processing can tell those overlapping inputs apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, one way a circuit can serve discrimination. Pattern recognition is the broader task of identifying a thing from a combination of inputs.

options.text: Recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.
options.why: That is invariance, the hardest form of the problem. Pattern recognition names the general task of identifying a thing from a combination across many inputs.

items.stem: What is the term for identifying something from a combination of activity across many inputs, no one of which identifies it alone?

options.text: Pattern recognition.
options.why: Correct. Pattern recognition is how the fish has to identify an eel, since no single receptor in its nostrils identifies an eel by itself.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. It names one thing a circuit can do, not the general task of identifying from a combination.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike so that a later stage can tell them apart. It serves discrimination; it is not the task itself.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal. It is a hard case of pattern recognition, not its definition.

items.stem: The worm’s copper-sensing neuron can be wired straight to turning away. Why can the small fish not get by with wiring each of its smell receptors straight to its escape muscles in the same way?

options.text: No receptor alone signals an eel, so a state that stands for the eel, whichever mixture produced it, has to arise somewhere downstream of the receptors.
options.why: Correct. The fish has to end up in a state that means “eel”, and none of its receptors can supply that state by itself. Pattern recognition needs something between the receptors and the muscles.

options.text: Receptor signals are too weak to drive a muscle on their own, so a stage that amplifies each receptor’s signal has to come between them and the muscles.
options.why: The strength of the signals is not the problem. Even a strong signal from one receptor would not mean “eel”, because no receptor responds to eels and only to eels.

options.text: Fish muscles respond only to signals from the brain, so receptor signals have to pass through the brain on their way, whatever those signals happen to mean.
options.why: The route is not the point. What has to arise between receptors and muscles is a state that stands for the eel, which no receptor supplies alone.

options.text: Wiring receptors to muscles would work for eels, but the fish would then have no way to learn anything new about the eels it smells.
options.why: Wiring each receptor to escape would not work for eels at all, since no receptor responds to eels and only to eels. The missing piece is a state that means “eel”.

items.stem: What is a representation?

options.text: An internal pattern of activity that stands for something in the world, so that what the animal does next depends on it.
options.why: Correct. A representation is the internal form in which information about the world is held, such as activity downstream of the fish’s receptors that stands for an eel.

options.text: How good an example of a category an item is, as when a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin is.
options.why: That is typicality, a fact about how people rate members of a category. A representation is a pattern of activity that stands for something, so that behavior depends on it.

options.text: A set of things treated as the same kind for some purpose, such as all the eels a fish has to flee from in its stream.
options.why: That is a category, a set of things in the world. A representation is the internal pattern of activity that stands for something in it.

options.text: A cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size.
options.why: That is tolerance, a property of a single cell’s response. A representation is a pattern of activity that stands for something in the world.

items.stem: What is the term for the internal form in which information about the world is held, such as a pattern of activity downstream of a fish’s receptors that stands for an eel, so that what the fish does next depends on it?

options.text: Representation.
options.why: Correct. A representation stands for something in the world, and what the animal does next depends on what it stands for.

options.text: Receptive field.
options.why: A receptive field describes which stimuli change one cell’s activity, and where in the sensory world they do it. It describes what drives a cell, not what a pattern stands for.

options.text: Category.
options.why: A category is a set of things treated as the same kind for some purpose. The eels are a category; the activity that stands for an eel is a representation.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. It is something done with stored patterns, not the name for a pattern that stands for something.

items.stem: Suppose two patterns of activity in a fish’s brain both stand for an eel. They occur in different places, and they look nothing alike. Can both count as representations of the eel?

options.text: Yes, if what the fish does next depends on what each one stands for; the definition puts no limit on where a pattern sits or what it looks like.
options.why: Correct. The definition is about what the pattern does for the animal, not about where it sits or what it looks like.

options.text: No, since a representation of an eel has to sit in the one part of the brain that handles smell, and the two patterns cannot both sit in that one place.
options.why: Nothing in the definition names a place. A pattern counts as a representation because of what it does for the animal, wherever it occurs.

options.text: No, since two patterns that look nothing alike cannot both stand for the same thing, so one of the two is not the eel’s representation.
options.why: The definition makes no demand about what a pattern looks like. What matters is that the animal’s next action depends on what the pattern stands for.

options.text: Yes, but only if each of the two patterns resembles the eel’s mixture of chemicals, the way a picture resembles the thing it shows.
options.why: The definition makes no demand that a pattern resemble what it stands for. It asks only that what the animal does next depend on what the pattern stands for.

items.stem: How is representation connected to which pairings an animal learns easily?

options.text: A new connection can only link things already represented, so how easily two things are paired depends in part on how each was represented beforehand.
options.why: Correct. The link is hedged on purpose: which pairings are learned easily is partly a question about representations, not wholly one.

options.text: How easily two things are paired depends entirely on how each was represented beforehand, so representation alone settles everything an animal can learn.
options.why: That hardens the claim. How easily two things are paired depends in part on how each was represented, and only in part.

options.text: Representations are formed by the pairings themselves, so how a thing is represented depends on what it has been paired with, and never the reverse.
options.why: The direction runs the other way. A new connection can only link things already represented, so representation comes before the pairing.

options.text: Pairings are learned equally easily whatever is represented, since a new connection can link any two inputs that occur together often enough.
options.why: A new connection can only link things the nervous system already represents. So what is represented matters to which pairings are learned easily.

items.stem: Suppose that nothing in a fish’s nervous system responds to some chemical in its stream, at any stage. A researcher repeatedly pairs that chemical with a threat. What should we expect?

options.text: The fish cannot come to link that chemical with the threat, since a new connection can only link things its nervous system already represents.
options.why: Correct. Learning a pairing means linking two things, and the chemical is not among the things the fish’s nervous system represents.

options.text: The fish learns the pairing as easily as any other, since a pairing depends only on how often the chemical and the threat occur together.
options.why: How often two things occur together matters, but only for things that are represented. A new connection cannot link something the nervous system does not represent at all.

options.text: The fish learns the pairing more easily than usual, since a chemical with no representation carries no old learning to overwrite.
options.why: Old learning is a separate concern. Here the obstacle is that there is nothing for a new connection to link the threat to.

options.text: The fish learns the pairing and, in doing so, comes to have a receptor for the chemical, since pairing creates whatever the nervous system needs.
options.why: Pairing links things already represented; it does not create receptors or representations. A new connection can only link what is already there.

items.stem: What is discrimination?

options.text: Treating differently the inputs that call for different responses, even when those inputs overlap.
options.why: Correct. The small fish has to flee from the eel and ignore the sucker, although most of what reaches its nostrils is the same in both cases.

options.text: Treating alike the inputs that call for the same response, even when those inputs barely overlap.
options.why: That is generalization, the other demand. Discrimination concerns inputs that call for different responses.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage of processing can tell them apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, a way a circuit can carry out discrimination. Discrimination is the demand itself, stated in terms of inputs and responses.

options.text: How far apart the evidence for “present” and the evidence for “absent” lie, whatever the criterion.
options.why: That is sensitivity, a quantity from signal detection theory. Discrimination is the demand that inputs calling for different responses be told apart.

items.stem: What is the term for treating differently the inputs that call for different responses, even when those inputs overlap?

options.text: Discrimination.
options.why: Correct. Discrimination is the demand that lets the fish flee from the eel and ignore the sucker, whose smells overlap.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is the opposite demand: treating alike the inputs that call for the same response, even when they barely overlap.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike so that a later stage can tell them apart. It is a way of carrying out discrimination, not the demand itself.

options.text: Sensitivity.
options.why: Sensitivity is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie, a quantity in signal detection theory. It is not the name of the demand.

items.stem: A harmless fish, the sucker, shares the stream with the eel, and its smell shares much of its chemistry with the eel’s. What does that mean for the small fish?

options.text: It has to flee from the eel and ignore the sucker, although most of what reaches its nostrils is the same in both cases.
options.why: Correct. That is the demand of discrimination: inputs calling for different responses have to be told apart, even when they overlap.

options.text: It has to flee from both of them alike, since smells that share most of their chemistry call for one and the same response.
options.why: Sharing chemistry does not make two smells call for the same response. The sucker is harmless, so the fish has to tell its smell apart from the eel’s.

options.text: It can tell the two apart with ease, since one receptor responds to the share of the eel’s chemistry that the sucker lacks.
options.why: No receptor responds to eels and only to eels. The overlap is exactly what makes telling the two apart hard.

options.text: It cannot tell the two apart at all, since two smells that share chemistry produce exactly the same activity in its nostrils.
options.why: Most of what reaches the nostrils is the same, not all of it. The fish has to tell the two apart despite the overlap.

items.stem: What is generalization?

options.text: Treating alike the inputs that call for the same response, even when those inputs barely overlap.
options.why: Correct. A large eel upstream and a small eel downstream give off quite different mixtures, but both call for the same response, flight.

options.text: Treating differently the inputs that call for different responses, even when those inputs overlap.
options.why: That is discrimination, the other demand. Generalization concerns inputs that call for the same response.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a partial input produces the full response.
options.why: That is pattern completion, a way a circuit can carry out generalization. Generalization is the demand itself, stated in terms of inputs and responses.

options.text: The fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs more and more from the input trained on.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, a measure of how generalization falls off. Generalization is the demand that inputs calling for the same response be treated alike.

items.stem: What is the term for treating alike the inputs that call for the same response, even when those inputs barely overlap?

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Correct. Generalization is the demand that has the fish flee from every eel, however different their mixtures of chemicals.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is the fall-off in responding as a new input differs more from the trained one. It measures generalization rather than naming the demand.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. It is one way a circuit can carry out generalization, not the demand itself.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance. It is a hard case, not the general demand.

items.stem: A large eel upstream and a small eel downstream give off quite different mixtures of chemicals. Which demand do the two of them place on the small fish?

options.text: Generalization, since both call for the same response, flight, although their mixtures of chemicals are quite different.
options.why: Correct. Inputs that call for the same response have to be treated alike, even if they barely overlap.

options.text: Discrimination, since their mixtures of chemicals are quite different, and inputs that differ have to be told apart.
options.why: Discrimination concerns inputs that call for different responses. Both eels call for flight, so they have to be treated alike, however different they smell.

options.text: Neither demand, since a large eel and a small eel are the same kind of thing, and so give off the same smell anyway.
options.why: The two eels give off quite different mixtures. That is exactly why treating them alike is a demand rather than something that happens by default.

options.text: Discrimination, since the fish has to flee from the larger eel and can safely keep feeding when it smells the smaller one.
options.why: Both eels are dangerous, and both call for the same response, flight. Treating them alike is what the fish needs.

items.stem: A rat that was made sick by one bait later avoids a second bait that tastes a little different. A student says the rat avoids the second bait only because it cannot tell the two baits apart. What is the better account?

options.text: The rat may tell the two apart perfectly well; avoiding the second is a bet that the two share a consequence.
options.why: Correct. Generalizing is not a failure to discriminate. What the rat cannot tell is whether the second bait will make it sick too, and treating the two alike is a bet that it will.

options.text: The student is right, since treating a new thing as an old one always means the animal has failed to tell the two apart.
options.why: That is the tempting reading, and it is the one rejected. An animal may tell two things apart perfectly well and still treat them alike.

options.text: The rat is discriminating, not generalizing, since it responds to the second bait differently than it responds to safe food.
options.why: The rat does tell bait from safe food, but the response in question is treating the second bait like the first. That is generalization.

options.text: The rat avoids the second bait because it has forgotten exactly how the first one tasted, so the two baits now seem the same to it.
options.why: Forgetting would be one more way of failing to tell the two apart, which is the student’s reading in another form. The rat may tell the baits apart perfectly well and still treat them alike, as a bet on a shared consequence.

items.stem: A child who got sick after eating one kind of red berry now refuses a slightly different red berry, though the child can easily see that the two berries differ. In a few sentences, explain why calling this generalization a failure would be a mistake.
items.answer: It is tempting to think of generalization as a failure, in which an animal treats a new thing as an old one because it cannot tell the two apart. But the child can tell the two berries apart perfectly well. What the child cannot tell is whether the second berry will cause sickness too. Refusing the second berry is a bet that the two share a consequence, which is what generalizing is. Treating the two alike is a bet on a shared consequence, not a failure to tell them apart.
rubric: Notes that the child can tell the two berries apart, so this is not a failure to discriminate.
Identifies what the child cannot tell: whether the second berry will also cause sickness.
Describes generalizing as a bet that two things share a consequence.

items.stem: How are discrimination and generalization related, for the small fish recognizing an eel?

options.text: They are two demands made at once on the same smells, and they push on those smells in opposite directions.
options.why: Correct. Both demands bear on the same inputs, and satisfying one pulls against satisfying the other.

options.text: They are two stages in a fixed order, and generalization can begin only once discrimination has been completed.
options.why: The two demands are made at the same time, not in sequence. That is why they pull against each other.

options.text: They are one demand described twice, since telling things apart and treating them alike are a single skill.
options.why: They are two demands, and they pull in opposite directions. Telling apart and treating alike are different things to ask of the same inputs.

options.text: They apply to different smells, discrimination to suckers and generalization to eels, so they never come into conflict.
options.why: Both apply to the eel’s smell. Telling the eel from the sucker and drawing every eel together act on the same smells, which is why they conflict.

items.stem: Suppose the eel’s smell and the sucker’s differ most on two kinds of receptor, and the fish learns to attend more closely to those two. A large eel and a small eel also differ on those same two kinds of receptor. What may happen?

options.text: The fish tells the eel from the sucker better, but may begin to treat the large eel and the small eel as different things.
options.why: Correct. Sharpening on the receptors where eel and sucker differ also sharpens where one eel differs from another, because the two demands push on the same inputs.

options.text: The fish tells the eel from the sucker better, and treats the large eel and the small eel alike more readily too, since attending closely helps both demands.
options.why: Attending more closely to those receptors helps discrimination, but it works against generalization, since the two eels differ there as well.

options.text: The fish treats the two eels alike more readily, but begins to confuse the eel with the sucker, since attending closely widens what counts as an eel.
options.why: Attending more closely is a sharpening, not a widening. Widening what counts as an eel is the change that would draw in the sucker.

options.text: Nothing changes for the two eels, since attending to some receptors affects how the fish responds to the sucker and never how it responds to eels.
options.why: The two eels differ on those same receptors, so sharpening there affects how the fish treats them as well.

items.stem: Someone proposes that the small fish could meet both demands by becoming more discriminating across the board, and then making up for it by becoming more general across the board. Why will that not work?

options.text: The fish needs the eel pulled apart from the sucker and every eel drawn together, for the same smells, so some differences must count for more and others for less.
options.why: Correct. Change across the board moves every difference the same way. What the fish needs is selective: the differences that separate eel from sucker must count for more, and those that separate one eel from another for less.

options.text: The proposal would work, since sharpening and widening cancel each other out once both are applied across the board, which leaves the fish exactly where it ought to be.
options.why: Change across the board treats every difference alike, so neither change can make the differences between eel and sucker count for more while the differences among eels count for less. That selective change is what the fish needs.

options.text: More generalization alone is what the fish needs, since every eel is dangerous and treating every eel alike is the whole of the problem.
options.why: Generalizing alone would lump the eel with the sucker, so the fish would flee from both or from neither. It needs both demands met.

options.text: More discrimination alone is what the fish needs, since a fish that tells every smell apart will never confuse an eel with a sucker again.
options.why: Discriminating alone would treat every eel as a new thing, so nothing learned about one eel would carry over to the next.

items.stem: What does the small fish’s world call for, and how are discrimination and generalization related to it?

options.text: A single mapping from patterns of receptor activity to responses, with discrimination and generalization as two demands on that one mapping.
options.why: Correct. This pattern means flee, that one means keep feeding. Discrimination and generalization are two demands on that single mapping.

options.text: Two separate mappings run side by side, one that discriminates and one that generalizes, with their two answers combined at the end.
options.why: There is one mapping from inputs to responses, and both demands bear on it. That is why they pull against each other.

options.text: A list of which receptor means which animal, with discrimination and generalization as two different ways of reading that list.
options.why: No receptor means “eel” on its own, so there is no such list. The input is a pattern across receptors, mapped to a response.

options.text: A single threshold on the most active receptor, with discrimination and generalization as two different settings of that threshold.
options.why: The input is a pattern across many receptors, not the activity of one. Both demands bear on the mapping from that pattern to a response.

items.stem: Guard bees at a hive entrance have to let in bees from their own hive and keep out bees from other hives. Nestmates’ smells vary a good deal from bee to bee, and a robber from a nearby hive can smell much like a nestmate. In a short paragraph, explain why the guards cannot satisfy both demands by becoming more discriminating, or more general, across the board, and say what they need instead.
items.answer: The guards face two demands at once on the same smells. Discrimination requires them to tell robbers from nestmates, although the smells overlap. Generalization requires them to treat every nestmate alike, although nestmates’ smells vary. Sharpening across the board, by attending more closely to every way the smells differ, would separate robbers from nestmates but would also split nestmates from one another, so some nestmates would be kept out. Widening across the board, so that every nestmate is let in, would also widen toward the robbers. Because the two demands push on the same inputs in opposite directions, the guards need some differences to come to count for more, those that separate robbers from nestmates, and others to count for less, those that vary among nestmates.
rubric: Names both demands as they apply here: telling robbers from nestmates, and treating all nestmates alike.
Explains that sharpening across the board would also split nestmates from one another.
Explains that widening across the board would also let robbers in.
Concludes that some differences have to come to count for more and others for less.

pools.title: How Alike, and Deciding Under Noise
pools.covers: reading §7.1.3, §7.1.4 · lecture 7.1 slides how_alike, four_outcomes, sensitivity_and_criterion, where_the_line_should_go

items.stem: What is a generalization gradient?

options.text: The fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs more and more from the input an animal was trained on.
options.why: Correct. Train a response to one input, then test on others, and the response weakens smoothly, often steeply, as the test input differs more from the trained one.

options.text: The rise in responding to one trained input as an animal is given more and more training trials with that same input.
options.why: That describes responding growing over training on a single input. A generalization gradient is measured across different test inputs, after the training is done.

options.text: The graded goodness of membership that makes some members of a category better examples of it than others are.
options.why: That is typicality, a graded property of category members that people rate. A generalization gradient is the fall-off in an animal’s responding to new inputs.

options.text: The fall-off in how often a decision is correct as the evidence for a target and against it come to overlap more.
options.why: Overlapping evidence is what signal detection theory deals with. A generalization gradient is about responding to inputs that differ from a trained one.

items.stem: An animal is trained to respond to one input. Its tendency to respond then falls off as a new input differs more and more from the trained one. What is that fall-off called?

options.text: Generalization gradient
options.why: Correct. The generalization gradient is the fall-off itself, measured by training on one input and testing on inputs that differ from it by different amounts.

options.text: Generalization
options.why: Generalization is the demand that inputs calling for the same response be treated alike. The gradient is the measured fall-off in that responding as inputs differ more.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization
options.why: That is generalization to inputs unlike anything a learner was trained on. The fall-off in responding as an input differs more is the generalization gradient.

options.text: Typicality
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category an item is, as people rate it. The fall-off in an animal’s responding to new inputs is the generalization gradient.

items.stem: A pigeon trained to peck at a yellow light pecks very often at yellow, a good deal less at yellow-green, and hardly at all at green. Which description fits this result?

options.text: A generalization gradient, in which responding falls off smoothly as the color differs more from the trained one.
options.why: Correct. The pecking falls off as the color differs more from the trained yellow, which is exactly what a generalization gradient describes.

options.text: A failure to discriminate, in which the pigeon pecks at yellow-green because it cannot tell yellow-green from yellow.
options.why: It is tempting to read generalization as failure, but responding to a new input as to a trained one can be a bet that the two share a consequence. Nothing here shows the pigeon cannot tell the colors apart.

options.text: A criterion, in which the pigeon has drawn a line between the colors it pecks at and the colors it ignores entirely.
options.why: A criterion is where a line is drawn along one axis of evidence for a yes-or-no decision. This result is graded, falling off steadily rather than switching at a line.

options.text: A typicality rating, in which yellow-green counts as a poorer example of the trained color than yellow itself does.
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category an item is, measured in people’s ratings. The pigeon’s result is a measure of responding to inputs that differ from a trained one.

items.stem: Researchers measured generalization gradients long before anyone spoke of representations. Why was that possible?

options.text: A gradient describes behavior, how strongly the trained response is given as the test input differs, and needs no claim about what is inside.
options.why: Correct. A generalization gradient plots how strongly the trained response is given against how the test input differs, so it can be measured without saying anything about what goes on inside the animal.

options.text: A gradient is a record of which neurons fire to each test input, and recording single neurons was possible long before representations were discussed.
options.why: A generalization gradient is not a record of neurons. It is measured from what the animal does, which is why it needs no claim about what goes on inside.

options.text: A gradient is a measure of the physical differences between test inputs, which instruments could record well before any theory of the mind existed.
options.why: The physical differences are not the gradient, and closeness in physical units turns out to predict generalization poorly. A gradient is measured from the animal’s responses.

options.text: A gradient is a count of the inputs an animal fails to tell apart, and counting such failures needs no theory of how inputs are told apart.
options.why: A gradient is not a count of failures. Generalizing can be a bet that two things share a consequence, made by an animal that tells them apart perfectly well.

items.stem: An engineer proposes to predict how an animal will generalize from a trained input by measuring, in physical units, how much each test input differs from it. What is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Closeness in physical units predicts generalization poorly, since the same physical difference can matter a great deal on one dimension and hardly at all on another.
options.why: Correct. The physical measure of a difference and the difference that governs generalization come apart, and they come apart differently on different dimensions.

options.text: Physical units cannot be measured precisely enough, so the small differences between nearby test inputs would be lost in the error of the instruments.
options.why: Precision is not the problem. Even measured perfectly, physical closeness is a poor predictor of how animals generalize.

options.text: Physical difference is the right measure, but it has to be taken inside the animal, as differences in receptor activity, rather than from the inputs themselves.
options.why: The point is not where a physical difference is measured. Which differences govern generalization has to be measured by watching what the animal does.

options.text: Physical difference works for sounds and lights but not for smells and tastes, since chemical inputs have no physical units in which they could be measured at all.
options.why: Chemicals can be measured physically too. The trouble is the same on every dimension: physical closeness does not predict well how animals generalize.

items.stem: A student wants to know which stream smells the small fish treats as more or less like an eel. She plans to analyze each smell chemically and rank the smells by how much their chemistry differs from an eel’s. Why would that ranking fall short?

options.text: The differences that make a smell more or less like an eel to the fish are not simply the physical ones, so they have to be measured by watching what the fish does.
options.why: Correct. Which differences govern generalization is not given by physical measurement. For the small fish it has to be measured from the fish’s own behavior.

options.text: The fish’s receptors respond to chemicals the analysis cannot detect, so a finer chemical analysis of each smell would give the ranking the student wants.
options.why: A finer analysis would still be a physical measure. The differences that govern generalization are not simply the physical ones, however finely those are measured.

options.text: The fish generalizes only to smells it cannot tell apart from an eel’s, so the ranking should instead list the smells by how often the fish confuses each of them with an eel’s.
options.why: Generalizing is not the same as failing to tell inputs apart. It can be a bet that two things share a consequence, made by an animal that tells them apart perfectly well.

options.text: The fish’s responses change from one sniff to the next because of noise, so no single ranking of the smells could describe how the fish treats them at all.
options.why: Noise makes each decision variable, but responding can still be measured across many trials. The trouble with the plan is that it measures chemistry rather than the fish.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how a researcher would measure a generalization gradient in an animal, why the measurement needs no claim about what goes on inside the animal, and why the physical differences between the test inputs cannot simply be assumed to be the ones that matter.
items.answer: The researcher trains the animal to give a response to one input, then tests it on inputs that differ from the trained one by different amounts, and records how strongly it gives the trained response to each. Responding falls off smoothly, and often steeply, as the input differs more, and that fall-off is the generalization gradient. It is a description of behavior, response strength against how the test input differs, so it needs no claim about representations, which is why it was measured long before anyone spoke of them. But closeness in physical units predicts generalization poorly. The same physical difference can matter a great deal on one dimension and hardly at all on another, and the pattern differs between species. So which differences count has to be measured by watching what the animal does.
rubric: Describes training a response to one input and testing on inputs that differ from it by different amounts.
Says responding falls off as the test input differs more from the trained one.
States that the gradient is a description of behavior and needs no claim about what goes on inside the animal.
States that physical closeness is a poor predictor, or that the same physical difference can matter on one dimension and not on another.
Concludes that which differences matter has to be measured from the animal’s behavior.

items.stem: What is signal detection theory?

options.text: A framework for decisions about whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence tells the two cases apart from where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn.
options.why: Correct. It was developed for faint signals on radar, and it is now used wherever a decision is about whether something is there.

options.text: A framework for decisions about which of several categories an input belongs to, which assigns the input to whichever category has stored examples it resembles most.
options.why: Sorting an input among categories by comparing it with stored examples is the job of a categorization model, such as an exemplar model. Signal detection theory is about deciding whether one thing is present.

options.text: A framework for measuring how an animal generalizes from one trained input, which records how its responding falls off as the test inputs differ from it more and more.
options.why: That describes measuring a generalization gradient. Signal detection theory separates how well evidence distinguishes present from absent from where the line is drawn.

options.text: A framework for building a separate detector for each thing in the world, which links one receptor to one response so that the receptor’s firing is itself the detection.
options.why: That describes a labeled line, the way the worm recognizes copper. Signal detection theory is a framework for deciding under noisy, overlapping evidence.

items.stem: What is the name of the framework for decisions about whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence distinguishes “present” from “absent” from where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn?

options.text: Signal detection theory
options.why: Correct. Signal detection theory pulls apart the two quantities, sensitivity and criterion, that percent correct mixes together.

options.text: Decision-bound model
options.why: A decision-bound model divides a space of inputs into regions, one for each response. It grew out of signal detection theory, but the framework named here is signal detection theory itself.

options.text: Pattern recognition
options.why: Pattern recognition is identifying something from a combination of activity across many inputs. The framework for yes-or-no decisions under noise is signal detection theory.

options.text: k-nearest-neighbor classification
options.why: That method assigns a new input to whichever category is most common among the stored examples most similar to it. The framework for deciding whether something is present is signal detection theory.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a hit?

options.text: Judging a target present when it is present.
options.why: Correct. A hit is one of the two correct outcomes: the target is there, and it is judged to be there.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: That is a false alarm, one of the two errors: something is judged to be there that is not.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: That is a miss, the other error: a target that is there goes undetected.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is absent.
options.why: That is a correct rejection, the other correct outcome: nothing is there, and nothing is judged to be there.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a miss?

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: Correct. A miss is the error in which a target that is there goes undetected.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: That is a false alarm, the other kind of error. A miss is failing to detect a target that is really there.

options.text: Failing to respond at all, because the evidence was too weak to register.
options.why: In signal detection theory every decision has an outcome, and “no” is a response. A miss is a “no” given when the target is present.

options.text: Setting the criterion in the wrong place, so that percent correct falls.
options.why: The criterion is where the line is drawn, not an outcome. A miss is one outcome of a single decision: a target present and judged absent.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a false alarm?

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: Correct. A false alarm is the error in which something is judged to be there that is not.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: That is a miss, the other kind of error. A false alarm is a “yes” given when no target is there.

options.text: Responding to a real target, but too late to be of use.
options.why: Timing plays no part in the four outcomes. A false alarm is defined by a “yes” when there is no target at all.

options.text: Any decision made with a criterion set lower than the best one.
options.why: A low criterion produces more false alarms, but the criterion is not an outcome. A false alarm is a single decision: target absent, judged present.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a correct rejection?

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is absent.
options.why: Correct. A correct rejection is the correct outcome in which nothing is there and nothing is judged to be there.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is present.
options.why: That is a hit, the other correct outcome. A correct rejection is a correct “no”.

options.text: Rejecting an input as the wrong kind of target.
options.why: The four outcomes concern whether a target is there, not which kind of target it is. A correct rejection is a “no” when nothing is there.

options.text: Changing a “yes” to “no” after a second look.
options.why: A correct rejection is not a revised decision. It is a single “no” given when no target is present.

items.stem: A spam filter lets a junk message through to the inbox. In signal detection terms, which outcome is that?

options.text: A miss
options.why: Correct. The target here is a junk message. It was present and was treated as absent, so the outcome is a miss.

options.text: A false alarm
options.why: A false alarm would be a real message sent to the junk folder, a target treated as present when it is absent.

options.text: A correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection would be a real message left in the inbox, no target present and none treated as there.

options.text: A hit
options.why: A hit would be a junk message caught and filtered out, a target present and treated as present.

items.stem: A witness is shown a single person and asked whether this is the man she saw at the scene. The person is innocent, but she says “that’s him”. In signal detection terms, which outcome is that?

options.text: A false alarm
options.why: Correct. The target, the man she saw, is not present, and she judges him present. That is a false alarm.

options.text: A hit
options.why: A hit would be naming the man she actually saw when he is shown to her. Here the person shown is someone else.

options.text: A miss
options.why: A miss would be failing to recognize the man she saw when he is shown to her, a target present and judged absent.

options.text: A correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection would be saying “that’s not him” about an innocent person. She said “yes” instead.

items.stem: Each time the small fish catches a whiff of something, it either flees or stays. Which pair of behaviors are the fish’s two kinds of error?

options.text: Staying put while an eel is near, and bolting when no eel is near.
options.why: Correct. Staying put beside an eel is a miss, and bolting from nothing is a false alarm.

options.text: Bolting from an eel that is near, and staying put when no eel is near.
options.why: Those are the two correct outcomes. Fleeing from an eel is a hit, and feeding calmly with no eel near is a correct rejection.

options.text: Staying put while an eel is near, and bolting from an eel that is near.
options.why: Staying beside an eel is a miss, an error, but fleeing from an eel is a hit, a correct outcome.

options.text: Bolting when no eel is near, and feeding calmly when no eel is near.
options.why: Bolting from nothing is a false alarm, an error, but feeding calmly when no eel is near is a correct rejection.

items.stem: Signal detection theory separates two quantities that are sometimes confused. What is the difference between sensitivity and the criterion?

options.text: Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie; the criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn.
options.why: Correct. Sensitivity, usually measured as d′, is the separation of the distributions. The criterion is a separate choice of where to draw the line across them.

options.text: Sensitivity is how little evidence is needed before saying “yes”; the criterion is how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie.
options.why: That swaps the two. How little evidence is needed for a “yes” is set by the criterion; how far apart the distributions lie is sensitivity.

options.text: Sensitivity is the proportion of targets that are detected; the criterion is the proportion of all decisions that turn out correct.
options.why: Both of those proportions shift when the line moves, so neither is sensitivity. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together.

options.text: Sensitivity is set by the difference between what a miss and a false alarm cost; the criterion is set by how noisy the receptors and neurons are.
options.why: That reverses where each comes from. Costs bear on where the criterion should go; noise in the evidence bears on how far apart the distributions lie.

items.stem: Two trainee radiologists read the same set of scans. Trainee A is right more often overall than Trainee B, but B calls “tumor” far more often than A. A supervisor concludes that A is better at telling tumors from healthy tissue. What should signal detection theory make the supervisor check first?

options.text: Whether the gap in percent correct comes from a difference in criterion, by comparing the two trainees’ sensitivity directly.
options.why: Correct. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together. B’s frequent “tumor” calls suggest a lower criterion, which can lower percent correct with no difference in sensitivity.

options.text: Whether B’s extra calls of “tumor” were mostly hits, since a higher hit rate on its own shows which trainee is the better reader.
options.why: A lower criterion raises the hit rate by itself, without any better reading. Hits alone cannot show sensitivity.

options.text: Whether A’s percent correct is high enough to pass, since percent correct already captures how well each trainee reads scans.
options.why: Percent correct is exactly the measure that mixes sensitivity with criterion, so it cannot settle which trainee reads scans better.

options.text: Whether A makes fewer false alarms, since the reader with fewer false alarms always has the better sensitivity of the two.
options.why: Fewer false alarms can come from a higher criterion alone. False alarms on their own no more measure sensitivity than hits do.

items.stem: On a face memory test, one person is right 84% of the time and another only 74%, yet both have a d′ of about 2.0. In a few sentences, explain how both can be true, and what this shows about percent correct as a measure.
items.answer: Sensitivity, measured as d′, is how far apart the evidence for studied faces and the evidence for new faces lie. The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn. The two people tell studied faces from new ones about equally well, so their sensitivity is the same. The second simply says “yes” more often. That gains a few hits, 49 instead of 42, but adds many more false alarms, 25 instead of 8, so percent correct falls. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together, and signal detection theory pulls them apart.
rubric: Treats d′ as sensitivity, how well the evidence separates studied from new faces, and says it is the same for both people.
Identifies the difference as one of criterion: the second person says “yes” more often.
Notes that saying “yes” more often here adds more false alarms than hits, which lowers percent correct.
Concludes that percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together.

items.stem: A clinic replaces its blood test with a new one. The new test comes back positive for more of the patients who have the disease, and also for more of the patients who do not. The maker advertises it as “more sensitive”. In signal detection terms, what does this pattern by itself show?

options.text: It fits a lower criterion, with more hits bought at the price of more false alarms, and on its own does not show any gain in sensitivity.
options.why: Correct. More hits together with more false alarms is exactly what moving the criterion does, and moving the criterion leaves sensitivity where it was.

options.text: It shows a gain in sensitivity, since detecting more of the patients who have the disease is what sensitivity means.
options.why: Detecting more patients who have the disease is a rise in hits, which a lower criterion produces on its own. Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions lie.

options.text: It shows a loss of sensitivity, since a test that flags more of the healthy patients must be telling the two groups apart less well.
options.why: More false alarms come with a lower criterion even when sensitivity is unchanged. The pattern alone does not show the distributions moving closer.

options.text: It shows a higher criterion, since the new test needs more evidence than the old one before it comes back positive.
options.why: A test that comes back positive more often, for patients with and without the disease, needs less evidence, not more. That is a lower criterion.

items.stem: A town must decide how much evidence of a tornado its warning siren should need before it sounds. According to signal detection theory, which two things should set that criterion?

options.text: What each outcome gains or loses, and how common tornadoes are.
options.why: Correct. Which criterion is best depends on what each outcome gains or loses, and on how common targets are.

options.text: How often the siren was right about tornadoes before, and how often it has sounded.
options.why: A past record of being right mixes sensitivity and criterion. The best criterion depends on the costs of each outcome and on how common targets are.

options.text: How loud the sirens are, and how many people live near each one.
options.why: Loudness and reach affect who hears a warning, not where the line between sounding and staying silent should be drawn.

options.text: Whatever setting makes the siren right most often, whatever errors cost.
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts. A missed tornado and a needless alarm do not cost the same.

items.stem: Suppose the small fish’s decisions about eels change. How does a change in its criterion differ from a change in its sensitivity in what each requires?

options.text: The criterion can move with no change in how the fish represents its input; sensitivity can improve only through a better representation.
options.why: Correct. The two quantities are different kinds of thing to change. Only sensitivity depends on how the input is represented.

options.text: The criterion can move only through a better representation of the input; sensitivity can change with no change in how the fish represents its input.
options.why: That swaps the two. Where the line is drawn can change with the representation untouched; how far apart the distributions lie cannot.

options.text: Both require a better representation of the input, since neither one can change unless the fish’s smell receptors are first replaced.
options.why: The criterion can move with no change in representation at all. Only sensitivity depends on a better representation of the input.

options.text: Neither requires any change in representation, since both are set entirely by the costs of misses and of false alarms.
options.why: Costs bear on where the best criterion lies, but they cannot move the distributions apart. Sensitivity improves only through a better representation.

items.stem: A baggage screener’s performance changes twice. First she is told that missing a weapon will cost her the job. Later, after months of practice, she can tell knives from hairbrushes on the screen in shapes that used to blur together. Which change is which?

options.text: The warning can move her criterion without altering her representation; the practice can raise her sensitivity through a better representation.
options.why: Correct. A new cost for misses moves where the line is drawn. Learning to pull apart shapes that used to blur together is a better representation, which is the only route to better sensitivity.

options.text: The warning raises her sensitivity by making her look harder at every bag; the practice moves her criterion by making her more willing to call a weapon.
options.why: That swaps the two. The warning changes what a miss costs, which bears on the criterion. The practice changes how well she tells the shapes apart.

options.text: Both changes raise her sensitivity, since each one leaves her catching more of the weapons that pass through the scanner.
options.why: Catching more weapons can come from a lower criterion alone. Only the practice changes how well she tells weapons from harmless objects.

options.text: Both changes move only her criterion, since sensitivity is fixed by the scanner and cannot be changed by practice.
options.why: Sensitivity can improve through a better representation of the input, and practice that pulls apart shapes that used to blur together provides one.

items.stem: Two detectors have the same distance between the centers of their two distributions of evidence, but in the second detector each distribution is much more spread out. How do their sensitivities compare?

options.text: The second detector has lower sensitivity, since d′ measures the distance between the centers in units of their spread.
options.why: Correct. d′ is the distance between the centers in units of the spread, so the same distance counts for less when the distributions are wider and overlap more.

options.text: The two detectors have equal sensitivity, since d′ is the distance between the centers, which has not changed, whatever the spread.
options.why: The distance alone is not d′. It is measured in units of the spread, so wider, more spread-out distributions give a smaller d′.

options.text: The second detector has higher sensitivity, since wider distributions cover more of the evidence and so catch more targets.
options.why: Wider distributions overlap more, which makes the two cases harder to tell apart. That is lower sensitivity, not higher.

options.text: Their sensitivities cannot be compared until a criterion is set, since sensitivity depends on where the line is drawn.
options.why: Sensitivity is how far apart the distributions lie, whatever the criterion. It can be compared without drawing any line.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is sensitivity?

options.text: How far apart the evidence for “present” and the evidence for “absent” lie, whatever the criterion happens to be.
options.why: Correct. Sensitivity, usually measured as d′, is the separation between the two distributions of evidence, and moving the criterion leaves it unchanged.

options.text: How little evidence is needed before a decision changes from “no” to “yes”, so that targets are seldom missed.
options.why: That describes a low criterion, which is what the everyday word “sensitive” often means. Sensitivity is the separation between the two distributions.

options.text: How often decisions turn out correct overall, counting the hits and correct rejections together against all decisions.
options.why: That is percent correct, which mixes sensitivity and criterion together. Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions lie.

options.text: How strongly a receptor responds to a weak input, so that faint targets produce a large signal at the very first stage.
options.why: A strong receptor response is not what signal detection theory means. Sensitivity is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the criterion?

options.text: The amount of evidence at which a decision changes from “no” to “yes”, so that moving it trades misses for false alarms.
options.why: Correct. The criterion is where the line is drawn, and moving it leaves sensitivity unchanged.

options.text: The separation between the evidence for “present” and for “absent”, so that raising it reduces misses and false alarms alike.
options.why: That describes sensitivity. Moving the criterion cannot reduce both kinds of error at once; it trades one for the other.

options.text: The proportion of decisions that turn out correct, so that raising it means fewer errors of either kind on the same task.
options.why: That describes percent correct, which mixes sensitivity and criterion together. The criterion is where the line is drawn.

options.text: The smallest difference between two inputs that an animal can tell apart, so that a lower one means finer discrimination.
options.why: A smallest detectable difference is a measure of discrimination. The criterion is the amount of evidence at which “no” turns to “yes”.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the name for the amount of evidence at which a decision changes from “no” to “yes”?

options.text: Criterion
options.why: Correct. The criterion is where the line is drawn along the evidence. Moving it trades misses for false alarms and leaves sensitivity unchanged.

options.text: Sensitivity
options.why: Sensitivity is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie. The point where “no” turns to “yes” is the criterion.

options.text: Decision boundary
options.why: A decision boundary is a line through a space of possible inputs, the kind a single unit draws. The criterion is a point along one axis of evidence.

options.text: Hit
options.why: A hit is one outcome of a single decision, a target present and judged present. The point where “no” turns to “yes” is the criterion.

items.stem: A trainer wants a sniffer dog to find more of the hidden explosives it is searching for. In a short paragraph, contrast two ways the dog’s performance could change, one through its criterion and one through its sensitivity. Say what each would require, and what moving the criterion would do to the dog’s false alarms.
items.answer: The dog’s criterion could be lowered, so that it signals on weaker evidence than before. That gives more hits and fewer misses, but also more false alarms, and it leaves sensitivity exactly where it was, because the distributions of evidence with and without explosives have not moved. Moving the criterion requires no change in how the dog represents what reaches its nose. Alternatively, the dog’s sensitivity could improve, so that the evidence from explosives and the evidence from everything else lie further apart. That can happen only through a better representation of the input, for example through training that pulls apart smells that used to blur together.
rubric: Describes lowering the criterion as signaling on weaker evidence, with more hits and fewer misses.
States that lowering the criterion also brings more false alarms.
States that moving the criterion leaves sensitivity unchanged and needs no change in representation.
States that sensitivity can improve only through a better representation of the input.

items.stem: What is a category?

options.text: A set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose, even when its members differ from one another.
options.why: Correct. The definition turns on use. Things form a category because they are treated as the same kind for some purpose, which is why a goal can hold a category together even when its members have almost nothing in common.

options.text: A set of things that all share a list of defining features, each one necessary and all of them together sufficient.
options.why: That is the classical view of what holds a category together, and it fits few everyday categories. A category is simply a set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose.

options.text: A pattern of activity that stands for something in the world, so that what an animal does next depends on it.
options.why: That is a representation. A category is the set of things in the world treated as the same kind, not the activity that stands for one of them.

options.text: A summary of a group of things, such as its average member, against which a new thing can be compared.
options.why: That is a prototype, a summary of a category rather than the category itself. A category is the set of things treated as the same kind.

items.stem: What is the term for a set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose?

options.text: Category.
options.why: Correct. A category is defined by use: its members are treated as the same kind for some purpose, though some are better examples than others.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is the demand that inputs calling for the same response be treated alike. It names a demand on responding, not the set of things that end up treated alike.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. It stands in for a category, and is not the set of things itself.

options.text: Typicality.
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category a member is. It describes the members of a set, not the set.

items.stem: Deciding whether an eel is present is a question about one target. According to the lecture, what does most recognition involve instead?

options.text: Sorting things into categories, sets treated as the same kind for some purpose, whose members are not all equally good examples.
options.why: Correct. The lecture turns from a fish detecting one target to the more common case. Most recognition is sorting into categories, and categories have structure of their own.
