options.text: Detecting one target after another, with the criterion moved for each new target according to what its outcomes gain or lose.
options.why: Moving a criterion is part of detecting a single target. The lecture’s point is that most recognition is sorting things into categories, which have structure of their own.

options.text: Responding through labeled lines, each one firing for a single kind of thing in the world and staying silent for everything else.
options.why: Labeled lines suit cases like the worm and copper, where one receptor is enough. Most of what matters arrives as patterns, and most recognition is sorting into categories.

options.text: Learning one new pairing at a time, between a single cue and the particular outcome that has followed that cue in the past.
options.why: Pairing single cues with outcomes is one kind of learning, and some categories defeat it. Most recognition, the lecture says, is sorting things into categories.

items.stem: What is typicality?

options.text: How good an example of a category a member is, as when a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is graded goodness of membership. A penguin is a bird, but a poorer example of one than a robin.

options.text: How many members a category has, as when there are many more kinds of bird in the world than kinds of penguin.
options.why: The size of a category is not its typicality. Typicality grades the members themselves: a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin, although both are birds.

options.text: How strongly a trained response is given to a new input, as the new input differs more and more from the trained one.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, a measure of behavior after training. Typicality is how good an example of its category a member is.

options.text: How far apart the evidence for a target and the evidence for no target lie, as when a fish with keen receptors tells eel from no eel well.
options.why: That is sensitivity, from signal detection theory. Typicality is about how good an example of a category each member is.

items.stem: Suppose people asked to rate members of the category fish call a trout an excellent example and a seahorse a poor one, while all agreeing that a seahorse is a fish. What does this pattern of ratings show?

options.text: The members of the category are not all equally good examples of it; goodness of membership is graded, which is typicality.
options.why: Correct. Both animals belong, and one is a better example than the other. That graded goodness of membership is typicality.

options.text: The seahorse has been placed outside the category, since a member rated a poor example has in effect been judged a non-member.
options.why: A poor rating does not put a member outside its category. A penguin is a bird, though a poorer example than a robin, and here the raters agree the seahorse is a fish.

options.text: The raters have trouble telling a seahorse from a trout, since a poor rating shows that two members are being confused with one another.
options.why: A seahorse is easy to tell from a trout, and a poor rating says nothing about confusion. It grades how good an example of a fish each one is.

options.text: The category has a definition that a trout meets in full and a seahorse meets only in part, and the ratings measure how much of it each meets.
options.why: A definition is met or not met, and under a definition every member belongs equally. The ratings measure something else: how good an example each member is.

items.stem: When people listed the attributes of twenty members of each of several categories, few or no attributes were listed for all twenty. How did the members of a category overlap instead?

options.text: Like faces in a family: one shares some features with a second, the second others with a third, and nothing runs through all.
options.why: Correct. That pattern is called family resemblance. Features are shared in overlapping pieces, and no single attribute runs through every member.

options.text: Like the terms of a definition: every member has a few core attributes in common with all the others, and they differ only in the rest.
options.why: That is what a definition would need, and it is what the attribute lists failed to find. Few or no attributes were listed for all twenty members.

options.text: Like the rungs of a ladder: each member has every attribute of the member below it, and then adds one more attribute of its own.
options.why: Nested attributes would give every member the attributes of the lowest rung, so some attributes would run through the whole set. Almost none did.

options.text: Like a crowd of strangers: members share no attributes with one another at all, and are grouped only by the name they are given.
options.why: Members did share features, just not the same features throughout. One shares some with a second, and the second shares others with a third.

items.stem: Suppose we counted, for each member of the category fruit, how many features it shares with other fruits and how many it shares with vegetables. Which member would the family-resemblance finding predict to be rated most typical?

options.text: The fruit that shares the most features with other fruits and the fewest with vegetables.
options.why: Correct. The most typical members were the ones sharing the most features with other members of their own category, and the fewest with members of neighboring categories.

options.text: The fruit that shares the most features with other fruits and the most with vegetables as well.
options.why: Sharing features with a neighboring category counts against typicality. The most typical members shared the most with their own category and the fewest with neighboring ones.

options.text: The fruit with a striking feature no other fruit has, which makes it the easiest one of all to remember.
options.why: A feature no other member has adds nothing to what a member shares with its category. Typicality went with sharing many features with members of one’s own category.

options.text: The fruit that shares the fewest features with anything at all, since it stands out most clearly from the rest.
options.why: Standing apart from everything makes a member atypical, not typical. The most typical members shared the most with their own category.

items.stem: A student reads that people rate a robin a far better example of a bird than a penguin, and concludes that people must sort things by comparing them with a summary of each category. What is wrong with the conclusion?

options.text: Several quite different accounts explain graded ratings equally well, so typicality alone cannot settle which is right.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is a fact any account of categories has to explain, but because several accounts explain it equally well, it cannot decide between them.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since only a summary of each category could make some members better examples than others.
options.why: A summary is one way to get graded examples, but not the only one. Several quite different accounts explain typicality equally well.

options.text: The ratings point the other way, since graded examples arise only when people compare things with every example they remember.
options.why: That swaps one unwarranted conclusion for another. Typicality is explained equally well by several accounts, so it favors none of them.

options.text: The ratings tell us little about categories, since they reflect how familiar each kind of animal happened to be to the students.
options.why: The ratings are a robust fact about human categories that any account has to explain. Their limit is that they cannot choose among the accounts.

items.stem: A magazine article reports that people agree on which birds are good examples of a bird, and concludes that the finding reveals how every animal sorts its world and which theory of categories is correct. What two cautions does the lecture attach to evidence of this kind?

options.text: The evidence comes from human beings, and since several quite different accounts explain it, it cannot decide between accounts on its own.
options.why: Correct. The lecture names both. Any account of categories has to explain typicality, but the evidence is human, and it does not favor one account over another.

options.text: The evidence comes from a single small group of students, and since the scale had only seven points, the grades are too coarse to use.
options.why: The ratings came from 209 students, and different groups agreed closely, so the finding is robust. The cautions concern whose categories it describes and what it can decide.

options.text: The evidence comes from birds alone, and since a bat was included by mistake, the ratings for other categories cannot be trusted either.
options.why: The ratings covered ten everyday categories, and the bat’s rating, close to the worst, is part of the finding rather than an error. The cautions are that the evidence is human and that it cannot choose among accounts.

options.text: The evidence comes from human beings, and since the ratings are graded, it shows that no bird belongs to the category fully.
options.why: The first half is right. But graded goodness of membership is not partial membership: a penguin is a bird, only a poorer example of one. The second caution is that several accounts explain typicality equally well, so it cannot decide between them.

items.stem: Typicality is a robust finding about human categories. In a few sentences, explain why every account of categories has to explain typicality, and why typicality still cannot show on its own which account is right.
items.answer: Typicality is graded goodness of membership: people rate a robin a far better example of a bird than a penguin, though both are birds, and different groups of raters agree closely. Because the finding is so robust, any account of how human categories work has to produce it, or that account is wrong about human categories. But several quite different accounts explain typicality equally well. A finding that all of them predict cannot favor one of them over the others, so deciding between the accounts needs evidence on which they disagree.
rubric: Defines typicality as graded goodness of membership, with an example such as the robin and the penguin.
Notes that the finding is robust, for instance that different groups of raters agree closely.
States that any account of categories must therefore explain it.
States that several quite different accounts explain it equally well.
Concludes that typicality alone cannot decide between those accounts.

items.stem: A tent, a box of matches, a first-aid kit, and a can opener have almost nothing in common, yet a person packing for a camping trip treats them as one kind of thing. What holds this category together?

options.text: A goal: all four are things the trip needs, treated as one kind for that purpose rather than for any resemblance.
options.why: Correct. Not every category is held together by resemblance among its members. Some are built around a goal, like things to take out of a burning house, and their members can have almost nothing in common.

options.text: A hidden defining feature, shared by all four, which a careful enough listing of their attributes would eventually reveal.
options.why: Nothing about the four objects has to be shared. The category is built around a goal, and its members are united by the purpose they serve.

options.text: A family resemblance, in which each item shares some features with the next, though no one feature runs through all four.
options.why: Family resemblance holds many categories together, but these four items have almost nothing in common, even in overlapping pieces. They are united by a purpose.

options.text: Nothing holds it together, since a set of things whose members do not resemble one another cannot be a category at all.
options.why: A category is a set of things treated as the same kind for some purpose, and resemblance is not required. Some categories are built around a goal.

items.stem: How does a category built around a goal differ from a category defined by a relation?

options.text: A goal-built category gathers things that serve one purpose; a relation-defined one gathers things by how they stand toward something else.
options.why: Correct. Things to take out of a burning house share a purpose; predators share what they do to other animals. In neither case does resemblance among the members hold the category together.

options.text: A goal-built category is held together by resemblance among its members; a relation-defined category is held together by a definition.
options.why: Neither kind is held together by resemblance, which is why both are examples of categories that resemblance does not explain. A goal unites one kind, a relation the other.

options.text: A goal-built category gathers things with almost nothing in common; a relation-defined one gathers things alike in appearance, as predators are.
options.why: The first half is right. But nothing about an animal’s own appearance makes it a predator, and predators can look nothing alike. A relation-defined category gathers things by how they stand toward something else.

options.text: A goal-built category is used only for sorting things; a relation-defined category is used only for inferring what cannot be seen.
options.why: Sorting and inferring unseen properties are both uses of categories in general, not marks of one kind. What separates the two kinds is what holds the members together: a purpose in one case, a relation in the other.

items.stem: Two berries smell almost exactly alike, but one kind makes an animal sick and the other does not. On the chapter’s view of recognition, what should decide whether the animal treats the two smells as one kind of thing?

options.text: Whether they share a consequence, since what matters is which inputs share a consequence, not only how alike they are.
options.why: Correct. Recognition is not only a matter of how alike inputs are. Two very alike smells with different consequences call for different treatment.

options.text: How alike the two smells are, since the more alike two inputs are, the more readily they must be treated as one kind.
options.why: That is the natural first answer, and resemblance does matter. But recognition is not only a matter of how alike inputs are; it turns on which inputs share a consequence.

options.text: Whether the two contain one defining chemical, since membership in a category is fixed by what all of its members contain.
options.why: That would make every category a definition, and many are not, such as categories built around a goal. Recognition turns on which inputs share a consequence.

options.text: Whether the two are equally typical, since only inputs that are equally good examples can belong to the same category.
options.why: Members of one category differ in typicality, as a robin and a penguin do. Typicality does not decide membership.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how categories built around a goal and categories defined by a relation show that recognition turns on more than how alike inputs are. Use one example of each other than those the chapter uses.
items.answer: Some categories are held together by a goal. Presents suitable for a young child’s birthday, such as a ball, a picture book, and a kite, have little in common, yet they are treated as one kind because they serve one purpose. Other categories are defined by a relation. Nothing about an animal’s own appearance makes it prey; what makes it prey is what other animals do to it. In both cases the members need not resemble one another at all. What unites them is a shared purpose or role, so recognizing a member is a matter of which inputs share a consequence, not only of how alike they are.
rubric: Gives a goal-built category not in the chapter, whose members have little in common.
Gives a relation-defined category not in the chapter, defined by how its members stand toward something else.
States that the members of such categories need not resemble one another.
Concludes that recognition turns on which inputs share a consequence, not only on how alike they are.

items.stem: What is the rule called in which one input is true, or the other, but not both?

options.text: Exclusive or.
options.why: Correct. It is often written XOR. The fruit-eating animal’s rule has this form: either smell alone means ripe fruit, and both together do not.

options.text: AND.
options.why: AND is true only when both inputs are true, which is exactly the case this rule excludes.

options.text: OR.
options.why: OR is true when one input is true or both are. The rule here is the same except that it is false when both are true.

options.text: NOT.
options.why: NOT reverses a single input. The rule here concerns two inputs, and it is true when exactly one of them is.

items.stem: Suppose a fruit smells right only when one chemical is at just the right strength: too little means unripe, and too much means rotten. Why does the chemical’s strength, on its own, fail to settle the answer?

options.text: More of the chemical is good news up to a point and bad news after it, so a stronger smell can mean better fruit or worse.
options.why: Correct. Below the right strength more of the chemical is welcome, and past it more is unwelcome, so a change in strength points in no consistent direction.

options.text: The chemical varies from sniff to sniff, so its strength is too noisy to separate ripe fruit from rotten fruit reliably.
options.why: Noise is a real problem for any detection, but it is not the problem here. Even measured perfectly, the strength is good news up to a point and bad news after it.

options.text: The chemical is present at the same strength in every fruit, so its strength cannot differ between ripe fruit and rotten.
options.why: The strength does differ, from too little to too much. The trouble is that more is good news up to a point and bad news after it.

options.text: The chemical carries information only together with a second smell, as in exclusive or, so its strength alone cannot matter.
options.why: The chapter says this case has the same character as exclusive or, not that it is exclusive or. One chemical is involved, and its strength alone does not point consistently either way.

items.stem: Suppose a plant-eating animal can safely eat a leaf only when its salt content is moderate: too little and the leaf lacks what the animal needs, too much and the leaf harms it. A student proposes the rule “the saltier, the better”. What is wrong with that rule?

options.text: Salt is good news only up to a point and bad news after it, so a rule that runs in one direction cannot be right.
options.why: Correct. This is a just-right-strength case. Salt carries the information, but its effect reverses past the ideal, so no rule that runs in one direction works throughout.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since salt is the one input here that carries all the information about whether the leaf is safe to eat.
options.why: Salt does carry the information, but not in one direction. More salt helps up to a point and harms after it, so “the saltier, the better” fails past that point.

options.text: The rule should be reversed, since a leaf with less salt in it is always safer for the animal to eat than a leaf with more.
options.why: Reversing the rule fails at the other end, since too little salt leaves the animal short of what it needs. Neither direction is right throughout.

options.text: The rule needs a second cue, since salt can carry information only in exclusive or with some other chemical in the leaf.
options.why: The case is like exclusive or in character, but it involves a single input. The problem is that the effect of salt reverses, not that a second cue is missing.

items.stem: What do the fruit exclusive-or case and the just-right-strength case have in common?

options.text: In each, no single input, taken on its own, points consistently toward one answer.
options.why: Correct. In the fruit case each smell is present as often without food as with it; in the second case more of the chemical is good news up to a point and bad news after it. Either way, no input on its own settles the answer.

options.text: Each is an instance of exclusive or, with too little and too much playing the parts of the two smells.
options.why: The chapter says the second case has the same character as exclusive or, not that it is exclusive or. One involves two smells, the other a single chemical.

options.text: Each involves two smells, one of which means ripe fruit and the other of which means rotten fruit.
options.why: In the fruit case either smell alone means ripe fruit, and the second case has only one chemical. Neither case gives each input a meaning of its own.

options.text: Each can be solved by adding up the evidence one input at a time, given enough experience with the fruit.
options.why: Adding up evidence one input at a time is exactly what fails in both, since no input on its own points toward the answer.

items.stem: In a few sentences, contrast a category in which each input carries information on its own with one in which only combinations of inputs do. Give a hypothetical example of each, other than the eel and the fallen fruit.
items.answer: In the first kind, a little more of one input makes the category a little more likely, whatever else is present. For a hypothetical bird, a little more of a sweet smell might make a berry a little more likely to be ripe, whatever its color. In the second kind, no input says anything on its own, and only the combination does. Suppose a hypothetical animal finds a nut good to eat when it is either heavy or dark, but not both: heavy and dark means rotten inside, and neither means empty. Heaviness is present in as many bad nuts as good ones, and so is darkness, so only the combination tells the animal what to do.
rubric: States that in the first kind, each input on its own makes the category more or less likely, whatever else is present.
States that in the second kind, no input on its own carries information, and only the combination does.
Gives a fresh example of the first kind.
Gives a fresh example of the second kind in which each input alone turns up as often with one outcome as with the other.

items.stem: Suppose an animal could learn only how often each single cue is followed by reward. Faced with a task in which every single cue is rewarded half the time, what should it be able to learn, and what did real animals do on such a task?

options.text: It should learn nothing useful from any one cue, and so fail the task; real animals learned the task anyway.
options.why: Correct. The single-cue account predicted that no animal could learn the task, and animals learned it anyway. Whatever they learned, it was not only about single cues.

options.text: It should learn the task quickly, since a reward on half of all trials is plenty to learn from; real animals were slower.
options.why: A cue rewarded half the time, whatever else is present, says nothing about which choice will pay. The single-cue account predicted failure, and animals succeeded.

options.text: It should learn the task only after very long training; real animals never learned it, however long they were trained.
options.why: The account predicted that no animal could learn the task at all, and the animals did learn it.

options.text: It should learn to choose at random, which is the best anything can do on such a task; real animals did the same.
options.why: Choosing at random is all the single-cue account leaves an animal, but real animals did better. They learned the task.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the evidence that animals and people can learn categories in which only combinations of cues predict the outcome, and say what account of learning that evidence counted against.
items.answer: Animal-learning researchers trained animals on discrimination tasks in which every single cue was rewarded half the time, so that only a combination of cues predicted the outcome. An account in which animals learn only about single cues predicted that no animal could learn such a task, since no single cue predicts the reward. Animals learned it anyway, and later studies found the same in a range of animals, from rats to monkeys. People can learn such categories too. In controlled experiments, categories that could be sorted by adding up evidence one feature at a time were no easier to learn than categories that could not. The animal results counted directly against the account in which learning is only about single cues, which had predicted failure.
rubric: Describes a task in which every single cue is rewarded half the time, so that only a combination of cues predicts the outcome.
States the single-cue account’s prediction that no animal could learn such a task.
Reports that animals learned it anyway, across a range from rats to monkeys.
Gives evidence from people, such as additive categories being no easier to learn than the others.

items.stem: In controlled experiments, how did people learn categories that could be sorted by adding up evidence one feature at a time, compared with categories that could not?

options.text: The additive categories were no easier to learn than the categories that could not be sorted that way.
options.why: Correct. People can learn categories that depend only on combinations, and in these experiments such categories were no harder than additive ones.

options.text: The additive categories were far easier, and people mostly failed to learn the ones that could not be sorted that way.
options.why: That is what an account built on single features would predict, and it is not what was found. Categories that depend on combinations were no harder.

options.text: The additive categories were harder, since people attend to combinations of features before they attend to single ones.
options.why: The finding was only that additive categories were no easier, not that they were harder. Nothing here says people attend to combinations first.

options.text: The additive categories could be learned by people, while the others could be learned only by trained animals.
options.why: People can learn categories that depend only on combinations too. In these experiments such categories were no harder than additive ones.

items.stem: What is invariance?

options.text: Recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.
options.why: Correct. An eel near and far, or a face seen from the front and from the side, produce inputs that barely overlap. Invariance is recognizing the one thing across changes like these.

options.text: A cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size.
options.why: That is tolerance, which single cells in the visual pathway show. Invariance is what the animal has to achieve: recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, one way a network builds in a little tolerance to shifts. Invariance is the demand itself, recognizing a thing across large changes in its input.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a faint or partial input produces the response the whole would.
options.why: That is pattern completion, proposed for circuits whose cells excite one another. Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.

items.stem: How can two smells of the same eel compare with the smell of a harmless sucker?

options.text: The two eel smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s, and still have to be treated as one thing.
options.why: Correct. One eel, close by and far away, gives off smells at very different strengths, and either smell can be more like the sucker’s than like the other.

options.text: The two eel smells always differ from each other less than either differs from the sucker’s, which is what lets them be treated as one thing.
options.why: That is the easy case, and it does not always hold. One eel’s smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s.

options.text: The two eel smells share nothing with the sucker’s, so telling the eel from the sucker is easy and only treating the eel smells alike is hard.
options.why: The sucker’s smell shares much of its chemistry with the eel’s. Both demands are hard here: telling the two fish apart, and treating the eel smells alike.

options.text: The two eel smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s, and so they have to be treated as two different things.
options.why: The smells do differ that much, but they still come from one eel and call for one response, flight. Treating them as two things would be a failure of invariance.

items.stem: Why is invariance described as discrimination and generalization at their hardest?

options.text: The smells that must be treated alike can differ more than those that must be told apart, so both demands bear down on the same inputs.
options.why: Correct. Generalization has to stretch across eel smells that barely overlap, while discrimination has to hold the sucker apart even when its smell is more like one eel smell than the eel smells are like each other.

options.text: The smells that must be told apart are so faint that a very low criterion is needed to pick them up, so a great many false alarms cannot be avoided.
options.why: That mixes in signal detection, where moving the criterion trades one error for the other. Invariance is about which inputs must be treated alike and which apart.

options.text: The smells of one eel change from moment to moment, so the fish has to start over each time and treat every new smell as a new thing.
options.why: Treating every eel smell as a new thing is the failure of a fish that only discriminates. Invariance is the demand that the changing smells be treated as one eel.

options.text: The smells that must be treated alike always overlap a great deal, so generalization is easy here and the discrimination is the hard part.
options.why: That reverses the difficulty. In invariance the inputs to be treated alike barely overlap, so generalization is hard as well.

items.stem: A crow on a fence sees a hawk circling high overhead as a small speck, and a minute later sees the same hawk gliding low, filling much of its view. The two images on its eyes have little in common. If the crow treats both as the same danger, which of these describes what it is achieving?

options.text: Invariance, because one hawk has produced two inputs that barely overlap and both call for the same response.
options.why: Correct. A change in distance changes the image a great deal, and recognizing the hawk across that change is invariance.

options.text: Discrimination, because the two images are so different that the crow has to tell them apart before it can respond.
options.why: Discrimination is telling apart inputs that call for different responses. These two images call for the same response, so treating them alike is what is needed.

options.text: Learning in sequence, because the crow saw the high hawk first and the low hawk later, with time between them.
options.why: The images arrive at different times, but nothing new is being learned here. The crow is recognizing one thing across a large change in its input.

options.text: Pattern completion, because the speck is a partial view of the hawk that the crow fills out into the whole bird.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. The speck is not part of the hawk’s image but a very different image of the whole hawk, and recognizing it is invariance.

items.stem: A familiar tune is played in a new key, a half step higher than usual. Its melody is unchanged, but every note is now a different pitch, and the new version shares few notes with the original. A different tune, played in the original key, shares many notes with the original. What does recognizing the familiar tune in its new key require?

options.text: Treating the two versions of the tune as one thing, though the original shares more notes with the different tune than the two versions share with each other.
options.why: Correct. This is the eel and the sucker in sound. One tune produces inputs that barely overlap, while a different tune shares more with the original than the two versions of the one tune share with each other.

options.text: Treating whichever tune shares the most notes with the original as the same tune, since shared notes are what make two inputs one thing.
options.why: That would pick the wrong tune. Invariance is hard precisely because what comes from one thing can share less than what comes from different things.

options.text: Treating the two versions of the tune as different tunes, since inputs that share almost nothing always call for different responses.
options.why: Inputs that barely overlap can still come from one thing and call for one response. That is the generalization side of invariance.

options.text: Treating all three as the same tune, since all of them are built from notes of the same kind and played on the same instrument.
options.why: That generalizes too far and gives up discrimination. The different tune must still be told apart, even though it shares many notes with the original.

items.stem: For the small fish’s nervous system, what does invariance mean?

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire for every eel smell, faint or strong, and stay quiet for the sucker’s smell.
options.why: Correct. The neuron’s firing has to follow the eel, not the strength or the particular mixture of the smell, and it has to stay quiet even when the sucker’s smell is more like one eel smell than the eel smells are like each other.

options.text: Some receptor in the nostrils has to respond to eels and only to eels, whether the eel’s smell is faint or strong.
options.why: No receptor stands for an eel; an eel is a pattern of activity across many receptors. The demand falls on a neuron downstream of them.

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire more strongly the stronger the smell is, so that faint smells from far away are ignored.
options.why: Firing that follows strength would miss the faint eel far away. Invariance asks for firing that follows the eel, faint or strong.

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire for whichever smell is most like the last eel smell, even when that smell is the sucker’s.
options.why: That neuron would send the fish fleeing from the sucker whenever its smell happened to be most like the last eel smell. The neuron has to stay quiet for the sucker even then.

items.stem: Suppose a neuron downstream of the fish’s smell receptors fires whenever the smell in the water is strong, and stays quiet whenever it is faint. Why does this neuron fail the demand that invariance makes?

options.text: It would not fire for an eel far away and could fire for a sucker close by, so its firing would not follow whether an eel is there.
options.why: Correct. An eel near and an eel far produce smells at very different strengths. A neuron that follows strength follows distance, not the eel.

options.text: It would meet generalization but fail discrimination, since it would treat strong smells alike, whether they come from an eel or from a sucker.
options.why: It does fail discrimination, but it fails generalization too. It would treat a faint eel and a strong eel differently, though both call for flight.

options.text: It is a single neuron, and invariance requires that no one neuron fire for every eel smell, only a pattern of activity across many.
options.why: Invariance is stated in exactly those terms: some neuron downstream has to fire for every eel smell. The trouble is what this particular neuron fires for.

options.text: It would meet the demand, since a strong smell usually means a nearby eel, and a nearby eel is the danger most worth fleeing from.
options.why: A distant eel still calls for flight while there is time to get away. And a strong smell could just as well come from a sucker close by.

items.stem: A young songbird has learned that a hawk’s outline overhead means danger. Later it learns about an owl, whose outline shares much with the hawk’s and with the outlines of harmless pigeons. Why does learning about the owl bear on what the bird already knows?

options.text: The owl has much in common with things learned earlier, so learning about it touches what is known about those things.
options.why: Correct. Things learned at different times often overlap, and when they do, learning about one bears on what is already known about the others.

options.text: Learning about the owl leaves old learning untouched, since each thing an animal learns about is kept apart from the rest.
options.why: Learning in sequence would be easy if that were so. Because the owl’s outline shares so much with the others, learning about it cannot be kept apart from them.

options.text: The owl was learned about later, and later learning replaces earlier learning whatever the two things have in common.
options.why: Order alone is not the problem; overlap is. And the requirement is that new learning add to old learning rather than replace it.

options.text: The owl is a predator like the hawk, so the bird simply treats the owl as a hawk and has nothing new to learn about it.
options.why: Treating the owl like the hawk would be generalization, but the bird is learning about the owl. Its overlap with the hawk and the pigeons is what makes that learning bear on the old.

items.stem: When an animal learns about one thing after another, what has to be true of the new learning?

options.text: It has to add to the old learning without overwriting it, so that what was learned before is kept.
options.why: Correct. That is the requirement learning in sequence states. Learning a new predator must not erase what the fish knows about eels.

options.text: It has to replace the old learning, so that the most recent encounter decides what the animal does.
options.why: Replacing old learning is exactly what must not happen. The fish that learns a new predator still needs what it knows about eels.

options.text: It has to wait until the old learning is complete, so that the two never go on at the same time.
options.why: The fish learns about other things in between its encounters with eels. The requirement is that new learning add to old, not wait for it.

options.text: It has to use receptors the old learning never used, so that the two cannot affect each other.
options.why: The new predator’s smell and the eel’s are carried by many of the same receptors. The requirement has to be met despite that overlap.

items.stem: Two foraging birds learn which berries to eat. Where the first lives, the edible and the bitter berries share almost none of their colors, sizes, and smells. Where the second lives, edible and bitter berries share most of their colors, sizes, and smells, in different combinations. For which bird does more of the reliable information lie in combinations of features?

options.text: The second, since the more the berries share features, the more of the reliable information lies in combinations of them.
options.why: Correct. When features are shared across edible and bitter berries, each single feature is followed by a good meal some of the time and not at others, and the combinations carry what is reliable.

options.text: The first, since features that the two kinds of berry do not share have to be combined before they can say anything about which to eat.
options.why: Where features are not shared, each one predicts the outcome on its own. A single color or smell is enough for the first bird.

options.text: Both equally, since how many features the berries share does not change where the reliable information about which to eat lies.
options.why: How much objects share is exactly what moves the reliable information. The more they share, the more of it lies in combinations.

options.text: Neither, since a bird learns only about single features, so even the second bird could not learn about combinations at all.
options.why: Animals do learn tasks in which only combinations predict the outcome. And the question is where the information lies, which the second bird’s berries put in combinations.

items.stem: A young bird has learned which butterflies are good to eat. It then learns about a new, bad-tasting kind, every one of whose colors and markings is also found on the good kinds, in different combinations. In a short paragraph, explain why learning about the new kind bears on what the bird already knows, why none of those colors or markings, taken alone, can now be relied on to predict a good meal, what the new learning has to do, and what trade-off that learning faces.
items.answer: The new butterfly’s colors and markings overlap with those of the kinds the bird already knows, so learning about it bears on what was learned about them. Each of those colors and markings now comes with a bad taste on some occasions and a good meal on others, so none of them alone predicts the outcome reliably, and only combinations do. The new learning has to add to the old without overwriting it: the bird must learn to avoid the new kind and still eat the good ones. This is the trade-off we called stability versus plasticity in Module 5, changing enough to learn something new while changing little enough to keep what was learned before.
rubric: Says the overlap in colors and markings makes learning about the new kind bear on old learning.
Says each shared color or marking is followed by a good meal on some occasions and a bad taste on others, so no single one is reliable and only combinations are.
States that new learning has to add to old learning without overwriting it.
Names stability versus plasticity and describes both sides of it.

pools.title: Definitions, Rules, and a Space of Inputs
pools.covers: reading §7.2.1, §7.2.2 · lecture 7.2 slides title, definitions_and_rules, a_space_of_inputs, three_families

items.stem: What is the classical view of categories?

options.text: The view that a category is defined by features that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient.
options.why: Correct. Everything with all of the defining features belongs to the category, and nothing without them does.

options.text: The view that a category is represented by one summary of its members, such as the average member.
options.why: That describes a prototype model, which stores a central tendency and sorts a new input by closeness to it. The classical view stores a definition.

options.text: The view that a category is represented by every member a person has stored, with new items compared to all of them.
options.why: That describes an exemplar model, which keeps the members themselves. The classical view lists defining features instead.

options.text: The view that members overlap the way faces in a family do, with no single feature running through the whole set.
options.why: That is family resemblance, the pattern found in everyday categories and part of the evidence against the classical view, not the view itself.

items.stem: What is the name for the account under which a category is defined by features that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for membership, so that everything with all of them belongs and nothing without them does?

options.text: Classical view.
options.why: Correct. It is the oldest answer to how categories might be formed, and for a long time it was the default account.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. A prototype model sorts by closeness to that summary, not by a list of defining features.

options.text: Exemplar.
options.why: An exemplar is a stored example of a category. An exemplar model sorts by summed similarity to stored members, with no defining features at all.

options.text: Decision-bound model.
options.why: A decision-bound model divides the feature space into regions and responds by region. A definition can be read that way, but the name for the account built on defining features is the classical view.

items.stem: A hiking club defines a “full member” as someone who has paid this year’s dues and has completed the safety course. Read as a classical definition, which statement follows?

options.text: Anyone who has done both is a full member, whatever else is true of them, and anyone who has done only one is not.
options.why: Correct. Each feature is individually necessary, so lacking either one excludes a person, and the two together are jointly sufficient, so nothing else is needed.

options.text: Someone who has done only one of the two is a partial member, closer to full membership than someone who has done neither.
options.why: That treats membership as graded. Under the classical view membership is all or none, so missing one necessary feature leaves a person out entirely.

options.text: Someone who has done both may still fall short if they are an unusual sort of member, since typical members count for most.
options.why: Typicality plays no part in a classical definition. The two features are jointly sufficient, so having both is enough, however unusual the member.

options.text: Someone who has done neither can still qualify if they share enough other features with the club’s most typical members.
options.why: That is family resemblance, which is how everyday categories often look. A classical definition makes each defining feature necessary.

items.stem: The lecture calls a classical definition “a more complex labeled line”. In what sense is a definition more complex than a labeled line such as the worm’s copper-sensing neuron?

options.text: A labeled line is a single test, while a definition is a set of such tests combined by a rule.
options.why: Correct. One kind of receptor responds and a response follows: that is a single test. A definition gathers several tests and combines them by a rule.

options.text: A labeled line answers to one receptor, while a definition answers to a pattern across many receptors that no rule can state.
options.why: A pattern that no single input identifies is what pattern recognition deals with. A definition is exactly a pattern that a rule does state.

options.text: A labeled line carries its label on the line itself, while a definition carries its label at the far end, in what it connects to.
options.why: That reverses the point about labeled lines. The label of a labeled line is at the far end, in what the line connects to, not on the line itself.

options.text: A labeled line is learned from experience, while a definition is fixed before any learning starts and never changes.
options.why: The chapter does not contrast labeled lines and definitions by how they arise. The contrast it draws is between one test and several tests combined by a rule.

items.stem: A rectangle is a closed figure with four straight sides and four right angles. If definitions are stacked, how is “right angle” handled?

options.text: It has a definition of its own in terms of simpler properties of lines, which rest in turn on tests a receptor can perform.
options.why: Correct. A defining feature need not be detected directly. Built this way, a definition is a hierarchy of tests, with receptor-level tests at the bottom.

options.text: It is detected directly by one kind of receptor that responds to right angles, so the rectangle needs no further levels below it.
options.why: Some tests at the very bottom are simple enough for a receptor. A right angle is not one of them; it is defined in terms of simpler properties.

options.text: It is left undefined, since only the category at the top of a definition needs a list of defining features.
options.why: Stacking means the reverse: each defining feature can have a definition of its own, level after level.

options.text: It is learned as the average of the right angles experienced so far, and each new corner is compared with that average.
options.why: Comparing with an average is what a prototype model does. In a stacked definition, each feature is itself defined by tests and a rule.

items.stem: A student tries to build a stacked definition of “tool”, working downward through simpler and simpler tests. What is most likely to make the attempt hard?

options.text: Each level must be definable from the one below, down to receptor tests, and for an everyday category that chain may be very hard to find.
options.why: Correct. For a square the chain reaches all the way down. For everyday categories such as bird or chair, it may be much harder to identify one.

options.text: Stacked definitions can combine their tests only by AND, and a category like “tool” would need other rules, such as exclusive or, at some level.
options.why: Rules are not limited to AND; exclusive or is a perfectly good rule. The difficulty lies in finding definitions at every level.

options.text: A hierarchy of tests would need a separate receptor for every kind of tool, and no animal has nearly that many kinds of receptor.
options.why: In a stacked definition only the bottom tests are done by receptors, and they are simple ones. The problem is defining each level from the one below.

options.text: A stacked definition can sort only the inputs it has already experienced, so any new kind of tool would fall outside it.
options.why: A definition sorts anything that passes its tests, new or not. The trouble is in building the chain of definitions in the first place.

items.stem: A critic argues that the classical view fails because definitions are too weak to compute anything complicated. How does the chapter answer the critic?

options.text: Definitions can use any rule and can be stacked, so the case against them rests on what people’s categories turn out to be like.
options.why: Correct. The case against the classical view does not rest on what definitions can compute. It rests on typicality and on how people’s categories are structured.

options.text: The critic is right, since definitions can combine tests only by AND, which is why they cannot capture categories that have exceptions.
options.why: Rules are not limited to AND, and definitions can be stacked into hierarchies. The weakness of definitions is not the case against them.

options.text: The critic is right, since a definition cannot capture a category with the shape of exclusive or, like the fruit that rots.
options.why: A definition can capture the fruit, since “smell A or smell B, but not both” is a perfectly good rule.

options.text: The critic is wrong, since people never use definitions at all, which leaves the computing power of definitions beside the point.
options.why: The chapter says some categories are probably learned as rules. The real reply is that the case against definitions concerns what categories are like.

items.stem: Suppose people rate 4 as a better example of an even number than 1,006, while agreeing that both are even and that every even number is equally even. By the chapter’s reasoning, what does this result show?

options.text: Graded ratings can exist alongside a definition, so typicality alone does not show that a category lacks one.
options.why: Correct. This mirrors the odd-number finding. People can know an exact definition and still rate some members as better examples.

options.text: Even number has no real definition, since graded ratings are the main evidence against the classical view.
options.why: Typicality is the main evidence against the classical view as a general account, but it cannot refute a definition alone, as numbers show.

options.text: People do not really understand what an even number is, since anyone who did would rate every member the same.
options.why: The people in such a study know the definition perfectly well. Graded ratings and an exact definition can coexist in one mind.

options.text: Numbers form a family resemblance, since small even numbers share more features with one another than large ones do.
options.why: Family resemblance describes categories with no feature running through every member. Every even number shares the defining feature.

items.stem: Why does one study’s finding about odd numbers matter to the case against the classical view?

options.text: People rated 3 a better odd number than 447 while knowing all odd numbers belong equally, so typicality alone cannot refute definitions.
options.why: Correct. Graded ratings can exist alongside a definition. Some categories are probably learned as rules, and others are not.

options.text: People rated 3 and 447 as equally good odd numbers, which confirmed that typicality disappears wherever a definition exists.
options.why: The finding was the reverse: people did rate some odd numbers as better examples than others.

options.text: People could not reliably say whether 447 was odd, which showed that even exact definitions are learned through family resemblance in the end.
options.why: The people knew the definition perfectly well. The finding was about graded ratings, not about uncertainty over membership.

options.text: People rated 3 a better odd number than 447, which showed that odd number has no exact definition after all.
options.why: Odd number plainly has an exact definition. The point of the finding is that graded ratings can coexist with one.

items.stem: What is a feature space?

options.text: A space with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point.
options.why: Correct. In a feature space, inputs that are alike land close together and inputs that are different land far apart.

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells of the tissue.
options.why: That is a topographic map, a layout of tissue. A feature space is a picture of inputs, with one axis per feature.

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes one cell’s activity.
options.why: That is a receptive field, a property of a single cell. A feature space places every input as a point.

options.text: The list of features that every member of a category has in common.
options.why: A list of shared features is what a classical definition would give. A feature space is a space, with an axis for each feature.

items.stem: What do we call a picture of inputs with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point?

options.text: Feature space.
options.why: Correct. A feature space turns sorting inputs into dividing a space into regions.

options.text: Feature engineering.
options.why: Feature engineering is deciding, before learning begins, what the inputs to a learning system will be. It chooses the axes; it is not the space.

options.text: Topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells.

options.text: Decision boundary.
options.why: A decision boundary is a line through the space of inputs, separating what a unit fires to from what it does not.

items.stem: The lecture says a feature space gives a picture to the mapping from inputs to responses that the fish’s world calls for. In that picture, what does the mapping become?

options.text: A division of the space into regions, one for each response, with a boundary between them.
options.why: Correct. The inputs that should get one response form a region, and the mapping divides the space with a boundary.

options.text: A single point for each response, placed at the average of the inputs that get that response.
options.why: One point per category at the average is a prototype. The mapping itself is a division of the whole space.

options.text: A threshold along each axis of the space, marking the strength at which each kind of receptor begins to fire.
options.why: A threshold on each axis would treat receptors one at a time. The mapping divides the space as a whole into regions.

options.text: A list of every input already experienced, each stored together with the response it received.
options.why: Storing every input is what an exemplar model does. The picture the feature space gives is a division into regions.

items.stem: What does it mean for two categories to be linearly separable?

options.text: One straight line or flat surface through the feature space puts all of one category on one side and all of the other on the other.
options.why: Correct. That property is linear separability, and it settles whether one straight cut is enough.

options.text: A single straight line through the feature space puts most of one category on one side and most of the other category on the other side.
options.why: Most is not enough. Two overlapping clouds can be mostly divided by one line and still not be linearly separable.

options.text: The points of the two categories do not overlap anywhere in the feature space.
options.why: Not overlapping is needed but not enough. The just-right fruit’s acceptable smells overlap none of the others, yet no straight line can wrap around that island.

options.text: Each category can be picked out by a single feature on its own, without any regard to the other features.
options.why: AND depends on two features together, and it is still linearly separable. One straight line may run across several axes at once.

items.stem: What is the name for the property of two categories that can be divided by a single straight line, or a single flat surface, through the feature space, with all of one category on one side and all of the other on the other?

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Correct. AND and OR have this property, which is why one unit could compute each of them; exclusive or does not.

options.text: Discrimination.
options.why: Discrimination is treating differently the inputs that call for different responses. It is a demand on the mapping, not a property of a division.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units, which makes it more likely that a straight boundary will work.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as distance or viewpoint.

items.stem: For a hypothetical bee, a flower is worth visiting when it has a sweet scent or a blue color, but not both. With one axis for the scent and one for the color, where do the four combinations fall, and can one straight line sort them?

options.text: The two cases worth visiting sit at opposite corners, as do the other two, so no straight line puts both of those corners on one side.
options.why: Correct. This is exclusive or. Any straight line that is tried leaves at least one case on the wrong side.

options.text: The two cases worth visiting sit side by side along one edge of the space, so one straight line can cut them off from the other two.
options.why: The two cases worth visiting are scent alone and color alone, which sit at opposite corners, not along one edge.

options.text: The cases worth visiting form an island in the middle of the space, so a straight line can cut off only one side of it.
options.why: An island in the middle is the just-right strength case. Here the four cases sit at the four corners of the space.

options.text: The four cases fall on a single straight line, so one threshold placed along that line sorts them correctly.
options.why: Two features that can each be present or absent give four corners of a square, not four points on a line.

items.stem: For the fruit where either smell alone means ripe fruit and both together mean rot, which added third input lets a single flat plane separate the ripe cases from the rest?

options.text: An input that is active only when both smells are present, the product of the two smells.
options.why: Correct. The product moves the rotting corner away from the other three, and then a single flat plane separates the ripe cases from the rest.

options.text: An input that reports the sum of the two smells, so that a stronger combined smell gets a larger value.
options.why: A sum is largest when both smells are present, which is why it can look like a fix. But on the sum the ripe cases fall between no fruit and rot. The input that moves the rotting corner away from the other three is one active only when both smells are present.

options.text: A second copy of smell A’s input, so that smell A is reported twice and counts for more than smell B.
options.why: A copy of smell A carries nothing that smell A did not already carry. The ripe cases still sit at opposite corners; what moves the rotting corner away is an input active only when both smells are present.

options.text: An input that reports smell B at a higher gain, so that small amounts of smell B register strongly.
options.why: Reporting smell B more strongly changes how far apart the cases sit along one axis, not which cases sit at opposite corners. What moves the rotting corner away is an input active only when both smells are present.

items.stem: A student says: “Exclusive or can never be solved by one straight boundary, whatever inputs we start from”. What is wrong with the student’s claim?

options.text: Separability depends on which features the space is built from; with the right added feature, one flat surface separates the cases.
options.why: Correct. Exclusive or is not linearly separable in the space of the two smells. Add the product of the two, and a single flat plane does the job.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; exclusive or can be solved only by a network with a hidden layer, never by any single straight boundary.
options.why: A hidden layer is one way of supplying new features. Once the inputs are re-represented, a single straight boundary can do the rest.

options.text: Exclusive or can be solved by one straight line in the original two-smell space, once a unit’s weights have been trained for long enough.
options.why: No amount of training gives one unit a line that puts both food corners on one side in the original space. What changes things is new features.

options.text: Exclusive or is linearly separable in the original two-smell space, as long as the straight line is drawn diagonally.
options.why: Every straight line in the two-smell space, diagonal or not, leaves at least one case on the wrong side.

items.stem: With the right features, the hard combination problems become easy to sort with one straight cut. What question does that leave open, and what answers are named?

options.text: Where such features come from: they can be learned, wired at random, or built in.
options.why: Correct. With the right features the hard problems are easy, so the open question becomes where the features come from.

options.text: Whether such features are real: they may be inputs no receptor reports, so the space is only a convenience.
options.why: The features can be real inputs, whether supplied by receptors or by later units. The open question is where useful ones come from.

options.text: Which family of algorithm to use: a decision bound, a prototype, or a set of stored exemplars.
options.why: The three families are a separate topic, about what is stored and consulted. The open question here is the source of useful features.

options.text: How many axes such features need: two can be pictured, three need a plane, and more cannot be divided.
options.why: A space with many axes can still be divided by a hyperplane. The open question is where useful features come from.

items.stem: Psychologists have proposed three broad families of algorithm that treat an input as a point in a feature space. What chiefly distinguishes the families from one another?

options.text: What has to be stored, and consulted, before a response can be made.
options.why: Correct. One family stores the boundary itself, and the others store something about the members of each category.

options.text: Whether they place inputs in a feature space at all, or work from definitions instead.
options.why: All three families treat an input as a point in a feature space. That is what they have in common.

options.text: Whether they end up drawing a boundary between categories, or manage to avoid drawing one.
options.why: Every family ends up drawing a boundary, whether it stores that boundary or not.

options.text: Whether they learn from experience, or have every category built in from the very start.
options.why: The families are not divided by learned versus built in. They differ in what is stored and consulted.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why most cognitive scientists do not take the classical view as the general account of categories, and why graded typicality alone does not settle the matter.
items.answer: The case against the classical view does not rest on what definitions can compute, since a definition can combine tests by any rule and can be stacked. It rests on what people’s categories are like. When people listed the attributes of twenty members of an everyday category, few or none were true of all twenty, so there is nothing for a definition to list. And a definition makes every member equally good, while people rated a robin a far better bird than a penguin. But typicality alone does not refute definitions. People rate 3 a better odd number than 447 while knowing that every odd number belongs equally. So graded ratings can exist alongside a definition, and some categories are probably learned as rules.
rubric: Says the case rests on what people’s categories are like, not on what definitions can compute.
Gives the attribute-listing finding: few or no attributes are shared by every member, so there is nothing to list.
Gives graded typicality (robin against penguin, or similar) as conflicting with every member belonging equally.
Gives the odd-number finding: graded ratings alongside an exact definition.
Concludes that typicality alone does not refute definitions, and that some categories may be learned as rules.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, use a square to explain how a definition can be built as a hierarchy of tests, and explain why the same construction may be much harder for an everyday category such as bird.
items.answer: A square is a closed figure with four straight sides of equal length and four right angles. None of those features is a single test. A right angle is itself defined in terms of simpler properties of lines, and those in terms of simpler properties still. So a stacked definition is a hierarchy of tests, with tests simple enough for a receptor to perform at the bottom, and each level combining the results of the level below by a rule. In Module 4’s terms, it is a hierarchy of units, each computing a truth table over the units beneath it. The hierarchy works only if every level can be defined in terms of the one below, all the way down to receptor tests. For a square that can be done. For bird it may be much harder to find a chain of definitions that reaches all the way down.
rubric: Gives the square’s defining features and notes that each can have a definition of its own.
Describes the result as a hierarchy, with receptor-level tests at the bottom.
Says each level combines the level below by a rule, or equivalently that each unit computes a truth table.
States the condition: every level must be definable down to tests a receptor can perform.
Says that for bird such a chain may be much harder to find, keeping the hedge rather than declaring it impossible.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the difference between two sniffs being close together in the small fish’s smell space and two sniffs calling for the same response. Use the eel and the sucker.
items.answer: Closeness in a feature space means the inputs are alike: the receptors respond to them in much the same way. Which response a sniff calls for depends on where it came from, an eel or a sucker. The eel and sucker clouds overlap at the edge, so a sucker sniff can sit right beside an eel sniff and still call for feeding rather than flight. The mapping divides the space into regions, one for each response, and where the boundary should run is set by which smells come from which fish and how much the two overlap. Because of the overlap, no single straight line puts every eel sniff on one side and every sucker sniff on the other; the clouds would be linearly separable only if they did not overlap.
rubric: Says closeness means the inputs are alike in how the receptors respond.
Says the response a sniff calls for depends on which fish produced it.
Uses the overlap of the eel and sucker clouds to show that neighbors can call for different responses.
Describes the mapping as regions with a boundary set by the smells and their overlap.
Notes that, with the overlap, the clouds are not linearly separable.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how three families of categorization algorithm that store different things can still be compared with one another, and why two models that draw the same boundary are hard to tell apart.
items.answer: The three families differ in what has to be stored, and consulted, before a response can be made. One stores the boundary itself, and the others store something about the members of each category. But every one of them ends up drawing a boundary between categories, whether it stores that boundary or not, so the boundaries give a common ground for comparing them. Two models that draw the same boundary sort every input the same way, so they are very hard to tell apart in data, even when they work very differently inside.
rubric: Says the families differ in what is stored and consulted before a response.
Says every family ends up drawing a boundary, whether or not it stores one.
Says the boundaries are what allow the families to be compared.
Explains that the same boundary means the same sorting, so data can barely separate the models.
Does not declare any family the winner.

items.stem: What is a decision-bound model of categorization?

options.text: A model that divides the feature space into regions, one for each response, and responds according to the region an input falls in.
options.why: Correct. A decision-bound model learns the boundary itself, and the side of the boundary an input lands on settles the response.

options.text: A model that stores one summary of each category, such as its average member, and assigns a new input to whichever summary is nearest.
options.why: That is a prototype model. It stores something about the members, and its boundary follows from what it stores rather than being learned directly.

options.text: A model that stores every member of each category, and assigns a new input to the category with the largest summed similarity to it.
options.why: That is an exemplar model. It stores the members themselves, while a decision-bound model stores the boundary instead.

options.text: A framework for deciding whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence tells the cases apart from where the line is drawn.
options.why: That is signal detection theory, the framework decision-bound theory grew out of. Its line is a criterion on one axis of evidence; a decision-bound model divides a whole feature space into regions, one for each response.

items.stem: What is the name for a model of categorization that learns the boundary itself, dividing the feature space into one region for each response and responding according to the region an input falls in?

options.text: Decision-bound model.
options.why: Correct. Of the three families, the decision-bound model is the one that stores the boundary rather than anything about the members.

options.text: Prototype model.
options.why: A prototype model stores one summary of each category and assigns an input to the closest one. Its boundary follows from those summaries; it is not stored.

options.text: Exemplar model.
options.why: An exemplar model stores every member and sums an input’s similarity to them. Its boundary follows from what it stores; it is not learned directly.

options.text: Signal detection theory.
options.why: Signal detection theory is the framework decision-bound theory grew out of, for deciding whether a target is present. The family that learns a boundary in a feature space is the decision-bound model.

items.stem: How is a decision bound related to the criterion of signal detection theory?

options.text: The criterion is a boundary drawn on a single axis of evidence, and a decision bound is that same idea extended to a feature space with many axes.
options.why: Correct. The criterion splits one evidence axis into “yes” and “no”. A decision bound splits a feature space with many axes into one region per response.

options.text: The criterion is a boundary in a space with many axes, and a decision bound is the simpler case of that same idea on a single axis of evidence.
options.why: This reverses the two. The criterion is the one-axis case, drawn along a single axis of evidence; the decision bound generalizes it to many axes.

options.text: The criterion measures how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie, and a decision bound measures that same distance across many axes.
options.why: How far apart the distributions lie is sensitivity, not the criterion. The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn, and a decision bound is that line in many dimensions.

options.text: The criterion and a decision bound are rival accounts, one for detecting a target and one for sorting categories, so neither is a case of the other.
options.why: They are not rivals. Decision-bound theory grew out of signal detection theory, and a decision bound is the criterion’s idea carried into a space with many axes.

items.stem: What is a unit’s decision boundary?

options.text: The line through the space of possible inputs that separates the combinations the unit fires to from the combinations it does not.
options.why: Correct. For a single unit the decision boundary is a straight line, with firing on one side and silence on the other.

options.text: The amount of evidence at which the unit’s response changes from “no” to “yes”, marked as one point on a single axis of evidence.
options.why: That is the criterion, a point on one evidence axis. The decision boundary is the set of inputs in the whole input space whose evidence sits at that criterion.

options.text: The distance between the unit’s responses to two categories, measured in units of how much those responses vary from trial to trial.
options.why: That describes sensitivity, measured as d′. The decision boundary is a line through the input space, not a distance between distributions.

options.text: The fall-off in the unit’s response as an input differs more and more from the input on which the unit was originally trained.
options.why: That describes a generalization gradient. The decision boundary is a sharp dividing line in the input space, with firing on one side only.

items.stem: A single unit of the kind in Module 4 fires to some combinations of its inputs and stays silent for the rest. What is the name for the straight line through the space of possible inputs that separates those two sets of combinations?

options.text: Decision boundary.
options.why: Correct. The decision boundary is the line that separates the combinations a unit fires to from the ones it does not.

options.text: Criterion.
options.why: The criterion is the amount of evidence at which a response changes, a point on one axis. The line through the input space is the decision boundary.

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Linear separability is a property of two categories, that one straight line can divide them. The line itself is the decision boundary.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is a smooth fall-off in responding with distance from a trained input, not a line separating firing from silence.

items.stem: Which change to a unit turns its decision boundary to a new angle, and which change slides the boundary without turning it?

options.text: Changing the weights turns the line, and changing the threshold or the baseline firing rate slides it.
options.why: Correct. The weights set the line’s angle; the threshold or baseline sets where along that angle the line sits.

options.text: Changing the threshold turns the line, and changing the weights or the baseline firing rate slides it.
options.why: This swaps the two. The weights set the balance among the inputs, which is the angle; the threshold sets how much evidence is needed, which is the position.

options.text: Changing the weights slides the line, and changing the threshold bends it into a curve around the inputs.
options.why: A single unit’s boundary never bends; it stays a straight line whatever its settings. The weights turn it and the threshold slides it.

options.text: Changing the baseline firing rate turns the line, and changing the weights leaves the line where it was.
options.why: The baseline firing rate works like the threshold and slides the line. The weights are what turn it.

items.stem: A unit with two inputs, each weighted 1, computes AND when its threshold is 1.5 and OR when its threshold is 0.5. Why can one unit compute both with no change at all to its weights?

options.text: The two computations’ lines are parallel, so going from one to the other only slides the line, which is what a change of threshold does.
options.why: Correct. AND and OR need lines at the same angle in different places, and the threshold is what slides a line from one place to another.

options.text: The two computations need lines at different angles, and a change of threshold is enough to turn a unit’s line to whatever angle is needed.
options.why: A change of threshold does not turn the line; changing the weights does. AND and OR need no turning, because their lines are parallel.

options.text: The two computations share a prototype at the center of the square, so the threshold only changes how close an input must come to that prototype.
options.why: A single unit stores no prototype. It draws one straight line set by its weights and threshold, and here only the threshold moves.

options.text: The two computations are both rules with a simple verbal form, and any rule with a verbal form can be computed by one unit at some threshold.
options.why: Exclusive or also has a simple verbal form, and no single unit computes it. What matters is that the lines for AND and OR are parallel.

items.stem: Put a single unit into the terms of signal detection theory. What in the unit plays the part of the evidence, and what plays the part of the criterion?

options.text: The unit’s weighted sum is its evidence, and its threshold is its criterion.
options.why: Correct. The weighted sum is how much evidence the inputs supply, and the threshold is the amount of evidence at which the unit’s response changes.

options.text: The unit’s threshold is its evidence, and its weighted sum is its criterion.
