options.why: This swaps the two. The threshold stays put while the weighted sum varies from input to input, so the sum is the evidence and the threshold the criterion.

options.text: The unit’s output, firing or silent, is its evidence, and its weights are its criterion.
options.why: Firing or silence is the response that follows the decision, not the evidence for it. The weights shape the evidence; the threshold is the criterion.

options.text: The unit’s weighted sum is its evidence, and the spread of that sum across trials is its criterion.
options.why: The spread of the evidence enters into sensitivity, which is measured in units of spread. The criterion is the threshold, where the line is drawn.

items.stem: A hummingbird drinks only from flowers whose nectar is neither too weak nor too strong, so the acceptable flowers form an island in the middle of its feature space, with unacceptable ones on every side. Which claim about modeling it with a decision-bound model is right?

options.text: A decision-bound model can draw a curved boundary that wraps around the island; only a single unit is held to one straight line.
options.why: Correct. Decision-bound models in psychology are not limited to straight lines. The single-line limit belongs to a single unit, the family’s simplest member.

options.text: No decision-bound model can capture it, because a decision bound is always one straight line, like the boundary of a single unit.
options.why: That carries a single unit’s limit over to the whole family. Decision-bound models in psychology can draw curved boundaries, including one around an island.

options.text: A decision-bound model can capture it only by turning its straight line until the line passes right through the middle of the island.
options.why: A straight line at any angle cuts off at most one side of an island. Capturing the island needs a boundary that curves around it.

options.text: A decision-bound model can capture it only if the island has a simple verbal form, since every decision bound has to be a rule.
options.why: Some decision bounds are rules with a verbal form, but many are not. Whether a bound can be put into words does not limit its shape.

items.stem: A unit with two inputs fires when the weighted sum of its inputs exceeds its threshold. In a few sentences, describe this unit as a decision-bound model in the terms of signal detection theory: say what its evidence and its criterion are, which inputs make up its decision boundary, and what happens to the boundary when the weights change and when the threshold changes.
items.answer: The unit’s weighted sum is its evidence, and its threshold is its criterion. Every combination of inputs that gives the same weighted sum lands on the same point of the evidence axis, so the decision boundary is exactly the set of inputs whose evidence sits at the criterion. In the space of the two inputs that set is a straight line, with firing on one side and silence on the other. Changing the weights turns the line to a new angle, and changing the threshold, or the baseline firing rate, slides it without turning it.
rubric: Identifies the weighted sum as the evidence.
Identifies the threshold as the criterion.
Says the boundary is the set of inputs whose weighted sum equals the threshold, a straight line.
Says changing the weights turns the line.
Says changing the threshold or baseline slides the line.

items.stem: In prototype and exemplar models of categorization, what is similarity?

options.text: Closeness between two inputs in a feature space, measured in a way, and in a space, that differs from one model to another.
options.why: Correct. Two inputs are similar when their points lie near each other, and closeness can be estimated in a number of different ways.

options.text: The proportion of defining features that two inputs share, so that two inputs sharing every defining feature are fully similar.
options.why: Counting shared defining features belongs to the classical view. Similarity in these models is closeness of points in a feature space.

options.text: How good an example of a category an input is, as when a robin is rated a better example of a bird than a penguin is.
options.why: That is typicality. Typicality can be explained by similarity, but similarity itself is closeness between two inputs.

options.text: The fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs more and more from the input that an animal was trained on.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, which in an exemplar model sets how much each example counts. Similarity is the closeness itself, and the gradient describes how responding falls as that closeness shrinks.

items.stem: Prototype and exemplar models both categorize a new input by its closeness to what they have stored, where closeness between two inputs is measured in a feature space and can be estimated in several ways. What is that closeness called?

options.text: Similarity.
options.why: Correct. Similarity is closeness in a feature space, and how it is measured, and in which space, differs from one model to another.

options.text: Typicality.
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category an item is. It is something similarity helps to explain, not closeness itself.

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Linear separability is a property of two categories that one straight line can divide. It says nothing about how close two inputs are.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is treating alike inputs that call for the same response. Closeness between inputs is one thing that can drive it, and that closeness is similarity.

items.stem: What is a prototype, in a prototype model of categorization?

options.text: A summary of a category, such as its average member, which a new input is compared with to find the category it is closest to.
options.why: Correct. A prototype is a category’s central tendency, and a prototype model assigns an input to whichever prototype it is closest to.

options.text: A stored example of a category, one of many kept, whose similarities to a new input are added up category by category.
options.why: That is an exemplar. An exemplar model keeps many examples per category, while a prototype model keeps one summary.

options.text: How good an example of a category an item is, as when a robin is rated a better example of a bird than a penguin is.
options.why: That is typicality. An item close to the prototype tends to be typical, but the prototype is the summary itself, such as the category’s average member.

options.text: A boundary stored for a category, dividing the feature space into the region where that category’s response is given and the rest.
options.why: A stored boundary belongs to a decision-bound model. A prototype model stores a summary, and its boundary follows from it.

items.stem: What is the name for a summary of a category, its central tendency, something like its average member, against which a new input is compared?

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: Correct. A prototype model stores one such summary for each category and assigns a new input to the closest.

options.text: Exemplar.
options.why: An exemplar is one stored example of a category, not a summary of all of them. An exemplar model keeps the members themselves.

options.text: Decision boundary.
options.why: A decision boundary is a line separating the inputs a unit fires to from the rest. It summarizes no category’s members.

options.text: Typicality.
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category an item is. An item close to the prototype is typical, but the summary itself is the prototype.

items.stem: What is an exemplar, in an exemplar model of categorization?

options.text: A stored example of a category; a new input goes to the category whose stored members it is most similar to in total.
options.why: Correct. An exemplar model keeps the members themselves, sums a new input’s similarity to them category by category, and picks the largest total.

options.text: A summary of a category, such as its average member; a new input goes to the category whose summary it lies closest to.
options.why: That is a prototype. A prototype model keeps one summary per category, while an exemplar model keeps every member.

options.text: A vote among the k stored examples nearest a new input, each counted equally; the input goes to the most common category among them.
options.why: That describes k-nearest-neighbor classification, a simple relative of the exemplar model. An exemplar is one stored member, and in an exemplar model every stored member contributes, weighted by similarity.

options.text: A defining feature of a category; a new input goes to the category whose defining features it has all of, and to no other.
options.why: Defining features belong to the classical view. An exemplar is a whole stored member, not a feature that members must have.

items.stem: Two learners have each seen the same hundred dogs and hundred cats. One keeps a single average dog and a single average cat; the other keeps all two hundred animals. A new animal is closer to the average dog than to the average cat, but it sits very close to a dozen of the stored cats and far from every one of the stored dogs. How do the two learners classify it?

options.text: The first calls it a dog, by closeness to the prototypes, and the second calls it a cat, by summed similarity to the stored members.
options.why: Correct. This is the kind of item later experiments built on purpose, where closeness to the prototype and closeness to particular examples point in different directions.

options.text: Both call it a dog, since summing similarity to every stored member always gives the same answer as comparing with the average.
options.why: Summing over members and comparing with an average can come apart. Here the stored cats it is close to carry the second learner’s total.

options.text: Both call it a cat, since the stored cats it closely resembles outweigh the average in either kind of model.
options.why: The first learner keeps no individual cats, only one average per category. By closeness to those averages, the new animal is a dog.

options.text: The first calls it a cat and the second a dog, since a prototype model weights nearby members heavily and an exemplar model does not.
options.why: This swaps the two. Weighting by nearby members is what an exemplar model does; a prototype model consults only the summaries.

items.stem: An exemplar model has stored three birds and three bats. A new animal’s similarities to the stored birds are 0.6, 0.1, and 0.1, and to the stored bats 0.3, 0.3, and 0.3. Which category does the model assign it to, and why?

options.text: Bat, because its summed similarity to the three stored bats, 0.9, is larger than its summed similarity to the three stored birds, 0.8.
options.why: Correct. An exemplar model adds up the similarity to every stored member, category by category, with each one counting according to how close it is.

options.text: Bird, because the most similar of the stored birds, at 0.6, beats every stored bat, and an exemplar model follows the one closest member.
options.why: Following only the closest member is k-nearest-neighbor classification with k of 1. An exemplar model sums similarity across all the stored members.

options.text: Bat, because three stored bats are similar to it, and each similar member gets one equal vote however similar it happens to be.
options.why: Equal votes belong to k-nearest-neighbor classification. In an exemplar model each stored member counts according to its similarity.

options.text: Bird, because an exemplar model counts only the stored members with a similarity above one half, and only one bird passes that mark.
options.why: An exemplar model sets no cutoff. Every stored member contributes, a nearby one a great deal and a distant one almost nothing.

items.stem: Suppose an animal trained on one tone treats the tone an octave above as more like the trained tone than tones that are physically closer, just below it. What does a case like this mean for how an exemplar model of that animal should compute similarity?

options.text: Similarity should be measured as distance in a psychological space recovered from how the animal treats pairs of tones, not in physical units.
options.why: Correct. Physical units tend to predict behavior poorly. A space recovered from the animal’s own behavior predicts it better.

options.text: Similarity should still be measured in physical units, since the octave is just a larger physical difference than it first appears to be.
options.why: The tones just below are physically closer by any measure of frequency. That is exactly why physical units fail to predict how the animal generalizes.

options.text: Similarity cannot be used for that animal at all, so the way it treats tones must be captured by a definition listing the octave as a defining feature.
options.why: The case shows that the space must change, not that similarity must be given up. Distance in a space recovered from behavior captures the octave.

options.text: Similarity should be measured from the average tone only, since only a prototype model can treat an octave as close to the tone that was trained.
options.why: Prototype and exemplar models face the same question about which space similarity is computed in. Neither handles the octave unless that space is right.

items.stem: Researchers want to build a similarity space for the way a dog treats ten different whistle sounds. How should they find the distances between the sounds?

options.text: Measure how far the dog treats each pair of whistles as the same, and place the sounds so that pairs the dog treats alike sit close together.
options.why: Correct. A psychological space is recovered from behavior itself, by measuring the extent to which the animal treats each pair of inputs as the same.

options.text: Measure the physical frequency of each whistle, and place the sounds so that pairs of whistles with nearby frequencies sit close together in the space.
options.why: Distance in physical units tends to predict behavior poorly. The space that predicts the dog’s behavior is recovered from that behavior.

options.text: Ask people to rate how similar each pair of whistles sounds, and assume the dog treats each pair the way the people do.
options.why: A space recovered from people’s judgments describes people. Species differ in which differences matter, so the dog’s space must come from the dog.

options.text: Count how many defining features each pair of whistles shares, and place the sounds so that pairs sharing more features sit closer.
options.why: Counting defining features belongs to the classical view. A psychological space is built from how the animal treats each pair of inputs.

items.stem: A new birdwatcher hears the songs of two kinds of warbler as nearly the same. After a season of learning which warbler is which, the birdwatcher hears the two songs as clearly different, though most other birdsongs sound no more different than before. How can that change be described in terms of the space the songs sit in?

options.text: Attention has stretched the space along the dimensions that separate the two warblers, so small differences along them became large distances.
options.why: Correct. Which dimensions count can itself be learned. When a task depends on one dimension, attention can stretch the space along it.

options.text: The whole space has been stretched evenly, so that every pair of birdsongs now sits further apart than the same pair of songs sat before the season.
options.why: An even stretch would make every pair of songs sound more different. Only the dimensions separating the warblers have changed.

options.text: A new prototype has been placed halfway between the two warbler songs, so that the two songs now fall on opposite sides of it.
options.why: Placing a prototype between two songs would not make them sound more different. The change is in the distances along particular dimensions.

options.text: The birdwatcher’s criterion for saying “different” has moved, so the same evidence now produces a “different” judgment more often.
options.why: Moving a criterion changes how often “different” is said, not how far apart the songs lie. The songs themselves now sit further apart.

items.stem: A dog is trained to come when it hears one particular whistle. In a short paragraph, explain why an exemplar model of the dog should compute similarity in a psychological space rather than in physical units, say how that space would be found, and describe how later training could change the space.
items.answer: Similarity measured in physical units, such as the frequencies of the whistles, tends not to predict how an animal generalizes, because the same physical difference can matter a great deal on one dimension and hardly at all on another. A better predictor is distance in a psychological space recovered from the dog’s own behavior, by measuring how far it treats each pair of whistles as the same and placing the whistles accordingly. That space can change with learning. If the dog is trained so that a difference along one dimension matters, attention can stretch the space along that dimension, so that small differences along it become large distances. For a nervous system, that would mean downstream neurons responding strongly along that dimension.
rubric: Says that similarity in physical units tends to predict behavior poorly.
Says the psychological space is recovered from how the animal treats pairs of inputs as the same.
Says attention can stretch the dimension that matters, turning small differences into large distances.
Gives the nervous-system reading: downstream neurons respond strongly along a stretched dimension.

items.stem: What is k-nearest-neighbor classification?

options.text: Assigning a new input to whichever category is most common among the k stored examples most similar to it, with k chosen in advance.
options.why: Correct. The classifier finds the k closest stored examples, such as 1, 5, or 15 of them, and takes the most common category among them.

options.text: Assigning a new input to whichever category has the largest summed similarity across every stored example, near or far.
options.why: Summing similarity over every stored example is an exemplar model. k-nearest-neighbor classification consults only the k closest.

options.text: Assigning a new input to whichever category’s average lies nearest, after the k most typical members are averaged.
options.why: Comparing with an average is a prototype model. k-nearest-neighbor classification counts categories among stored examples and averages nothing.

options.text: Assigning a new input to whichever side of a learned boundary it falls on, with the boundary placed k steps away from each category’s nearest member.
options.why: A learned boundary belongs to a decision-bound model. In k-nearest-neighbor classification the boundary follows from the stored examples.

items.stem: What is the name for a method that finds a fixed number of stored examples most similar to a new input, the number chosen in advance, and assigns the input to whichever category is most common among them?

options.text: k-nearest-neighbor classification.
options.why: Correct. k is the number chosen in advance, and the input goes to the most common category among the k most similar examples.

options.text: Exemplar.
options.why: An exemplar is one stored member, and an exemplar model sums similarity over every stored example, weighted by closeness.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a whole category. Counting categories among the closest stored examples is a different method.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning has units inhibit one another until one wins and moves toward the input. It sorts nothing by counting stored examples.

items.stem: A k-nearest-neighbor classifier with k = 5 sorts mushrooms into safe and poisonous. Among a new mushroom’s five nearest stored examples, three are safe and two are poisonous, although the two poisonous ones are much closer to it than any of the safe ones. What answer does the classifier give, and why?

options.text: Safe, because each of the five nearest examples gets one equal vote, however close it is, and safe has three of the five votes.
options.why: Correct. A k-nearest-neighbor classifier gives the k closest examples one equal vote each, and the rest no vote at all.

options.text: Poisonous, because the two closest examples outweigh the three further ones, since each example counts according to how close it is.
options.why: Weighting each example by its closeness is what an exemplar model does. A k-nearest-neighbor classifier gives the k closest equal votes.

options.text: Poisonous, because a k-nearest-neighbor classifier follows the single closest example and uses the other four only to break ties.
options.why: Following the single closest example is the special case k = 1. With k = 5, all five nearest examples vote, equally.

options.text: No answer at all, because the classifier needs every stored mushroom to vote before it can assign the new one to a category.
options.why: Hearing from every stored example is closer to an exemplar model. A k-nearest-neighbor classifier consults only the k closest.

items.stem: People rate a sparrow a better example of a bird than an ostrich. A student offers this as evidence that people categorize by prototypes rather than by stored exemplars. What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: Both models explain typicality, since a typical member is close to the prototype and also close to many stored examples.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is a fact any account must explain, but prototype and exemplar models both explain it, so it cannot tell them apart.

options.text: Typicality counts against both models, since it shows that people categorize by a definition in which each member belongs equally.
options.why: A definition makes every member equally good, so typicality is evidence against the classical view as a general account, not against these two models.

options.text: Typicality favors exemplar models instead, since stored examples alone can make one member closer to the others than another.
options.why: A typical member is close to the prototype too. Neither model has typicality to itself.

options.text: Typicality concerns ratings, not categorization, so it says nothing about how people sort things.
options.why: Typicality is a fact any account of categories has to explain. It simply fails to separate these two models, because both explain it.

items.stem: People classified the never-seen originals of two dot patterns nearly as well as the distortions they had studied, which first looked like strong support for prototypes. Why does an exemplar model predict the same result?

options.text: Each original sits in the middle of its own distortions, so it is similar to many of the stored distortions at once.
options.why: Correct. Summed similarity is high for an item close to many stored examples, and an original is close to all of its distortions.

options.text: Each original is stored as an exemplar during learning, since a model that keeps every member also keeps the pattern it was made from.
options.why: The originals were never shown, so an exemplar model cannot have stored them. It predicts the result from the distortions alone.

options.text: Each original is far from all of its distortions, so it falls into the right category by elimination.
options.why: An original is close to its distortions, not far from them. That closeness to many stored examples is what drives the prediction.

options.text: Each original is averaged into the stored examples once testing begins, which turns the exemplar model into a prototype model.
options.why: An exemplar model averages nothing. It predicts the result while staying an exemplar model, which is why the result does not settle which model is right.

items.stem: Typicality and the dot-pattern result both look at first like support for prototype models. In a short paragraph, explain why neither one can decide between prototype and exemplar models.
items.answer: A typical member of a category sits close to many other members, near the middle of the category. So it is close to the prototype, and it is also close to many stored examples, which means both models predict that it will count as a good member. In the dot-pattern study, people classified the undistorted originals, which they had never seen, nearly as well as the distortions they had studied. A prototype model predicts that, because an original is like the average of its distortions. But an exemplar model predicts it too, because each original sits in the middle of its distortions and is similar to many of them at once. In both cases the two models make the same prediction, so the result cannot tell them apart.
rubric: Says a typical member is close to the prototype and also to many stored examples.
Describes the dot-pattern result: never-seen originals classified nearly as well as studied distortions.
Explains the exemplar prediction: each original is similar to many of its distortions at once.
Concludes that the two models predict the same result in both cases, so neither result settles which model is right.

items.stem: Three pairs of categories are offered to a model that keeps exactly one prototype per category. Pairs A and B can each be divided by one straight line through the feature space; pair C cannot. Which pairs are ruled out, whatever prototypes the model ends up with?

options.text: Pair C alone, since a model with one prototype per category shares a single unit’s limit to linearly separable categories.
options.why: Correct. A one-prototype model draws a straight boundary, so it can only sort categories that one straight line can divide, and pair C is not one of them.

options.text: No pair at all, since a prototype can be placed anywhere in the feature space and so can come to fit any category, given enough training on its members.
options.why: Placing a prototype anywhere still yields a straight boundary halfway between two prototypes. No placement sorts a pair one line cannot divide.

options.text: Pairs A and B, since categories that one straight line can divide are exactly the ones that a single summary cannot hold together.
options.why: This reverses the limit. A summary is what fails on categories no line divides; with one prototype each, a pair like C can even average to the same point.

options.text: All three pairs, since a prototype model has no boundary of its own and sorts only by how typical each member is.
options.why: A nearest-prototype model does draw a boundary, a straight one halfway between its prototypes. Its limit rules out only categories that no straight line can divide.

items.stem: A prototype model is built so that whenever an item does not fit any of its existing prototypes well, it adds a new prototype for that item’s category. Is this model still limited to linearly separable categories?

options.text: No; models that keep several prototypes for each category are not limited to straight lines, so the one-prototype limit does not apply.
options.why: Correct. The limit to linearly separable categories belongs to models with one prototype per category, not to prototype models as a family.

options.text: Yes; every prototype model is limited to a straight line halfway between its prototypes, however many it keeps for each category.
options.why: That holds for one prototype per category. Models that keep several prototypes for each category are not limited to straight lines.

options.text: Yes; adding prototypes changes where the line runs but cannot change its shape, just as weighting the features only tilts the line.
options.why: Weighting does only tilt a one-prototype boundary, but adding prototypes is a different change. It lets the boundary bend around the categories.

options.text: No; adding prototypes turns the model into a decision-bound model, which stores its boundary rather than any summary of members.
options.why: The model still stores summaries, only more of them. It escapes the limit by keeping several prototypes, not by storing a boundary.

items.stem: For the fruit where either smell alone means ripe fruit and both together mean rot, the two categories average to the same point. Why can an exemplar model still sort a new input that matches the “smell A only” case?

options.text: It keeps the cases themselves, so an input matching “smell A only” is close to a stored ripe case, whatever the average says.
options.why: Correct. An exemplar model has no one-prototype limit, because it compares a new input with the stored cases rather than with an average.

options.text: It stores a curved boundary learned directly from the four cases, so the average plays no part in where an input falls.
options.why: A stored boundary belongs to a decision-bound model. An exemplar model stores the cases, and its boundary follows from them.

options.text: It adds a third input for the product of the two smells, which moves the rotting case away from the other three cases.
options.why: A product input would also solve the problem, but that is a change of features, not what an exemplar model does. It keeps the cases.

options.text: It weights smell A more heavily than smell B, which tilts the line between the averages until the cases fall on the right sides.
options.why: Weighting tilts a line between averages, but here the averages are one point, and no straight line sorts the cases anyway.

items.stem: If the three families draw boundaries of different shapes in principle, why has it been hard in practice to tell which one people use?

options.text: Each family contains many specific models, and models from separate families can end up drawing much the same boundary between categories.
options.why: Correct. Two models that draw the same boundary will be hard to tell apart from behavior, even when they work very differently inside.

options.text: People’s categories tend to be linearly separable, so the families draw the same straight line for most categories people learn.
options.why: People can learn categories that no straight line divides, including one with the shape of exclusive or. The difficulty lies elsewhere.

options.text: The families cannot be tested on animals, so the evidence comes from people’s typicality ratings, which each family explains.
options.why: Experiments have tested both human and animal learning. Typicality does fail to separate the models, but it is not the only evidence.

options.text: The families make no predictions about behavior at all, since they describe only what is stored and not how an input is sorted.
options.why: Each family says how an input is sorted, which is why each draws a boundary. The trouble is that different models can draw the same one.

items.stem: Two models of how a bee sorts flowers work very differently inside. One stores a single summary of each kind of flower; the other is a single unit with a learned straight boundary. Both end up drawing the same straight line between rewarding and unrewarding flowers. What follows?

options.text: Data on the bee’s choices cannot easily separate the two models, since models that draw the same boundary sort every flower the same way.
options.why: Correct. Two models that draw the same boundary will be hard to tell apart from behavior, however differently they work inside.

options.text: Data on the bee’s choices will favor the summary model, since storing a summary of each kind of flower is the more natural thing for a bee to do.
options.why: Which procedure seems more natural is not evidence. With the same boundary, the bee’s choices fit both models equally well.

options.text: Data on the bee’s choices will favor the single unit, since only a unit with a learned line can sort flowers along a straight boundary.
options.why: A nearest-prototype model also draws a straight boundary. That shared line is exactly why behavior cannot separate the two.

options.text: Data on the bee’s choices can separate the models at once, by checking whether the bee treats some flowers as better examples than others.
options.why: Graded typicality is something several different models explain. It does not separate two models that draw the same boundary.

items.stem: A classmate says, “The experiments are in: people categorize by exemplars, not prototypes”. How does that claim compare with the state of the evidence?

options.text: It overstates it; decades of work have produced no agreement on which family describes people, and many researchers think people use more than one.
options.why: Correct. The pitted comparisons mostly, but not always, favored exemplars, and that is far from a settled answer.

options.text: It is right; once experiments pitted the two models against each other, every result favored exemplar models over prototype models.
options.why: Not every result favored exemplars; the comparisons did so mostly, but not always. And no agreement has emerged about which family describes people.

options.text: It is backward; the experiments favored prototypes, since people classified never-seen originals nearly as well as the distorted items they had studied.
options.why: An exemplar model predicts the dot-pattern result too, so it does not favor prototypes. The later comparisons mostly favored exemplars.

options.text: It is beside the point; no experiment can bear on the question, since the two families draw exactly the same boundary in every case.
options.why: The families draw different boundaries in principle, and experiments were built to separate them. The trouble is that the results have not settled it.

items.stem: When the chapter speaks of a network, what does it mean?

options.text: An artificial neural network: a model built from units and weighted connections of the kind in Module 4, run on a computer.
options.why: Correct. A network here always means an artificial one, a model that describes an algorithm.

options.text: A set of real neurons wired together in a brain region, together with the synapses that carry signals from one of those neurons to the next.
options.why: Real neurons wired together are a circuit or a region. A network, as the term is used here, is an artificial neural network run on a computer.

options.text: Any model of categorization at all, including the prototype and exemplar models that psychologists have proposed.
options.why: Prototype and exemplar models are not networks as such. A network is a model built from units and weighted connections.

options.text: A diagram of the brain’s areas and the pathways between them, drawn from measurements of where signals travel in tissue.
options.why: A map of brain areas describes tissue. A network, as the term is used here, is a model of units and weighted connections run on a computer.

items.stem: Put into network terms, in the chapter’s own translation rather than the psychologists’, what does an exemplar model behave like?

options.text: A layer of units between the input and the decision, one unit for each stored example, each responding to inputs close to its own example.
options.why: Correct. Each example unit responds to inputs near its example, which is the network version of summing similarity to stored members.

options.text: A single unit whose weights are set to the average of the stored examples, firing whenever an input is close enough to that average.
options.why: A unit tuned to an average is closer to a one-prototype model. An exemplar model keeps one unit for every stored example.

options.text: A layer of units wired at random and never trained, each combining a random handful of the inputs, with learning only at the connections to the output.
options.why: A random, untrained layer is the original perceptron’s middle layer. The exemplar layer has one unit tuned to each stored example.

options.text: A sheet of units that inhibit one another until one wins, with the winning unit moving its weights a little toward the input.
options.why: That is competitive learning. The exemplar layer is not a competition; every example unit responds according to how close an input is.

items.stem: A plant is safe to eat when its leaves are either spotted or ridged, but not both, and unsafe when they are both or neither. In a short paragraph, explain why a model that keeps one prototype for each category cannot learn to sort these plants, and why an exemplar model can.
items.answer: This is exclusive or. Picture the four cases in a feature space with one axis for spots and one for ridges. The two safe cases sit at opposite corners, so their average is the center of the square. The two unsafe cases sit at the other two corners, and their average is the same point. Two categories with the same prototype cannot be told apart by their prototypes, so a one-prototype model fails. More generally, a model with one prototype per category draws a straight boundary and can only sort categories that are linearly separable, and these are not. An exemplar model keeps the cases themselves. A new plant with spots and no ridges is close to the stored safe case with spots only, whatever the average says, so its boundary can curve to follow the stored cases.
rubric: Identifies the pattern as exclusive or, or as not linearly separable.
Says each category’s cases lie at opposite corners, so both prototypes land at the same central point.
Says a model with one prototype per category is limited to linearly separable categories.
Says an exemplar model keeps the cases, so a new input is close to a stored case of the right category.

items.stem: In principle, the three families of categorization model look easy to compare. In a short paragraph, explain why, and then give the reasons that telling them apart has been hard in practice, and say where the question stands.
items.answer: In principle the three families are different algorithms that draw boundaries of different shapes: the simplest prototype model a straight line, an exemplar model a curve that follows the stored examples, and a decision-bound model whatever boundary it has learned. That makes them look easy to compare. In practice it has been hard. Each family contains many specific models, and some prototype models keep several prototypes per category, so they are not limited to straight lines. It has been argued that for any prototype model an exemplar model could be built that behaves the same way, and the reverse. And two models that draw the same boundary will be hard to tell apart from behavior, even when they work very differently inside. Decades of experiments have produced no agreement about which family best describes people, and many researchers now think people use more than one.
rubric: States the in-principle picture: the families draw boundaries of different shapes.
Names at least one practical difficulty: many models per family, or prototype models with several prototypes.
Names the argued mimicry between families, or that models drawing the same boundary are hard to tell apart from behavior.
Says there is no agreement, without keying either family as the winner.
Mentions that many researchers think people use more than one.

pools.title: Hidden Layers, and Who Sets Their Weights

items.stem: What is a hidden layer?

options.text: A layer of units between a network’s input and its output, driven directly by neither the world nor the response.
options.why: Correct. Hidden units are not driven directly by the world, and their activity does not directly drive behavior. What they stand for depends on their weights.

options.text: A layer of units driven directly by the world, with one unit for each kind of receptor, feeding the rest of the network.
options.why: That describes a network’s input layer. A hidden layer sits between the input and the output, and the world does not drive its units directly.

options.text: A layer of units whose activity drives the response directly, with one unit for each answer the network can give.
options.why: That describes a network’s output layer. A hidden layer’s activity reaches behavior only through the output, never directly.

options.text: A layer of units hidden from the experimenter, whose activity cannot be recorded and so has to be inferred from the output.
options.why: “Hidden” does not mean unobservable; every unit’s activity in a network can be read. Hidden units are the ones between input and output, driven directly by neither the world nor the response.

items.stem: What is the name for a set of units between a network’s input and its output, driven directly by neither the world nor the response, whose units come to stand for combinations of the inputs?

options.text: A hidden layer.
options.why: Correct. Hidden units sit between input and output, and what they stand for depends on their weights.

options.text: A distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation is a kind of code, a pattern of activity across many units. Hidden units may carry one, but the set of units between input and output is a hidden layer.

options.text: A topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement in which neighboring cells handle neighboring points in the world. It names a layout, not a position between input and output.

options.text: A feature space.
options.why: A feature space is a space with one axis per feature, in which each input is a point. It describes inputs, not a set of units inside a network.

items.stem: A network computes exclusive or for the fruit. Its first hidden unit computes OR, its second computes NOT-AND, and its output unit computes AND over the two hidden units. What happens when both smells are present, meaning the fruit is rotting?

options.text: The OR unit fires and the NOT-AND unit is silent, so the output unit stays silent.
options.why: Correct. With both smells present, OR fires and NOT-AND does not, since NOT-AND fires unless both are present. AND needs both hidden units, so the output is silent.

options.text: Both hidden units fire, since each smell drives each hidden unit, so the output unit fires.
options.why: NOT-AND fires unless both smells are present, so here it is silent. That silence is exactly what keeps the output off for rotting fruit.

options.text: Neither hidden unit fires, since the two smells cancel out, so the output unit stays silent.
options.why: The output is silent, but not for this reason. OR fires whenever either smell is present, including when both are.

options.text: The OR unit is silent and the NOT-AND unit fires, so the output unit stays silent.
options.why: That swaps the two hidden units. OR fires when either smell is present, and NOT-AND is the one that falls silent when both are.

items.stem: A songbird should answer a call that has either a trill or a rising note, but not both, and ignore calls with neither. A network built to signal “answer” has two hidden units feeding an output unit that computes AND. Which pair of hidden units would make the network correct?

options.text: One that fires when either feature is present, and one that fires unless both are present.
options.why: Correct. That is OR and NOT-AND. Both fire only when exactly one feature is present, so AND over them gives exclusive or.

options.text: One that fires only when both features are present, and one that fires only when neither is present.
options.why: Those two units never fire together, so an AND output over them would never fire at all.

options.text: One that fires when the trill is present, and one that fires when the rising note is present.
options.why: Copying the two inputs gives the output nothing new. AND over them fires only when both features are present, which is the case to ignore.

options.text: One that fires when either feature is present, and one that fires only when both are present.
options.why: OR and AND fire together only when both features are present, so the output would answer exactly the wrong calls.

items.stem: A student says the logical, boundary, and geometric readings of the exclusive-or network are rival accounts of how it works, so at most one can be right. What does the chapter say about the three readings?

options.text: They describe one fact: the hidden layer re-represents the input, so that the last step, one straight line, is easy.
options.why: Correct. Composed truth tables, a band between two lines, and remapped points are three descriptions of the same re-representation.

options.text: The logical reading is the right one, since the units compute truth tables, and the other two are loose pictures of it.
options.why: Each reading is exact in its own terms, and none is privileged. All three describe the hidden layer re-representing the input.

options.text: The geometric reading is the right one, since only it shows the ripe cases landing on one point, and the other two are mistaken.
options.why: The geometric reading is one description among three, and the other two are not mistaken. All three describe one re-representation.

options.text: The boundary reading is the right one for the hidden units, and the logical reading is the right one for the output unit.
options.why: The readings are not divided among units. Each describes the whole network, and all three describe one fact.

items.stem: A network for the fruit has two hidden units, one computing OR and one computing NOT-AND, and an output unit computing AND over them. In a short paragraph, work through what the network does with each of the four combinations of the two smells, and say what the hidden layer has done that makes the last step easy.
items.answer: With neither smell present, the OR unit is silent and the NOT-AND unit fires, so the AND output is silent: no fruit. With smell A alone, or smell B alone, the OR unit fires and so does the NOT-AND unit, so the output fires: ripe fruit. With both smells present, the OR unit fires but the NOT-AND unit is silent, so the output is silent: rotting fruit. The hidden layer has re-represented the input. In the space of hidden-unit activity, the two ripe cases land on the same point, so the output needs only one straight line, AND, to separate them from the other two.
rubric: Gets neither smell right: OR silent, NOT-AND fires, output silent.
Gets either smell alone right: both hidden units fire, output fires.
Gets both smells right: OR fires, NOT-AND silent, output silent.
Says the hidden layer re-represents the input, so that a single unit or a single straight line can do the last step.

items.stem: What was true of the original perceptron’s middle layer?

options.text: It was wired at random and never trained, and learning happened only at the output.
options.why: Correct. The perceptron already had a layer between input and output. Only the connections to the output were adjusted.

options.text: It did not exist, since the perceptron connected its inputs straight to its output unit.
options.why: A common belief, but the perceptron did have a middle layer. What it lacked was any training of that layer.

options.text: It was trained by passing errors back from the output, though too slowly to be of much use.
options.why: Passing errors back is backpropagation, which came later. The perceptron’s middle layer was never trained at all.

options.text: It was trained by competition, each middle unit moving its weights toward the inputs it won.
options.why: Competition is a third way to set hidden weights. The perceptron’s middle layer was fixed at random.

items.stem: A network that sorts spoken vowels gives a wrong answer. The delta rule can adjust the weights into its output units. Why can the same rule not be applied directly to its hidden units?

options.text: The rule needs each unit’s correct output, and no one knows what a hidden unit’s correct output should be.
options.why: Correct. The output has a correct answer to compare against. A hidden unit has none, which is exactly the problem training a hidden layer runs into.

options.text: Hidden units have no adjustable weights of their own, so there is nothing for the rule to change.
options.why: Hidden units do have weights, and what they stand for depends on those weights. The trouble is that there is no correct output to compare them with.

options.text: Hidden units are driven directly by the sounds, so their activity is fixed by the input and cannot be learned.
options.why: Hidden units are driven directly by neither the world nor the response. Their weights can change; the difficulty is knowing in which direction.

options.text: Hidden units fire too rarely for their output to be compared with anything, so their errors cannot be measured.
options.why: How often a hidden unit fires is not the obstacle. Even a unit that fires often has no known correct output to compare against.

items.stem: How does structural credit assignment differ from the credit assignment problem of Module 5?

options.text: Module 5’s problem is in time, which action caused a later outcome; the structural one is in space, which connections deep inside caused an output error.
options.why: Correct. The structural problem is the same question asked about position inside a network rather than about when something happened.

options.text: Module 5’s problem is in space, which connections deep inside caused an output error; the structural one is in time, which earlier action caused a later outcome.
options.why: That reverses them. Module 5’s credit assignment concerns outcomes that arrive later; the structural version concerns connections deep inside a network.

options.text: Module 5’s problem concerns rewards that arrive at once; the structural one concerns punishments that arrive only after a long and variable delay.
options.why: Neither problem is defined by reward versus punishment. One is about time, the other about where inside a network the responsible connections are.

options.text: Module 5’s problem concerns a single unit with no hidden layer; the structural one concerns whole animals choosing among actions.
options.why: That has it backward as well. Choosing among actions over time is Module 5’s problem; connections inside a network are the structural one.

items.stem: What is structural credit assignment?

options.text: Working out which connections inside a network were responsible for an error at its output.
options.why: Correct. It is credit assignment in space rather than in time: when the output is wrong, which connections deep inside were responsible.

options.text: Working out which of several earlier actions was responsible for an outcome that arrived later.
options.why: That is credit assignment in time, the version in Module 5. The structural version asks about connections inside a network.

options.text: Passing each output’s error backward through the network to compute an error for every hidden unit.
options.why: That is backpropagation, one answer to structural credit assignment. The term itself names the problem, not the answer.

options.text: Letting units compete for each input so that only the winner’s connections are credited and changed.
options.why: That is competitive learning, another answer to the problem. Structural credit assignment names the problem those answers address.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a rule like the delta rule can train a network’s output units but not, by itself, its hidden units, and say how backpropagation gets around the difficulty.
items.answer: The delta rule compares a unit’s output with the correct answer and adjusts its weights to make the correct answer more likely. An output unit has a correct answer, so the comparison can be made. A hidden unit does not: no one knows what each hidden unit’s correct output should be. So when the output is wrong, there is the problem of working out which connections deep inside the network were responsible, which is structural credit assignment. Backpropagation answers it by computing each hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through, so that the delta rule’s kind of update can be applied at every layer.
rubric: Says the delta rule compares a unit’s output with a correct answer.
Says no one knows the correct output for a hidden unit.
Names or describes structural credit assignment: which connections deep inside the network were responsible for the output’s error.
Says backpropagation computes a hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections.

items.stem: What is backpropagation?

options.text: An extension of the delta rule to networks with hidden layers, computing each hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds.
options.why: Correct. The errors are passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through.

options.text: A way of setting hidden weights that needs no teacher, in which units compete for each input and only the winner moves its weights toward it.
options.why: That is competitive learning. Backpropagation depends on an error measured against a target.

options.text: A way of leaving hidden weights fixed at random, in which only the connections from the hidden layer to the output are trained.
options.why: That is the perceptron’s answer, fixed random wiring with a trained output. Backpropagation changes every weight in the network.

options.text: A way of storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, in which activity runs around a circuit’s own connections. Backpropagation passes errors back from outputs to hidden units.

items.stem: What is the name for an extension of the delta rule to networks with hidden layers, in which each hidden unit’s error is computed from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through?

options.text: Backpropagation.
options.why: Correct. It is one of the three broad answers to structural credit assignment, and it changes every weight in the network.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning needs no teacher and no error. Only the winning unit moves its weights, toward the input.

options.text: Structural credit assignment.
options.why: Structural credit assignment is the problem backpropagation answers: which connections inside a network were responsible for an error.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association stores patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells. It passes no errors back from an output.

items.stem: During backpropagation, a hidden unit is completely silent on one training example, although the output unit it feeds has a large error. On that example, what happens to the connection from the silent hidden unit to the output unit?

options.text: It does not change, because each change is proportional to the receiving unit’s error times the sending unit’s activity, which is zero.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation keeps the delta rule’s update: error at the receiving unit times activity of the sending unit. A silent sender contributed nothing, so its connection is not changed on that example.

options.text: It changes the most of any connection in the network on that example, since a silent hidden unit is the likeliest cause of a large error at the output.
options.why: A silent sending unit contributed nothing to the output on that example. Under the delta rule’s update, its connection does not change.

options.text: It changes by the full size of the output’s error, since a connection’s change depends only on the error at the receiving unit.
options.why: The error at the receiving unit is only one factor. It is multiplied by the sending unit’s activity, and here that activity is zero.

options.text: It is rewired at random, since backpropagation replaces the connections of hidden units that fail to respond.
options.why: Backpropagation never rewires anything at random. Random wiring belongs to the perceptron’s middle layer, which is set once and never changed; backpropagation adjusts weights by error times activity.

items.stem: An engineer wants a network to learn which combinations of sensor readings signal that a bridge is unsafe, without listing those combinations in advance. If the network is trained by backpropagation, what is the method’s strength, and what does it require?

options.text: Training finds the combinations the task needs, but every output needs a target to compare against.
options.why: Correct. That is backpropagation’s strength and its cost: it finds the combinations the task needs, and every output needs a target.

options.text: Training finds clusters of readings that overlap, with no target, but they may not be the clusters that matter for safety.
options.why: That is the strength and limit of competitive learning, which needs no teacher and finds overlap rather than what the task needs.

options.text: No training of the hidden layer is needed, but it takes a great many units and no needed combination is guaranteed.
options.why: That describes fixed random wiring with a trained output. Backpropagation trains the hidden layer too.

options.text: Training finds the combinations the task needs, and its outputs need no target, since the readings alone are enough.
options.why: Backpropagation does find the needed combinations, but not from readings alone. Every output needs a target to compare against, here whether the bridge was unsafe.

items.stem: A network is given hours of recorded birdsong, with the task of predicting each next note. No one labels anything. Can backpropagation train this network, and if so, where do the targets come from?

options.text: Yes; the target for each prediction is the next note itself, as in the prediction learning of Module 5.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation needs a target for every output, but the target need not come from a teacher. The world’s next input supplies it.

options.text: No; backpropagation needs a teacher to label every example, so unlabeled recordings cannot supply any targets.
options.why: Every output needs a target, but a teacher is only one source. In prediction learning, the next input is the target.

options.text: Yes; the network’s output units compete for each note, and the winner’s response serves as the target for the rest.
options.why: Competition sets weights with no target at all, and it is a different answer. In prediction learning, the target is the next note.

options.text: No; without labels only the connections to the output can be trained, as in the perceptron’s random middle layer.
options.why: The perceptron trains only its output connections by design, not for lack of labels. Prediction supplies targets for backpropagation.

items.stem: An engineer builds a network whose 5,000 middle units each receive a random handful of its 20 inputs. Those connections are never changed; only the connections from the middle units to the output are trained. Which answer to who sets the hidden weights is this?

options.text: Nothing sets them: the middle layer stays as it was first wired, and only the output connections are trained.
options.why: Correct. That is the original perceptron’s answer, a large middle layer wired at random and never trained.

options.text: Backpropagation: the output’s error is passed back through the connections, so the middle units’ weights are trained too.
options.why: Backpropagation would change every weight, including those into the middle units. Here they never change.

options.text: Competitive learning: the middle units compete for each input, and each winner moves a little toward it.
options.why: In competitive learning the winner’s weights change. Here the middle layer’s weights never change at all.

options.text: Hand-setting: the engineer chose each middle unit’s handful of inputs to suit the task in advance.
options.why: The middle units’ inputs were chosen at random, not to suit the task. No one arranged which combinations they respond to.

items.stem: What is dimensionality expansion?

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units, which makes it likelier that one straight boundary can separate the cases that matter.
options.why: Correct. A straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions than in a space with few.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart more easily than it could tell the original inputs apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which is about overlap between inputs. Dimensionality expansion is about the number of units an input is spread across.

options.text: Activity in which only a small proportion of the units are strongly active for any one input, whatever the number of units.
options.why: That is sparse coding, which works well alongside expansion. Dimensionality expansion is the spreading itself, onto many more units.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, which builds in tolerance to small shifts. Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units.

items.stem: A company wants a device that sorts scent mixtures by combinations of chemicals that no single sensor reports. Its engineers propose a very large middle layer wired at random and never trained, with only the connections to the output trained. In a short paragraph, explain why this design might work, what kind of activity in the middle layer would help, and what its weaknesses are.
items.answer: With many more middle units than sensors, each combining a random handful of sensor readings, some units are likely to respond to the combinations that matter without anyone arranging it. Spreading the input across many more units is dimensionality expansion, and a straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions than in a space with few, so a single trained output layer may be enough. The expansion works best if the code is sparse, with only a few middle units active for any one input. The weaknesses are that it takes a great many units, and nothing guarantees that the combinations the task needs will be among the random ones.
rubric: Says random units each combine a handful of inputs, so useful combinations are likely to turn up by chance.
Names dimensionality expansion, or describes spreading the input across many more units.
Says a straight boundary can separate more sets of points in a space of many dimensions than of few.
Says the expansion works best with sparse activity, only a few units active for any one input.
Names a weakness: it needs a great many units, or there is no guarantee the needed combinations appear.

items.stem: What is the cost of backpropagation, and what is the cost of fixed random wiring with a trained output?

options.text: Backpropagation needs a target for every output; random wiring needs a great many units, with no guarantee the needed combinations appear.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation finds the needed combinations but must have targets. Random wiring needs no training of the hidden layer but may not contain what the task needs.

options.text: Backpropagation needs a great many units, with no guarantee the needed combinations appear; random wiring needs a target for every one of its outputs.
options.why: That swaps the two costs. Random wiring is the one that needs many units and offers no guarantee; backpropagation is the one that needs targets.

options.text: Backpropagation finds only how the inputs overlap, not what the task needs; random wiring needs a teacher for every hidden unit.
options.why: Finding overlap rather than what the task needs is the limit of competitive learning. Random wiring never trains its hidden units at all.

options.text: Backpropagation trains only the connections to the output; random wiring changes every weight in the network on each example.
options.why: That reverses which weights change. Backpropagation changes every weight; random wiring changes only the connections to the output.

items.stem: What is competitive learning?

options.text: Learning in which units receiving the same input inhibit one another until one wins, and only the winner moves its weights toward the input.
options.why: Correct. It needs no teacher, and the winner’s step toward the input is a Hebbian one, kept in check because only the winner learns.

options.text: Learning in which each hidden unit’s error is computed from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through those very same connections.
options.why: That is backpropagation, which needs a target for every output. Competitive learning needs no teacher.

options.text: Learning in which a large middle layer is wired at random, and only the connections from that layer to the output are adjusted.
options.why: That is fixed random wiring with a trained output, the perceptron’s answer. In competitive learning, the winning unit’s own weights change.

options.text: Learning in which the connections among a circuit’s active cells are strengthened, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, used for pattern completion. Competitive learning moves only a winning unit’s weights toward the input.

items.stem: Several units all receive the same input from a microphone. For each sound, the units inhibit one another until one is left active, and then a Hebbian step moves weights a little toward the sound. What keeps that Hebbian step in check?

options.text: Only the winning unit moves its weights, and only by a small step toward each input; the other units do not change.
options.why: Correct. A Hebbian step strengthens what is active together. Limiting it to the single winner keeps it in check.

options.text: An error measured against a target pulls each unit’s weights back whenever they move too far.
options.why: No target or error is involved; competitive learning needs no teacher. The check comes from only the winner learning.

options.text: The weights into these units are fixed at random, so that only the connections to an output can change.
options.why: Fixed random weights are a different answer. Here the winner’s own weights do change, and only the winner’s.

options.text: Every unit moves toward each sound, but by an amount scaled by how much that unit’s output would change with its input.
options.why: Scaling by how much a unit’s output would change is part of backpropagation. In competition, the losing units do not move at all.

items.stem: What is a topographic map?

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so the tissue’s layout mirrors what it represents.
options.why: Correct. Competitive learning can produce one from experience alone, when the winner’s neighbors also move toward each input.

options.text: A space with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point and inputs that are alike land close together in it.
options.why: That is a feature space, a description of inputs. A topographic map is a layout of cells in tissue.

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes one cell’s activity, together with the kind of stimulus that changes it.
options.why: That is a receptive field, which belongs to a single cell. A topographic map is how many cells are laid out relative to one another.

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things.
options.why: That is a distributed representation, which says nothing about where cells sit. A topographic map concerns the layout of the cells.

items.stem: A competitive network is trained on recordings of calls from two frog species, one toxic to a predator and one safe to eat. The recordings differ most in loudness, which depends on how far away each frog was, not on its species. What is the risk?

options.text: The units may form clusters by loudness, since competition finds how inputs overlap, which is not always what the animal needs.
options.why: Correct. Competition finds the structure in how inputs overlap. Here that structure is distance, and the species, which matters, may go unrepresented.

options.text: The units cannot form any clusters, by loudness or by species, since competitive learning needs a label telling it which species each call came from.
options.why: Competitive learning needs no teacher or label. It will form clusters; the risk is that they follow loudness rather than species.

options.text: The units are certain to form clusters by species, since competition always finds the structure that matters for survival.
options.why: Competition finds how inputs overlap, whatever matters. When loudness dominates the overlap, the clusters may follow loudness.

options.text: The units will each respond to every call equally, since only the winner learns and so no unit wins often enough.
options.why: Only the winner learns, but over many inputs each unit wins for some calls and settles at a cluster’s center. The risk is which clusters form.

items.stem: On a single training example, which weights change under each of the three answers to who sets a hidden layer’s weights?

options.text: Error-driven learning changes every weight; random wiring changes only the hidden-to-output connections; competition changes only the winner’s.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation reaches every layer, the perceptron’s answer touches only the output connections, and competition moves only the winning unit.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes only the hidden-to-output connections; random wiring changes every weight; competition changes only the winner’s.
options.why: That swaps the first two. Error-driven learning passes the error back through every layer, and random wiring never changes its middle layer.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes every weight; random wiring changes only the winner’s; competition changes only the hidden-to-output connections.
options.why: That swaps the last two. Random wiring trains only the output connections, and competition moves only the winning unit’s weights.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes only the winner’s weights; random wiring changes every weight; competition changes only the hidden-to-output connections.
options.why: None of the three is matched correctly. Error-driven learning changes every weight, random wiring only the output connections, and competition only the winner.

items.stem: What is a localist representation?

options.text: A code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which unit is active is itself the information.
options.why: Correct. It takes Module 3’s point all the way: part of a spike’s meaning lies in which cell fired it.

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, each unit taking part in many things.
options.why: That is a distributed representation, the other broad possibility for what a hidden unit stands for.

options.text: A code in which only a small proportion of the units are strongly active at any one moment.
options.why: That is sparse coding. A localist code is defined by each thing having its own unit, not by how many units are active.

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring units handle neighboring points in the world, mirroring its layout.
options.why: That is a topographic map, which concerns where cells sit. A localist code concerns whether each thing has a unit of its own.

items.stem: What is a distributed representation?

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things.
options.why: Correct. Because similar things share active units, a distributed code makes them look similar without extra work.

options.text: A code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which one unit is active is itself all of the information carried.
options.why: That is a localist representation. In a distributed code, no single unit stands for a thing.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, so that a straight boundary separates more cases.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion, which is about the number of units. A distributed code is about how each thing is represented across them.

options.text: A layer of units between a network’s input and its output, whose units come to stand for various combinations of all the inputs.
options.why: That is a hidden layer. A hidden layer’s units may carry a distributed code, but the code and the layer are different things.

items.stem: What is the name for a code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things?

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: Correct. Such codes degrade gracefully and pack many patterns into few units.

options.text: Localist representation.
options.why: A localist representation gives each thing its own unit, the opposite arrangement.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units. It names the spreading, not a code in which each unit serves many things.

options.text: Sparse coding.
options.why: Sparse coding is about how few units are active at once. The code described is defined by each unit serving many things.

items.stem: Every spike is the same size, so part of a spike’s meaning lies in which cell fired it. How does a localist code relate to that point?

options.text: It takes the point all the way: each thing has its own unit, so which unit is active becomes the whole of the information.
options.why: Correct. In a localist code, knowing which unit fired is knowing what is represented.

options.text: It sets the point aside: since spikes are all one size, a localist code carries its information in how many spikes there are.
options.why: Counting spikes is not what makes a code localist. A localist code rests on which unit is active.

options.text: It reverses the point: a localist code spreads each thing’s meaning across many cells, so no one cell matters.
options.why: Spreading each thing across many cells is a distributed code. A localist code puts each thing in its own unit.

options.text: It depends on the point being false: a localist code needs spikes of different sizes to tell its things apart.
options.why: A localist code works because the identity of the cell carries the meaning. It needs no difference in spike size.

items.stem: In one network, a sparrow and a finch are represented by patterns that share many active units, while a sparrow and a trout share few. What is learned about sparrows carries over to finches far more than to trout, with no extra mechanism added. Which property of the code explains this?

options.text: In a distributed code similar things share active units, so they look similar without any extra work.
options.why: Correct. That is one strength of distributed codes: similarity comes for free from the overlap between patterns.

options.text: In a localist code each animal has its own unit, so what is learned about one unit spreads to its neighbors.
options.why: In a localist code each animal’s unit is separate, which keeps things cleanly apart. Overlapping patterns are what carry similarity.

options.text: In a sparse code few units are active, so the sparrow and the trout share too few for learning to reach the trout.
options.why: Sparseness is about how many units are active, and it would not explain the carrying over to finches. Shared active units do.

options.text: In a topographic map the sparrow and finch units sit side by side, so learning about one spills onto the other with no extra work.
options.why: Nothing in the description places units side by side; the animals are patterns across units. Shared active units carry the similarity.

items.stem: Two networks each represent 200 words with 200 units. In the first, each word has a unit of its own; in the second, each word is a pattern across many of the 200 units. Ten units are destroyed in each network. What is the likeliest result?

options.text: The first loses about ten words outright; the second still represents every word, each a little less clearly.
options.why: Correct. In a localist code each word is its own unit, so losing a unit loses the word it stood for. A distributed code degrades gracefully: each word is spread across many units, and losing ten of 200 blurs every word a little rather than removing any.

options.text: The first still represents every word, each a little less clearly; the second loses about ten words outright.
options.why: That reverses the two codes. Losing a unit in a localist code loses its word; a distributed code degrades gracefully.

options.text: Both lose about ten words outright, since ten of the 200 units are gone from each network and each unit held one word.
options.why: Only in the first network does each unit hold one word. In the second, every unit takes part in many words.

options.text: Neither loses anything, since the remaining units in each network take over the work of the ones destroyed.
options.why: Nothing in either code moves the work of lost units to others. The second network degrades a little; the first loses words.

items.stem: Localist and distributed codes each have their own strengths. Which strength belongs to localist codes?

options.text: They are easy to read, and they keep things cleanly apart.
options.why: Correct. With one unit per thing, which unit is active can be read off directly, and different things never share units.

options.text: They make similar things look similar without any extra work.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes, where similar things share active units.

options.text: They degrade gracefully when some of their units are lost.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes, where each thing is spread across many units.

options.text: They pack many patterns into comparatively few units.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes. A localist code needs a unit for every thing.

items.stem: A student argues, “Distributed codes degrade gracefully and pack many patterns into few units, so brains must use distributed codes”. What does the chapter conclude about which code brains use?

options.text: Which kind brains use is still argued, whatever the strengths of each kind, and a mixture of the two is a serious option.
options.why: Correct. Each kind has strengths, and listing them does not settle what brains do. A mixture of the two is taken seriously.

options.text: Brains use distributed codes, as the student says, since graceful degradation is exactly what lost neurons would require.
options.why: The strengths are real, but strengths alone do not settle what brains do. Which code brains use is still argued.

options.text: Brains use localist codes, since a spike’s meaning lies partly in which cell fired it, and localist codes take that all the way.
options.why: That point about spikes motivates localist codes but does not settle the question. Which code brains use is still argued.
