options.text: Brains use neither kind, since hidden units exist only in artificial networks and have no counterpart among neurons.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter rules brains out of either code. Which they use, or whether they use a mixture of the two, is still argued.

pools.title: Shared Weights: Invariance, Interference, and Small Changes
pools.covers: reading §7.2.9, §7.2.10, §7.2.11 · lecture 7.2 slides stacking_layers_for_invariance, what_shared_weights_cost, fooled_and_far_from_home

items.stem: What is convolution, in a network that recognizes images?

options.text: Applying one small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in the input, so that a feature is found wherever it falls.
options.why: Correct. A detector for a short vertical edge, for example, is copied across the whole image, with the same weights in every copy.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood of positions, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, which usually follows convolution. Convolution is the copying of one detector to every position in the input.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, each of those units combining a random handful of the original inputs.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion, the random-wiring answer to who sets a hidden layer’s weights. Convolution copies one detector everywhere.

options.text: Letting units that receive the same input inhibit one another until one of them wins, so that only the winning unit moves its weights.
options.why: That is competitive learning, one way of setting weights. Convolution is about where a detector is applied, not about how its weights are set.

items.stem: What is the name for applying the same small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in an input, so that a feature is found wherever it falls?

options.text: Convolution.
options.why: Correct. Because the detector is the same everywhere, the feature can be found at any position, and the map of where it was found moves with the input.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling combines detections over a small neighborhood so that a small shift stops mattering. Copying one detector to every position is convolution.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units, often through random wiring. It does not copy one detector across positions.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning is a way of setting weights with no teacher, by letting units compete. It says nothing about copying a detector across positions.

items.stem: A network finds a short vertical edge in an image. The image is then shifted a little to the right. How do convolution and pooling each respond to the shift?

options.text: Convolution’s map of where the edge was found moves right with the image; pooling over a neighborhood gives the same output again.
options.why: Correct. Convolution alone makes the response move along with the input. Pooling is the step that makes a small shift stop changing the output.

options.text: Convolution’s map of where the edge was found stays where it was; pooling then moves its own output to the right to follow the image.
options.why: That reverses the two. The feature map moves with the input, and pooling is what holds the output steady across a small shift.

options.text: Both give exactly the same output as before, since each of them was built so that a shift in position makes no difference at all.
options.why: Convolution alone does not make the response unchanged by a shift; it makes the response move along. Pooling removes small shifts, and imperfectly.

options.text: Both move their output to the right along with the image, since neither of them does anything to remove the effect of a shift.
options.why: Convolution does move with the input, but pooling combines detections across a neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes its output.

items.stem: A network that watches a bird feeder applies a detector for the curve of a beak at every position in each camera frame, with the same weights everywhere. A sparrow hops from the left side of the frame to the right. What happens to the map of where the beak curve was found?

options.text: The detection turns up at a new place in the map, following the beak across to the far side of the frame as it hops.
options.why: Correct. Because the same detector is applied everywhere, the beak curve is found wherever it falls, and the map of where it was found shifts with the input.

options.text: The detection drops out of the map, since the detector was trained on beaks that sat on the left side of the frame.
options.why: That would be true of a detector placed at one position only. Convolution copies the detector to every position, so the curve is found anywhere.

options.text: The detection stays at the same place in the map, since copying the detector everywhere makes its output ignore position.
options.why: Copying the detector makes the feature findable anywhere, but the map still records where it was found, so the detection moves with the beak.

options.text: The detection spreads out across the whole map, since every copy of the detector now responds a little to the sparrow.
options.why: Each copy responds to the beak curve only where the curve falls within that copy’s own small region. The result is one detection, at the new position.

items.stem: What is pooling, in a network that recognizes images?

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input stops mattering to the output.
options.why: Correct. Pooling usually follows convolution. Convolution makes the response move with a shift, and pooling makes a small shift stop mattering.

options.text: Applying one small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in the input, so that a feature is found anywhere.
options.why: That is convolution. On its own it makes the response move with a shift; pooling is the step that makes a small shift stop mattering.

options.text: Keeping a single cell’s preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes in its position or its size.
options.why: That is tolerance, a property of cells in the ventral stream. Pooling is an operation in a network, which builds in tolerance to small shifts and nothing for size.

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can bring back the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, proposed for the piriform cortex. Pooling combines detections over a neighborhood so that small shifts do not matter.

items.stem: A network that sorts photographs of leaves has several rounds of convolution and pooling stacked on one another. Its first layer responds to short edges in small parts of the image. What should we expect of the units several rounds higher?

options.text: They respond to combinations of the features below, such as edges joined into a lobe, over a wider region, with more tolerance of small shifts.
options.why: Correct. Each round responds to combinations of the features in the layer below, over a wider region of the input, and tolerates small shifts and distortions a little more.

options.text: They respond to the same short edges as the first layer, over the same small region, since every layer copies one detector across positions.
options.why: Each layer does copy its detectors across positions, but the detectors differ from layer to layer. Higher layers combine lower features over wider regions.

options.text: They respond to any leaf at any size, angle, or distance, since stacking enough rounds of convolution and pooling builds in complete invariance.
options.why: Stacking adds tolerance to small shifts and distortions, a little at a time. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size, rotation, or viewpoint.

options.text: They respond to the whole image at once with no regard to its parts, since pooling throws away which features were present in the layer below.
options.why: Pooling gives up a little of exactly where a feature was, not whether it was there. Higher layers still respond to combinations of the features below.

items.stem: The bet built into a convolutional network is that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears. For which of these tasks is that bet least likely to be right?

options.text: Reading the temperature from photographs of a thermometer, where the top of the red column stands for a different temperature at each height.
options.why: Correct. Here the same feature, the top of the red column, means a different thing at each position in the image, so the bet that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears is wrong for this task.

options.text: Finding cracks in photographs of a concrete wall, where a crack is a crack whether it runs near the top or near the bottom.
options.why: A crack means the same thing anywhere in the photograph. This is a task where the convolutional bet is right, and when it is right it helps a network learn.

options.text: Reading handwritten zip-code digits from envelopes, where a 7 written a little to the left or to the right is still a 7.
options.why: This is the task of the digit-reading network, and there the bet was right: the network made fewer errors on unseen digits than a fully connected network with about as many weights.

options.text: Spotting ripe berries in photographs of a bush, where a red berry is ripe whether it hangs high or low on the branch.
options.why: A ripe berry is ripe wherever it hangs, so the feature means the same thing everywhere, and the convolutional bet helps.

items.stem: What is an inductive bias?

options.text: A tendency to find some things easier to learn than others, which is established before the learning itself begins.
options.why: Correct. It can come from an animal’s lineage or from what it has already learned, and in a convolutional network it is built into the wiring.

options.text: A tendency to fit the training examples so closely, accidents and all, that performance on new examples suffers.
options.why: That is overfitting, which happens during learning. An inductive bias is in place before learning begins, and when it is right it helps.

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape, found in networks trained on photographs.
options.why: That is texture bias, a tendency in how a trained network categorizes images. An inductive bias is a tendency in what is easier to learn, in place before the learning begins.

options.text: A tendency to respond less and less to a new input the more it differs from the input that the animal was trained on.
options.why: That describes a generalization gradient, a pattern in behavior measured after training. An inductive bias is set before learning begins.

items.stem: A network built with convolution and pooling is trained only on photographs of cats seen side-on at one size, and is then tested on new photographs. To which change in a cat does its architecture alone give it some tolerance?

options.text: The cat shifted a little to the left or right in the frame, though even that is handled imperfectly.
options.why: Correct. Convolution and pooling build in tolerance to one kind of change, a shift in position, and imperfectly.

options.text: The cat much closer to the camera, so that it fills twice as much of the frame as it did in training.
options.why: That is a change in size. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size.

options.text: The cat photographed upside down, so that every edge in the image is turned to a new orientation.
options.why: That is a rotation. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for rotation; networks mostly get it from training examples that include rotations.

options.text: The cat photographed from the front, so that the outline of its body is quite unlike the side view.
options.why: That is a change of viewpoint, and convolution and pooling build in nothing for viewpoint.

items.stem: For the small fish, an eel can appear to its left or to its right, near or far, and from the front or from the side. Which of these changes would convolution and pooling build any tolerance to?

options.text: Only the eel to the left or the right, which is a shift; near and far is a change in size, and the two angles are a change of viewpoint.
options.why: Correct. Convolution and pooling build in tolerance to a shift in position, imperfectly, and nothing for size, rotation, or viewpoint.

options.text: Only the eel near and far, since pooling over a neighborhood absorbs a change in size the same way it absorbs a small change in position.
options.why: Near and far is a change in size, and convolution and pooling build in nothing for size. The change they do cover is a shift in position.

options.text: All three of them, since enough stacked rounds of convolution and pooling build in tolerance to position, size, and viewpoint alike.
options.why: Stacking adds tolerance to small shifts and distortions a little at a time, but nothing for size or viewpoint.

options.text: Not even the eel to the left or the right, since convolution makes the response move along with the input and so removes no change.
options.why: Convolution alone does make the response move with a shift, but pooling then makes a small shift stop mattering. Together they give tolerance to shifts.

items.stem: A classmate argues: “Networks recognize objects across size and rotation because they were trained on rescaled and rotated copies of their images. So animals must recognize things across such changes in the same way”. What does the chapter say about this argument?

options.text: Whether training of that kind is enough to explain how animals manage changes of size and rotation is still a live dispute among researchers.
options.why: Correct. The first half of the argument is a fair description of networks. The step to animals is exactly what remains disputed, in either direction.

options.text: The argument is likely right, since the chapter presents varied training as the leading explanation of how animals manage such changes.
options.why: The chapter presents varied training as how artificial networks mostly get there, not as the leading account of animals. For animals the question is a live dispute.

options.text: The argument is likely wrong, since the chapter presents built-in wiring as the leading explanation of how animals manage such changes.
options.why: The chapter favors neither side for animals. Whether training of this kind is enough to explain how animals do it is left as a live dispute.

options.text: The argument is wrong, since networks get their tolerance to size and rotation from convolution and pooling, not from their training images.
options.why: Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size or rotation; networks mostly get those from varied training examples. The step to animals is what is disputed.

items.stem: A network built from convolution followed by pooling is shown a photograph of a beetle, and then the same photograph with the beetle shifted a few positions to the right. In a few sentences, explain what convolution does with the shift, what pooling adds, and which changes to the beetle this architecture would still give the network no help with.
items.answer: Convolution applies the same small detector, with the same weights, at every position, so each feature of the beetle is found wherever it falls. When the beetle shifts, the map of where each feature was found shifts with it. So convolution alone does not make the response unchanged; it makes the response move along with the input. Pooling then combines the detections over a small neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes the pooled output. Together they give some tolerance to shifts in position, though imperfectly. They build in nothing for other changes, such as the beetle seen larger or smaller, rotated, or from another viewpoint. Networks mostly get those from training images that already include them.
rubric: Says convolution applies one detector, with the same weights, at every position, so a feature is found wherever it falls.
Says the convolution map moves with the shift rather than staying unchanged.
Says pooling combines detections over a small neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes the output.
Names at least one change the architecture builds in nothing for: size, rotation, or viewpoint.
Keeps the tolerance to shift limited or imperfect, rather than complete.

items.stem: What is catastrophic interference?

options.text: A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights that the old ones needed.
options.why: Correct. In a classic demonstration, a network that had learned the addition facts about ones began answering them as twos after a single pass through the twos.

options.text: A loss of accuracy on new examples after a network has fit its training examples so closely that it has learned even their accidents along with them.
options.why: That is overfitting, which is about doing poorly on new examples of the same kind. Catastrophic interference is old learning wiped out by newer learning.

options.text: A confident wrong answer to an input that has been changed slightly and deliberately, often in a way that a person looking at it would not notice.
options.why: That describes an adversarial example. Catastrophic interference concerns what happens to old learning when a network learns something new afterward.

options.text: A weakness in handling inputs unlike anything a network was trained on, such as numbers with many more digits than any that appeared in training.
options.why: That is weak out-of-distribution generalization. Catastrophic interference is a loss of old learning, triggered by learning in sequence.

items.stem: What is the name for a drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights that the old patterns depended on?

options.text: Catastrophic interference.
options.why: Correct. The trigger is learning in sequence; trained on everything at once, the same network can learn it all.

options.text: Overfitting.
options.why: Overfitting is fitting the training examples so closely that new examples suffer. It is not a loss of earlier learning to later learning.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization is generalizing to inputs unlike any in training. It says nothing about old learning being lost.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, so a later stage can tell them apart. It is not a loss of old learning.

items.stem: A network trained to recognize the calls of ten frog species is then trained further on the calls of ten bird species. Its accuracy on the frogs drops. What is the general reason for problems of this kind?

options.text: The same units carry both sets of patterns, so learning the birds moves weights that recognizing the frogs depended on.
options.why: Correct. When the patterns a learner stores are carried by the same units, learning a new pattern moves weights that an old pattern depends on.

options.text: The network ran out of room, so the bird calls had to take over the units that had been set aside for the frogs.
options.why: With shared weights no unit is set aside for one species. Every weight takes part in many input–output pairs, and that is the source of the problem.

options.text: The frog calls were kept in their own part of the network, which faded because nothing activated it during the bird training.
options.why: Nothing in the account involves fading with disuse. The old learning is disturbed because new learning moves the very weights it depended on.

options.text: The frog training had overfit the ten frog species, so any later training was bound to expose how fragile that learning was.
options.why: Overfitting is doing poorly on new examples of the same kind. Here the frogs themselves were lost, because learning the birds moved weights the frogs depended on.

items.stem: In one patch, blue round flowers and yellow star-shaped flowers carry nectar, while blue star-shaped flowers and yellow round flowers carry none. One learner tracks only single features; another can also represent combinations of features. How do they compare?

options.text: The combination learner can come to rely on “blue and round”, which is always rewarded, and the single-feature learner keeps undoing its own weights.
options.why: Correct. Each single feature here is rewarded half the time, but a combination can be reliably rewarded even when none of its parts is. Representing it stops the interference.

options.text: The single-feature learner does better, since tracking “blue” and “round” separately gives it twice as many chances to be rewarded.
options.why: Each single feature is rewarded on half its occasions and unrewarded on the rest, so its weight keeps going up and down.

options.text: The two learners do equally well, since a combination like “blue and round” carries no more than the sum of what each of its parts predicts.
options.why: If a combination were only a sum of its parts, nothing could solve this patch. Representing the combination as its own thing is what stops the interference.

options.text: Neither learner can succeed, since no learner that changes its weights with reward can use cues that are each rewarded half the time.
options.why: A learner that represents combinations can do it, because each combination is reliably rewarded even though no single feature is.

items.stem: A network that recognizes handwritten letters reads a new person’s writing well. Trained afterward on a new alphabet, it loses much of the old one. How does the chapter relate these two behaviors?

options.text: They are one effect seen from two sides: each weight serves many input–output pairs, which carries learning to new inputs and lets new learning alter old answers.
options.why: Correct. Weight sharing is why similar inputs get similar outputs without any extra work, and also why changing the weights for new pairs changes the answers to old ones.

options.text: They are two separate effects with two separate causes: generalization comes from the variety of the training letters, and interference from having too few hidden units.
options.why: The chapter traces both to one property, weights that each take part in many input–output pairs, not to the variety of the training set or the size of the network.

options.text: They trade off against each other: the better a network generalizes to new inputs, the less it will suffer from interference when it later learns something else entirely.
options.why: They go together, not against each other. The sharing that gives generalization is the same sharing that lets new learning disturb old learning.

options.text: They are both forms of overfitting: the network fits each set of training letters so closely that it cannot treat any other letters properly.
options.why: Overfitting is doing poorly on new examples after fitting the training set too closely. This network generalizes well, so overfitting is not the story.

items.stem: A network must learn to name twenty birds and twenty frogs from their calls. On one schedule, the bird and frog calls are mixed together from the start. On another, all the birds come first and then all the frogs. How do the outcomes compare?

options.text: Mixed together, it can master all forty; birds first and frogs second, it loses much of the birds as it learns the frogs.
options.why: Correct. The trigger for catastrophic interference is learning in sequence. Trained on everything at once, the same network learns it all.

options.text: Mixed together, it learns neither set well, since the two sets keep pulling its weights in opposite directions at once.
options.why: Trained on all the calls at once, a network finds weights that serve both sets. The trouble comes when the sets arrive in sequence.

options.text: The two schedules end in the same place, since the network hears exactly the same calls in both and only their order differs.
options.why: The order is what matters. Learning in sequence is the trigger for catastrophic interference.

options.text: Birds first and frogs second gives the better result, since learning one set fully before the next keeps the two from mixing.
options.why: That is how it might seem, but sequence is the trigger. The network moves its weights to suit the newest set, whatever the old set needed.

items.stem: When people learn a new list of associations that conflicts with an old one, how does what happens to their old list compare with what happens in a network trained the same way?

options.text: Both lose some of the old list, but people lose far less: they still recall more than half of it after mastering the new one.
options.why: Correct. In a classic study people kept more than half the old list, while the network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one.

options.text: People lose none of the old list, since human memory keeps each list in its own separate store, while the network loses all of it.
options.why: People forget too. The difference between people and networks is in how much is lost, not in whether anything is.

options.text: Both lose about the same amount, since people and networks forget conflicting lists by the same means and at about the same rate.
options.why: People lose far less. They kept more than half the old list, while the network lost all of its old list early in the new learning.

options.text: The network loses less than people do, since it can hold far more associations at once than a person can keep in memory.
options.why: That reverses the finding. The network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why generalization and catastrophic interference can be called the same effect seen from two sides, and why learning in sequence is what triggers the interference.
items.answer: In a network, every weight takes part in many different input–output pairs. That sharing is why similar inputs get similar outputs without any extra work, which is generalization. It is also why changing the weights to fit new pairs changes the answers to old ones, which is interference. So both come from one property. The interference becomes catastrophic when learning happens in sequence. Trained on one set and then another, the network moves its weights to wherever suits the newest set, regardless of where the old set needed them to be. Trained on all the facts at once, the same network learns them all.
rubric: Names the shared property: each weight takes part in many input–output pairs.
Links that sharing to generalization, with similar inputs getting similar outputs.
Links the same sharing to interference, with weight changes for new pairs changing old answers.
Says learning in sequence is the trigger, with the weights moving to suit the newest set.
Says that training on everything at once lets the same network learn it all.

items.stem: A classmate says: “Catastrophic interference proves that networks learn nothing like people, because people never lose old learning when they learn something new”. In a few sentences, say what is right and what is wrong in that claim.
items.answer: The classmate is right that the difference is real and large. In a classic study, people still recalled more than half of an old list after mastering a new one that conflicted with it, while a network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one. But it is wrong that people never lose old learning. When people learn a new list of associations that conflicts with an old one, they lose some of the old list too. So the difference between people and networks lies in how much is lost, not in whether anything is. How brains keep most of their old learning is a separate question, and the network results do not answer it.
rubric: Says people do lose some of an old list when they learn a conflicting new one.
Says the difference between people and networks is in how much is lost.
Gives evidence of the size of the difference, such as people keeping more than half of the old list while the network lost all of it.
Does not claim that the network results explain how brains limit the loss.

items.stem: What is an adversarial example?

options.text: An input changed slightly and deliberately, so that a network gives a confident wrong answer, by a change that can be too slight for a person to see.
options.why: Correct. The change at each pixel can be about as small as an image file can record, and imperceptible to a person, while the network’s answer changes completely.

options.text: An input unlike anything in a network’s training examples, so that the network’s answer to it is much less reliable.
options.why: That describes an out-of-distribution input. An adversarial example is a familiar kind of input with a tiny, deliberate change.

options.text: An image whose surface texture comes from one object and whose shape comes from another, used to test what a network relies on.
options.why: Pictures like that were used to measure texture bias. An adversarial example is an input changed slightly and on purpose.

options.text: A training example that a network fits so closely, accidents included, that it then does worse on new examples.
options.why: That describes overfitting. An adversarial example is an input deliberately altered to produce a confident wrong answer.

items.stem: What is the name for an input changed slightly and deliberately, so that a network gives a confident wrong answer, by a change that can be too slight for a person to see?

options.text: Adversarial example.
options.why: Correct. The panda photograph that a network labeled “gibbon” after a carefully chosen pattern was added is a well-known case.

options.text: Texture bias.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize by surface over shape. It is not an input altered to produce a wrong answer.

options.text: False alarm.
options.why: A false alarm is judging a target present when it is absent. An adversarial example can produce a wrong answer, but the term names the altered input.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization is generalizing to inputs unlike anything in training. An adversarial example is a familiar input with a tiny, deliberate change.

items.stem: On one explanation of adversarial examples, how can a change too small to notice at any one pixel still change a network’s answer?

options.text: A unit sums thousands of weighted inputs, so nudging each slightly in the direction its weight favors adds up until the sum crosses the boundary.
options.why: Correct. No single pixel moves much, but every tiny change pushes the sum the same way, and the total carries the input across the boundary.

options.text: A single pixel changed by a large amount can carry the whole weighted sum across the decision boundary, while the other pixels stay exactly as they were.
options.why: On this explanation no single pixel moves much. It is the many tiny changes together that carry the sum across the boundary.

options.text: The tiny changes make the image look like a different object to the network’s first layer, whose detectors then respond to the new object’s shape.
options.why: The change alters no shape that anyone could see. The explanation turns on a weighted sum over many inputs, not on a new shape.

options.text: The tiny changes are scattered at random, and among enough random changes some are bound to push the answer over into a different category.
options.why: Direction matters on this explanation. Random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer.

items.stem: A study guide states that adversarial examples are “caused by tiny nudges adding up across thousands of inputs, as researchers have established”. How does the chapter’s account differ?

options.text: It gives the many-small-nudges account as one explanation, notes that a different cause was first proposed, and calls it still debated.
options.why: Correct. The account makes the effect easy to understand, and the single-unit result fits it, but the explanation is not settled.

options.text: It rejects the many-small-nudges account, since a single unit that sums its inputs turned out to be impossible to fool by nudging them.
options.why: A single unit was fooled, on 99 percent of nudged inputs. The chapter keeps the account as one explanation, still debated.

options.text: It agrees with the study guide, adding only that the account came from the same researchers who first reported adversarial examples.
options.why: The researchers who first reported adversarial examples proposed a different cause. The account is still debated.

options.text: It traces adversarial examples instead to the training images, the same cause that it gives for texture bias in standard networks.
options.why: The training images are the source the chapter gives for texture bias. For adversarial examples, the cause is still debated.

items.stem: What is texture bias?

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape, found in networks trained on standard sets of photographs.
options.why: Correct. Given a picture with a cat’s shape and an elephant’s skin, such networks mostly said “elephant”, where people say “cat”.

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their outline rather than their surface, found in people shown pictures whose shape and texture conflict.
options.why: That is the opposite tendency, the one people show: they chose shape about 96 percent of the time.

options.text: A tendency, built into convolutional networks by their wiring, to find a feature equally well wherever in an image it happens to appear.
options.why: That is the convolutional bet, an inductive bias in the architecture. Texture bias came from the training images, not the architecture.

options.text: A tendency to give confident wrong answers to images that have been changed slightly and on purpose, in ways a person would not notice.
options.why: That describes what adversarial examples produce. Texture bias is about relying on surface texture rather than shape.

items.stem: A picture has the outline of a dog, filled in with the surface texture of tree bark. What would people, and a network trained on a standard collection of photographs, most likely say it is?

options.text: People would mostly say “dog”, going by shape, while the network would more likely name something with that bark texture.
options.why: Correct. People chose shape about 96 percent of the time in such pictures; networks trained on standard photographs chose shape only 17 to 43 percent of the time.

options.text: Both would mostly say “dog”, since people and networks trained on photographs both rely on an object’s outline above all.
options.why: People rely on shape, but networks trained on standard photographs mostly go by texture. That difference is texture bias.

options.text: People would mostly go by the bark texture, while the network would more likely say “dog”, going by the outline.
options.why: That reverses the finding. People go by shape; networks trained on standard photographs mostly go by texture.

options.text: Both would mostly name something with the bark texture, since texture covers far more of the picture than the outline does.
options.why: People mostly go by shape even when texture covers the picture. Only the networks mostly went by texture.

items.stem: Researchers trained the same network architecture on two sets of photographs: a standard collection, and the same photographs repainted in the styles of different paintings, which scrambled their textures. What did the comparison show about where texture bias comes from?

options.text: From the training images rather than the architecture: on repainted photographs, the same architecture learned to go by shape far more often.
options.why: Correct. The same architecture chose shape 81 percent of the time instead of 22. Only the training images had changed.

options.text: From the architecture rather than the training images: the same architecture went by texture after training on both sets of photographs alike.
options.why: The repainted training made a large difference, which could not happen if the bias were fixed by the architecture.

options.text: From the repainting itself: training on the repainted photographs led the network to go by texture even more often than before.
options.why: The effect ran the other way. With textures scrambled, the network went by shape far more often.

options.text: From the number of photographs: the repainted set was larger, and a larger set of any kind reduces texture bias by itself.
options.why: The two sets held the same photographs, repainted. What changed was whether texture went with the category, not how many images there were.

items.stem: A team’s network sorts beetles by species, and they find that it relies on the texture of the beetles’ shells rather than their body shape. One member says a new architecture is the only possible fix. In light of the repainting result, what is the best reply?

options.text: Changing the training images so shell texture no longer goes with the label may move the network toward outline, since what it learns depends on experience.
options.why: Correct. The same architecture moved from texture toward shape when only its training images changed. What a classifier learns is not set by its build alone.

options.text: Nothing can be done about it, since every network built from convolution and pooling relies on surface texture whatever images it is trained on.
options.why: The repainting result shows otherwise: the same architecture relied on shape far more often after training on texture-scrambled images.

options.text: A new architecture is indeed the one real fix, since the repainting result showed that texture bias is wired into the architecture of these networks.
options.why: The repainting result showed the reverse. Texture bias came from the training images rather than from the architecture.

options.text: Adding many more photographs from the same collection would probably help, since texture bias tends to shrink as a training set grows larger.
options.why: More images of the same kind keep texture going with species. The repainting worked by breaking that link, not by adding more images.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the many-small-nudges explanation of adversarial examples, why the direction of the change matters, and how firmly the explanation is established.
items.answer: A unit computes a weighted sum over its inputs, and an image has many thousands of inputs. If every input is moved a tiny amount, each in the direction its weight favors, the tiny changes add up. No single pixel moves much, but the total crosses the decision boundary. On this explanation even a single unit should be fooled, and it is: a unit that told 3s from 7s accurately misclassified almost all inputs nudged along its own weights. The direction is what matters, since random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer. But this is one explanation. The researchers who first reported adversarial examples proposed a different cause, and the matter is still debated.
rubric: Says a unit computes a weighted sum over very many inputs.
Says nudging every input slightly in the direction its weight favors makes the tiny changes add up and cross the boundary.
Says random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer, so direction matters.
Says the explanation is one account that is still debated, not an established cause.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what texture bias is, and how comparing networks trained on standard and on repainted photographs located its source. What does the result show about what a classifier learns?
items.answer: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape. Given a picture with a cat’s shape and an elephant’s skin, people say “cat”, while networks trained on a standard collection of photographs mostly said “elephant”. When the same architecture was trained on photographs repainted in the styles of different paintings, which scrambled their textures, it chose shape far more often, 81 percent of the time instead of 22. The architecture stayed the same and only the training images changed, so the bias came from the training images, not the architecture. What a classifier learns depends on its experience, and not only on how it is built.
rubric: Defines texture bias as categorizing by surface texture rather than shape.
Describes the comparison: the same architecture, trained on standard versus texture-scrambled photographs.
States that training on the repainted photographs made the network go by shape far more often.
Concludes that the bias came from the training images rather than the architecture.
States that what a classifier learns depends on its experience, not only on how it is built.

pools.title: Kinds of Failure, and What Has to Be Built In
pools.covers: reading §7.2.12, §7.2.13, §7.2.14 · lecture 7.2 slides fooled_and_far_from_home, gaps_or_something_missing, what_has_to_be_built_in

items.stem: What is overfitting?

options.text: Fitting the training examples so closely, accidents included, that performance on new examples suffers.
options.why: Correct. An overfit network does well on the examples it was trained on and poorly on new ones, because it has fit accidents that new examples do not share.

options.text: Failing to fit the training examples at all, so that performance is poor on old and new examples alike.
options.why: That is a failure to learn anything, not overfitting. An overfit network does well on its training examples; the trouble shows up only on new ones.

options.text: Giving a confident wrong answer to an input that someone has changed slightly and deliberately.
options.why: That describes an adversarial example. Overfitting is about the gap between performance on the training examples and performance on new ones.

options.text: Losing old learning drastically when new patterns are learned after old ones, because shared weights move.
options.why: That is catastrophic interference, which appears when learning happens in sequence. Overfitting is fitting the accidents of the training examples too closely.

items.stem: When an artificial classifier is built, what is its training set?

options.text: The examples the learner learns from, as distinct from any examples kept apart to evaluate it afterward.
options.why: Correct. The training set is the examples a learner learns from. A separate test set is kept apart and used only for evaluation.

options.text: The examples kept apart from training and used only afterward to evaluate how well the learner does.
options.why: That describes the test set. The training set is what the learner learns from, and it is exactly what the test set must be kept apart from.

options.text: The inputs an engineer decides on before learning begins, chosen because they carry the structure that matters.
options.why: Choosing the inputs before learning begins is feature engineering. The training set is the collection of examples the learner then learns from.

options.text: The inputs unlike anything the learner has seen, used to measure how far its performance carries.
options.why: Inputs unlike anything in training are what out-of-distribution generalization is about. The training set is the familiar material itself.

items.stem: What is a test set?

options.text: Examples kept apart from training, never used to adjust the learner, and used only to evaluate it.
options.why: Correct. Because a network can fit its training examples and still do poorly on new ones, classifiers are scored on examples they never learned from.

options.text: The examples a learner learned from, run through it again at the end to check what it learned.
options.why: Scoring a learner on its own training examples is exactly what a test set exists to avoid, since a network can fit those examples and still do poorly on new ones.

options.text: A set of inputs unlike anything in training, gathered to measure how far a learner can extrapolate.
options.why: A test set is usually drawn from the same collection as the training set, so it holds inputs like the training examples, not unlike them.

options.text: A set of inputs changed slightly and deliberately, gathered to find out whether a network can be fooled.
options.why: Slightly and deliberately changed inputs are adversarial examples. A test set is just ordinary examples that were held back from training.

items.stem: A teacher builds a final exam by copying questions word for word from the practice sets the class worked through. A student who memorized the practice answers scores 98 percent. By the reasoning used for artificial classifiers, why is that score a poor measure of what the student learned?

options.text: The exam reused the very examples the student learned from, so it cannot separate fitting them from doing well on new ones.
options.why: Correct. That is why classifiers are scored on a test set kept apart from training. A score on the training examples cannot show whether the learner fit their accidents or learned something that carries over.

options.text: The exam held questions unlike anything practiced, so it measured out-of-distribution generalization instead of what was learned.
options.why: The questions were copied from the practice sets, so they were the most familiar inputs possible, not unfamiliar ones. The trouble is that they were the training examples themselves.

options.text: The exam scored the student too highly, and any score above 90 percent is evidence of overfitting, whatever questions are used.
options.why: No score is a sign of overfitting by itself. What matters is whether the examples scored were kept apart from the examples learned from.

options.text: The exam measured how readily the student answered, which is a criterion, while learning is a matter of sensitivity alone.
options.why: Criterion and sensitivity are a real distinction, from signal detection theory, but they are not the issue here. The exam fails because it reused the training examples.

items.stem: A network is trained and tested on handwritten digits collected from forms in one country, and scores 99 percent on its test set. It is then used on digits from a country where a seven carries a crossbar and a one has a long upward stroke. Why should the test score not be taken as a guide to how it will do there?

options.text: Its test set came from the same collection as its training set, so it measured inputs like those it trained on.
options.why: Correct. Even a good test-set score is a score on inputs like the training set. Digits in an unfamiliar style lie outside that collection, where current classifiers are much weaker.

options.text: Its test score was earned on digits it had already been trained on, since a test set reuses the training examples.
options.why: A test set is kept apart and never used in training, so the score was earned on new digits. The problem is that the new digits were of the same kind as the training digits.

options.text: Its test set was too small, and more digits from the same forms would have revealed how it handles the new styles.
options.why: More digits from the same forms would still be in the familiar style. No amount of familiar material shows how a classifier does on inputs unlike anything in training.

options.text: Its test score is a measure of overfitting, and a network that scores so well on a test set has always overfit.
options.why: A high test score is evidence against overfitting, since overfitting shows up as poor performance on new examples. The limitation lies in what kind of new examples the test set held.

items.stem: What is out-of-distribution generalization?

options.text: Generalization to inputs unlike anything a learner was trained on, beyond the collection its examples came from.
options.why: Correct. It goes beyond doing well on a test set, which holds new inputs from the same collection as the training examples.

options.text: Generalization to new inputs drawn from the same collection as the training examples, as in a test set.
options.why: That is what a good test-set score shows. Out-of-distribution generalization is the harder case, inputs unlike anything in training.

options.text: The fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs more and more from the input trained on.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, a description of how responding declines with difference. Out-of-distribution generalization is the ability to handle inputs far from training at all.

options.text: Fitting the accidents of the training examples, so that performance on any new example suffers.
options.why: That is overfitting. Out-of-distribution generalization is an ability, the one current classifiers are much weaker at than at handling familiar inputs.

items.stem: What is the name for generalizing to inputs unlike anything in a learner’s training?

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Correct. Current classifiers are much weaker at it than at handling inputs among their familiar examples.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of viewpoint. It can fail out of distribution, but it names a different demand.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is the fall-off in responding as a new input differs more from a trained one. It describes behavior; it is not the name for generalizing far from training.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. It works from familiar patterns rather than inputs unlike anything learned.

items.stem: A network learns to tell cats from dogs from many thousands of daylight photographs of adult animals of many breeds. Which new photograph is it most likely to label correctly?

options.text: A daylight photograph of an adult cat of an unfamiliar breed that looks much like the breeds in its training.
options.why: Correct. Current classifiers interpolate well among familiar examples and extrapolate poorly beyond them. A new cat that resembles the training cats lands among familiar examples.

options.text: An infrared photograph of an adult cat taken at night by a wildlife camera, whose outline matches the cats in its training.
options.why: A matching outline does not make the input familiar. An infrared image at night is unlike anything in training, which is where current classifiers extrapolate poorly.

options.text: A child’s crayon drawing of a cat, since a drawing shows only the features shared by all breeds and none of the accidents.
options.why: A drawing is far from every daylight photograph the network learned from. Having fewer accidents does not bring an input closer to the training examples.

options.text: A blurred daylight photograph of a kitten, since blurring removes the fine detail where overfitting usually takes hold.
options.why: Blur and youth both move the input away from the training examples. Overfitting is not removed by degrading a new input.

items.stem: Not every failure of current classifiers is the same kind of failure. Which group does the chapter class as gaps in pattern recognition itself, gaps a better classifier could in principle close?

options.text: Adversarial examples, texture bias, overfitting, and failure out of distribution.
options.why: Correct. These four are gaps in pattern recognition itself. Catastrophic interference is a gap of a different kind, in the learning procedure, and the remaining failures look like marks of later capacities.

options.text: Adversarial examples, catastrophic interference, overfitting, and reasoning about causes.
options.why: Catastrophic interference lies in the learning procedure, and reasoning about causes looks like a mark of a capacity that pattern recognition alone does not supply.

options.text: Systematicity, reasoning about causes, and knowing what an object is like beyond recognizing it.
options.why: These three are the ones that look like marks of capacities pattern recognition alone does not supply. A better classifier is not expected to close them by itself.

options.text: Catastrophic interference, texture bias, systematicity, and failure out of distribution.
options.why: Texture bias and failure out of distribution belong in the group, but catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure, and systematicity looks like a mark of a later capacity.

items.stem: A network learns to recognize twenty kinds of birds by their songs. It is then trained only on twenty kinds of frogs by their calls, and afterward it misnames most of the birds. How does the chapter classify a failure of this kind?

options.text: As a gap in the learning procedure, which appears when learning happens in sequence, one set after another.
options.why: Correct. This is catastrophic interference. Trained on birds and frogs together, the same network could learn both; trained on one and then the other, the new learning moves weights the old depended on.

options.text: As a gap in pattern recognition itself, of the same kind as overfitting and texture bias.
options.why: Overfitting and texture bias are gaps in pattern recognition itself. Losing the birds after learning the frogs lies in how the learning was done, in sequence.

options.text: As a mark of a later capacity, of the same kind as systematicity and reasoning about causes.
options.why: Marks of later capacities are things pattern recognition alone may not supply. The network could recognize the birds; it lost that ability through the order of its training.

options.text: As a failure out of distribution, since the bird songs became unfamiliar while the frogs were being learned.
options.why: The bird songs are the same inputs the network was trained on. They did not move away from training; the weights that handled them moved.

items.stem: Overfitting and catastrophic interference both leave a network doing badly on inputs it ought to handle. Why does the chapter sort them as different kinds of failure?

options.text: Overfitting is a gap in pattern recognition; catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure, appearing with learning in sequence.
options.why: Correct. A better classifier could in principle close the gaps in pattern recognition. Catastrophic interference is about the order of learning: the same network trained on everything at once does not suffer it.

options.text: Overfitting is a mark of a capacity pattern recognition does not supply, while catastrophic interference is a gap a better classifier could close.
options.why: That reverses the sorting and misplaces both. Overfitting is a gap in pattern recognition, and catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure.

options.text: Overfitting happens only in animals, while catastrophic interference happens only in artificial networks trained by backpropagation.
options.why: Overfitting is described for artificial classifiers, and people forget too when they learn conflicting lists in sequence. The difference is in the kind of gap, not in who has it.

options.text: Overfitting comes from the training data, while catastrophic interference comes from small deliberate changes made after training ends.
options.why: Small deliberate changes produce adversarial examples. Catastrophic interference comes from new learning moving weights that old learning depended on.

items.stem: A classifier correctly labels a photograph of a refrigerator. Why might knowing that the refrigerator is heavy and rigid, and what would happen if it were pushed, be a different matter?

options.text: Recognizing it is pattern recognition, but knowing what it is like and what pushing it would do may draw on something more.
options.why: Correct. Failures here look like marks of capacities that pattern recognition alone does not supply, and the chapter keeps the hedge: knowing these things may draw on something more.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy is pattern recognition, but recognizing it in a photograph is a mark of a later capacity.
options.why: That reverses the two. Recognizing the refrigerator is the pattern recognition; knowing what it is like goes beyond its pattern.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy needs a test set kept apart from training, while recognizing it needs only a training set.
options.why: Training and test sets are about scoring a classifier fairly. They do not separate recognizing an object from knowing what it is like.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy is a kind of texture bias, since weight shows up in the surface texture of a photograph.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize by surface texture rather than shape. Weight and what happens when something is pushed are not in a photograph’s texture.

items.stem: What is systematicity?

options.text: The ability to combine known parts in new ways, so that understanding one combination brings understanding of others made from the same parts.
options.why: Correct. Anyone who understands “the eel chased the fish” also understands “the fish chased the eel”. Systematicity may draw on something more than pattern recognition.

options.text: The ability to recognize one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.
options.why: That is invariance. Systematicity is about combining known parts in new ways, not about recognizing one thing across changes.

options.text: The ability to recover a whole stored pattern from only part of it, as when a faint or partial trace of a familiar smell brings back the whole.
options.why: That is pattern completion. Systematicity is about understanding new combinations of known parts.

options.text: The ability to sort things by a definition, with every member of a category having every one of the defining features.
options.why: Sorting by necessary and sufficient features is the classical view of categories. Systematicity is about combining parts, not about defining a category.

items.stem: What is the name for the ability to combine known parts in new ways, so that understanding one combination brings with it the understanding of others built from the same parts?

options.text: Systematicity.
options.why: Correct. Systematicity may draw on something more than pattern recognition, which is why its absence in a network looks like a mark of a later capacity.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is treating alike the inputs that call for the same response. Understanding a new combination of known parts is a different ability.

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation is a code in which each thing is a pattern across many units. It is a kind of code, not an ability to combine parts into new wholes.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Systematicity builds new wholes from known parts rather than restoring old ones.

items.stem: A robot has learned to carry out the instruction “put the cup on the box”. Without any further training, it also carries out “put the box on the cup” correctly. What capacity does the second success show?

options.text: Systematicity, combining known parts in new ways.
options.why: Correct. Understanding one arrangement of the parts brings with it understanding of another made from the same parts, as with “the eel chased the fish” and “the fish chased the eel”.

options.text: Generalization, treating alike inputs that call for one response.
options.why: The two instructions call for different responses, so this is not treating them alike. The robot combined the same parts in a new way and acted on the new combination.

options.text: Invariance, recognizing one thing across large changes.
options.why: The two instructions are not one thing seen differently; they mean different things. What the robot shows is the ability to understand a new combination.

options.text: Pattern completion, recovering a whole from part of it.
options.why: Nothing here was partial. The robot received a complete new instruction built from known parts and understood it.

items.stem: Reasoning about causes, language, and the use of symbols are taken up separately in the course, not treated as further problems of pattern recognition. What is the reason for setting them apart?

options.text: Failures in them look like marks of capacities pattern recognition alone does not supply, as each may draw on something more.
options.why: Correct. Causes and planning, language, and symbols are each taken up in a later module of their own, because they may need more than recognizing patterns.

options.text: Failures in them are gaps in pattern recognition itself, which a better classifier could close without anything new being added.
options.why: Those gaps are adversarial examples, texture bias, overfitting, and failure out of distribution. Causes, language, and symbols are set apart because they may need something more.

options.text: Failures in them are gaps in the learning procedure, which appear only when the parts of a task are learned in sequence.
options.why: That describes catastrophic interference. The capacities set apart here are not about the order of learning; they may draw on something beyond pattern recognition.

options.text: Failures in them come from the input space, which pattern recognition takes as given and so cannot be asked to explain.
options.why: The input space is one of the candidates for what is built in, and it matters for pattern recognition too. It is not why causes, language, and symbols are set apart.

items.stem: A whale and a submarine are much alike in shape, size, and the ability to dive deep. They are very different in what they are made of and in how they came to exist. What argument about similarity does this pair illustrate?

options.text: Anything is similar to anything else in some respect, so similarity alone cannot say which respects matter.
options.why: Correct. This is the argument illustrated by the cloud and the white feather: alike in color and in floating, unlike in size and use. Similarity does not say which comparisons count.

options.text: Two things alike in shape are always in the same category, so shape is the respect that matters most.
options.why: The whale and the submarine are alike in shape and are plainly not the same kind of thing. The argument is that similarity alone cannot pick out which respects matter.

options.text: Similarity measured in physical units predicts generalization well, so the shared size settles the category.
options.why: Closeness in physical units is not a good predictor of how animals generalize. And the pair shows that physical likeness leaves the category unsettled.

options.text: Two things are similar only when their prototypes match, so a whale and a submarine cannot be compared at all.
options.why: Prototypes are one way of using similarity, not a condition for it. The whale and the submarine can be compared in many respects; the trouble is choosing among them.

items.stem: On the alternative to similarity that the chapter describes, what holds a category together?

options.text: A theory, an understanding of why the category’s members have the particular features they do.
options.why: Correct. On this alternative, members belong together because of why they have their features, not just because they resemble one another. It is one alternative, and the question is still debated.

options.text: A prototype, the average member that each new input is compared with to assign its category.
options.why: A prototype is a summary used by a similarity-based model. The alternative replaces similarity with an understanding of why members have their features.

options.text: A definition, a list of features each member must have and that together guarantee membership.
options.why: A definition belongs to the classical view. The alternative described here is a theory about why members have the features they do.

options.text: A decision boundary, a single line through the feature space with every member on one side.
options.why: A decision boundary divides a feature space. The alternative to similarity is not a boundary but an understanding of why members have their features.

items.stem: A lemon is coated and scented so that it looks, feels, and smells exactly like an orange. Inside, it still has lemon juice and lemon seeds. On the view that a category is held together by a theory, why might a person still call it a lemon?

options.text: What makes it a lemon is what it is underneath, the reason for its features, which goes beyond its outward pattern.
options.why: Correct. On the theory view, membership follows an understanding of why members have their features. Knowing what the fruit is underneath goes beyond its pattern, as with the raccoon changed to look like a skunk.

options.text: It sits closest to the lemon prototype in a feature space built from its color, its surface texture, and its smell.
options.why: In color, texture, and smell, the coated fruit now matches an orange. Closeness on those features points the wrong way; the theory view looks beneath them.

options.text: It is out of distribution for the person, who falls back on the nearest familiar category, which is the lemon.
options.why: Out-of-distribution failure is about inputs unlike anything in training, and it describes classifiers. The theory view explains the answer by what the fruit is underneath.

options.text: Its surface features carry texture bias, so the person relies on its shape, which is still the shape of a lemon.
options.why: The fruit was made to look exactly like an orange, shape included. The theory view rests the answer on what the fruit is underneath, not on any surface feature.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why texture bias and catastrophic interference are sorted as different kinds of failure, and then name and describe a failure of a third kind.
items.answer: Texture bias is a gap in pattern recognition itself, produced by the training data, and a better classifier could in principle close it. Catastrophic interference is a gap of a different kind. It lies in the learning procedure, and it appears when learning happens in sequence: the same network trained on everything at once does not suffer it. A third kind of failure looks like a mark of a capacity that pattern recognition alone does not supply. Systematicity is one: anyone who understands “the eel chased the fish” also understands “the fish chased the eel”, and that may draw on something more than recognizing patterns.
rubric: Classes texture bias as a gap in pattern recognition that a better classifier could in principle close.
Classes catastrophic interference as a gap in the learning procedure, appearing when learning happens in sequence.
Names a mark of a later capacity: knowing what an object is like, reasoning about causes, or systematicity.
Describes that third kind as something pattern recognition alone may not supply, keeping the hedge.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the argument that similarity cannot be what holds a category together, describe one alternative, and say how settled the question is.
items.answer: Prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models all rest on similarity. Some researchers argue that similarity cannot be what holds a category together, because anything is similar to anything else in some respect. A cloud and a white feather are very similar in color and in floating, and very different in size and in what they can be used for, so similarity alone cannot say which respects matter. On one alternative, a category is held together by a theory, an understanding of why its members have the features they do; older children said a raccoon changed to look like a skunk was still a raccoon. The question is not settled. For a fish’s smells similarity may carry most of the load, and for human concepts the share is still debated.
rubric: States that prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models all rest on similarity.
Gives the argument that anything is similar to anything in some respect, so similarity cannot say which respects matter, with an example.
Describes the theory alternative: an understanding of why members have the features they do.
Says the question is open, with similarity perhaps carrying most of the load for a fish’s smells and debated for human concepts.

items.stem: Two researchers argue about whether a songbird’s fear of hawks is innate or learned. Following the main lesson of the nativism debate, what question would move their argument forward?

options.text: What exactly is claimed to be built in: the bird’s receptors, its wiring, its learning rule, or a detector for hawks.
options.why: Correct. The useful question is not whether a capacity is innate or learned, but what exactly is claimed to be built in, because the candidates differ enormously. Pattern recognition lets us list them precisely.

options.text: Whether the fear is innate or learned, settled once and for all by measuring how strongly adult birds react to hawks.
options.why: Asking innate or learned is the framing the nativism debate teaches us to move past. And the strength of an adult’s reaction cannot tell a ready-made detector from a learned one.

options.text: Whether the fear is useful to the bird, since useful capacities tend to be built in and less useful ones have to be learned.
options.why: Usefulness does not decide what is built in; learned capacities are useful too. The productive question is which of the candidates is being claimed.

options.text: Whether the fear varies from one bird to another, since a capacity that varies between individuals must be a learned one.
options.why: Built-in features can vary between individuals, and learned ones can be very uniform. The productive question is what exactly is claimed to be built in.

items.stem: Many flowers carry patterns that reflect ultraviolet light. Bees have receptors that respond to ultraviolet light, and the human eye does not. Two flowers differ only in their ultraviolet patterns. What follows for a person trying to learn to tell them apart by eye?

options.text: No amount of training will help, since no receptor the person has responds to the two flowers differently.
options.why: Correct. Which receptors an animal has determines which feature space it starts in and which differences it can register at all. The input space is the first way knowledge can be built in.

options.text: Enough training will help, since a hidden layer can come to stand for any difference that exists among the inputs.
options.why: A hidden layer recodes the differences its inputs carry. If no receptor responds differently to the two flowers, there is no difference in the input for it to recode.

options.text: Training will help if it is spread out over time, since learning in sequence protects old learning from new.
options.why: Learning in sequence is what causes catastrophic interference, not what prevents it. And no schedule of training can register a difference no receptor responds to.

options.text: Training will help once the person’s criterion for calling the flowers different is lowered, so weaker evidence is accepted.
options.why: Moving the criterion never changes sensitivity. With no receptor responding differently, the evidence for the two flowers is the same, wherever the criterion sits.

items.stem: Convolution and a large random expansion layer, like the one in the fruit fly’s brain, are both ways knowledge can be built in. What kind of built-in knowledge are they?

options.text: Architectural biases, assumptions about the task placed in the wiring before learning starts.
options.why: Correct. Convolution assumes a feature means the same thing wherever it appears, and a random expansion layer assumes useful combinations will turn up among many random ones.

options.text: Learning rules, which set what each weight change depends on after the system starts to learn.
options.why: A learning rule is the third candidate. Convolution and random expansion are fixed in the wiring before learning starts, which makes them architectural biases.

options.text: Input spaces, which set which differences in the world a system can register at all, before anything is learned.
options.why: The input space is set by the receptors. Convolution and random expansion operate on inputs already registered, through how the units are wired.

options.text: Specific content, detectors already wired for one particular thing in the world, such as a predator.
options.why: Specific content is a detector for one particular thing. Convolution and random expansion are general assumptions about any task, not detectors for particular things.

items.stem: Two networks receive exactly the same inputs. One is trained by backpropagation and the other by competitive learning. Why do they come to represent different things?

options.text: The two rules respond to different information, so the learning rule is itself part of what is built in.
options.why: Correct. The learning rule, what a weight change depends on, is the third way knowledge can be built in. Different rules, given the same inputs, come to represent different things.

options.text: The two networks were given different feature engineering, so their inputs carried different structure.
options.why: The inputs were exactly the same, so no difference in feature engineering is involved. The difference lies in what each rule’s weight changes depend on.

options.text: Competitive learning needs a target for every output, and it learns whatever reduces error on the task.
options.why: That describes backpropagation. Competitive learning needs no teacher; units compete, and only the winner moves its weights toward the input.

options.text: Backpropagation gives each thing its own unit, while competitive learning spreads each thing across many units.
options.why: Neither rule is defined by whether its code is localist or distributed. The two differ in the information their weight changes depend on.

items.stem: A rat links a new flavor with illness after a single pairing, even with hours between them, but hardly links a flavor with a shock at all. Which way of building knowledge in does this illustrate?

options.text: The learning rule, since the pattern shows which pairings the rat’s learning links most readily.
options.why: Correct. Animals differ in what their learning rules link most readily, and that difference is in place before the rat ever tastes the flavor.

options.text: The input space, since the pattern shows which flavors the rat’s receptors can register before it links them to anything.
options.why: The rat registers the flavor in both cases. What differs is which pairings its learning links readily, illness yes and shock hardly at all.

options.text: An architectural bias, since the pattern shows how the rat’s taste receptors are wired to each other.
options.why: Nothing here concerns how receptors are wired to one another. The asymmetry is in what the rat’s learning links.

options.text: Specific content, since the pattern shows a detector already wired for one particular food.
options.why: The rat avoids the flavor only after it has been paired with illness, so this is not a ready-made detector for one food. What is built in is a readiness to link flavor with illness.

items.stem: Newborn human babies, in their first hour, turn their eyes further to follow a pattern arranged like a face than to follow one with the same parts scrambled. Which candidate for what is built in does this bear on?

options.text: Specific content, something already wired to respond to one particular kind of thing.
options.why: Correct. The fourth candidate is specific content, such as a detector already wired for one particular predator, or caregiver. A preference for face-like patterns in the first hour bears on it.

options.text: The input space, since newborns have face receptors in the eye that adults lose.
options.why: The two patterns have the same parts, so they reach the same receptors. What differs is the arrangement, which is why this bears on specific content.

options.text: A learning rule, since the babies learned what faces look like during their first hour.
options.why: The chapter offers the first-hour result as evidence about specific content, a response to one particular arrangement of parts, not as an example of a learning rule. A learning rule is what a weight change depends on, as in the rat’s readiness to link a flavor with illness.

options.text: An architectural bias, since convolution finds a face wherever it falls in view.
options.why: Convolution is an assumption about networks, that a feature means the same thing anywhere. The newborn result is about a preference for one particular arrangement.

items.stem: With 10 input features there are 45 possible pairs, 120 possible triples, and more than a thousand possible combinations of all sizes, and a fish has many dozens of kinds of smell receptor. What does this arithmetic count against?

options.text: Building everything in, since a ready-made detector for every combination is out of the question.
options.why: Correct. That is the first of two reasons against building everything in. The number of combinations grows explosively, and which few will matter cannot be settled in advance.

options.text: Learning about combinations at all, since no learner could search through more than a thousand possibilities.
options.why: The same arithmetic is why learning is valuable: learning can arrive at the combinations a task needs without anyone listing them in advance.

options.text: Using hidden layers, since each possible combination would need a hidden unit of its own.
options.why: Hidden layers are valuable for exactly this reason. Learning in them arrives at the few combinations needed, not at every possible one.

options.text: Having receptors at all, since a receptor can respond to only one feature of a smell at a time.
options.why: Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in. The arithmetic is about detectors for combinations of what receptors register.

items.stem: A predatory fish of a kind that has never lived in a certain lake is released into it. Which minnows in the lake are more likely to end up avoiding its smell?

options.text: Minnows whose avoidance of predator smells is learned, since learning can follow a change that a detector fitted to the ancestors’ predators cannot.
