options.why: Correct. That is the second reason against building everything in: when the world changes, with a new predator or a new food, a built-in detector cannot follow, and learning can. It is a claim about a changed world, not a verdict that learning beats building in everywhere.

options.text: Minnows with a built-in detector for predators, since a built-in detector responds faster than any learned one.
options.why: Speed is not what the chapter compares. A detector that fits the ancestors’ predators has no reason to respond to a predator its ancestors never encountered.

options.text: Minnows with more kinds of smell receptor, since more receptors give a detector for every combination.
options.why: More receptors make the number of possible combinations larger, not smaller. A detector for every combination is out of the question.

options.text: Minnows whose built-in predator detectors are the most finely tuned, since a sharper detector for the ancestors’ predators also catches new ones.
options.why: A detector tuned more finely to the ancestors’ predators fits that past still more closely, and does nothing for a predator the lineage never encountered. When the world changes, a built-in detector cannot follow, and learning can.

items.stem: In what sense is building in too much described as “a kind of overfitting”?

options.text: A built-in solution fits the world the lineage lived in, as an overfit network fits its training set, and fails when that world changes.
options.why: Correct. The lineage’s past plays the part of the training set. A built-in detector fits it well, and when a new predator or a new food arrives the detector cannot follow.

options.text: A built-in solution fits the animal’s own early experience so closely that its later experience can no longer change anything.
options.why: A built-in solution comes from the lineage, not from the animal’s own experience. The overfitting is to the lineage’s past.

options.text: A built-in solution adds so many detectors that the animal reacts to harmless things, raising its rate of false alarms.
options.why: False alarms are a matter of the criterion, from signal detection theory. The overfitting in question is fitting a world that may no longer exist.

options.text: A built-in solution fits its predators so closely that small deliberate changes to their smell fool it, as adversarial examples fool a network.
options.why: Adversarial examples are a different failure. The comparison with overfitting is about fitting the past, which fails when the world changes.

items.stem: In machine learning, what is feature engineering?

options.text: Deciding, before any learning begins, what the inputs to a learning system will be, the built-in side of the choice.
options.why: Correct. It is the machine-learning name for the built-in side of the choice between building in and learning.

options.text: Adjusting a network’s hidden weights during training so that its hidden units come to stand for useful features.
options.why: That is learning in a hidden layer, by backpropagation for example. Feature engineering is decided before learning begins.

options.text: Building into a network’s wiring the assumption that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears.
options.why: That is convolution, an architectural bias. Feature engineering is about what the inputs will be, not how the units are wired.

options.text: Copying each training image shifted, rotated, or rescaled, so that a network sees more variety in training.
options.why: That is a way of training networks across changes of size and angle, and it changes the training examples. Feature engineering decides what kind of input the learner receives.

items.stem: Researchers who disagree about nativism are often disagreeing about different items among the four candidates. Where are the live disputes?

options.text: Over how much specific content must be supplied in advance, and how much a general architecture and learning rule can extract.
options.why: Correct. Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in, and few doubt that some architectural biases are. The disputes are over specific content and what general learning can extract.

options.text: Over whether receptors are built in, and whether architectural biases such as convolution are in place before learning starts.
options.why: These are the least disputed candidates. Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in, and few doubt that some architectural biases are.

options.text: Over whether anything is built in, since the four candidates are about equally contested among researchers who study them.
options.why: The candidates are not equally contested. Receptors and some architectural biases are barely doubted; the disputes are over specific content and general learning.

options.text: Over whether learning rules exist, since what a weight change depends on has not been shown to differ between animals.
options.why: Learning rules do differ between animals: a rat links flavor with illness far more readily than with shock. The live disputes lie elsewhere.

items.stem: Wild minnows of two species both flee from the odor of pike. What would show whether either species’ reaction comes from a ready-made detector or a learned one?

options.text: Raising fish of each species that never encounter a pike, then testing whether they react the first time they smell its odor.
options.why: Correct. A ready-made detector and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, and only experiments on animals raised without the experience can tell them apart. The answer can differ by species.

options.text: Timing how fast wild fish of each species flee, to see whether a ready-made detector gives a faster escape than a learned one.
options.why: The two kinds of detector can produce the same behavior, so watching wild fish react cannot tell them apart. The test needs fish raised without the experience.

options.text: Counting each species’ kinds of smell receptor, since a species with more kinds of receptor must have learned its reaction.
options.why: The number of receptor kinds does not reveal whether a reaction was learned. Only fish raised without ever encountering a pike can show that.

options.text: Testing wild fish with pike odor mixed among other smells, since a learned detector fails whenever its odor is mixed.
options.why: Nothing suggests that learned detectors fail on mixtures. What separates the two is whether the reaction appears without any experience of pike.

items.stem: In a few sentences, give the two reasons that building everything in is not a good solution, and explain why one of them is described as a kind of overfitting.
items.answer: The first reason is size. The number of possible combinations of features grows explosively: with 10 features there are 45 pairs, 120 triples, and more than a thousand combinations of all sizes, and a fish has many dozens of kinds of smell receptor. A detector for every combination is out of the question, and which few will matter cannot be settled in advance. The second reason is change. A built-in solution fits the world the animal’s ancestors lived in, and when that world changes, with a new predator or a new food, a built-in detector cannot follow, while learning can. That is like overfitting: as an overfit network fits its training examples and does poorly on new ones, a built-in solution fits the lineage’s past and does poorly when the world changes.
rubric: Gives size as one reason: the number of combinations grows explosively, so a detector for every combination is out of the question.
Gives change as the other reason: a built-in solution fits the ancestors’ world and cannot follow a new predator or food.
Says that learning can follow a changed world where a built-in detector cannot.
Explains the overfitting comparison: fitting the lineage’s past as an overfit network fits its training examples.

items.stem: Wild fish of a newly studied species flee from the odor of a predatory crab. In a short paragraph, describe an experiment that would show whether the reaction comes from a ready-made detector or a learned one, explain why watching wild adults cannot settle the question, and say how the reaction might be learned if it is.
items.answer: A ready-made detector and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, so wild adults, which have probably encountered crabs or their odor, cannot tell them apart. The experiment is to raise fish of this species without ever encountering the crab, and test whether they react the first time they smell its odor. If they react, there is evidence of a ready-made detector; if they do not, the reaction is probably learned. If it is learned, one way is associative learning: a fish that smells the crab at the same time as chemicals released from the injured skin of another fish of its own kind comes to avoid the crab’s odor afterward. The answer could differ from one species to another, as it does among fish.
rubric: States that a ready-made and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, so wild adults cannot settle it.
Proposes raising fish without any encounter with the crab and testing their reaction on first exposure to its odor.
Describes a learned route: pairing the predator’s odor with chemicals from the injured skin of a fish of the same kind.
Notes that the answer can differ between species, keeping it hedged.

pools.title: The Oldest Cortex: Separating and Completing Smells
pools.covers: reading §7.3.1, §7.3.2, §7.3.3 · lecture 7.3 slides title, the_oldest_cortex, pulling_similar_smells_apart, completing_from_part

items.stem: What is the piriform cortex?

options.text: The three-layered olfactory cortex of mammals, which receives the olfactory bulb’s output directly, without a relay in the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. In mammals the piriform cortex is the first cortex a smell reaches. It is older in form than the neocortex, and its input arrives straight from the olfactory bulb.

options.text: The six-layered sheet that makes up most of the mammalian pallium, which receives signals from the eyes, the skin, and the ears through the thalamus.
options.why: That describes the neocortex. The piriform cortex has three layers, not six, and smell reaches it without passing through a relay in the thalamus.

options.text: The first stop for signals from the nose, which gathers them before sending its own output on to the cortex for the next stage of work on a smell.
options.why: That is the olfactory bulb. The bulb sends its output to the piriform cortex, which is the cortex that receives it.

options.text: The structure in the insect brain where smell inputs are spread across many more cells, through connections that appear random, with learning at its output.
options.why: That is the mushroom body. It resembles the piriform cortex in some ways, but it belongs to an insect, and the piriform cortex belongs to a mammal.

items.stem: What is the name for the three-layered sheet in mammals that receives the olfactory bulb’s output directly, without a relay in the thalamus?

options.text: Piriform cortex.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex is the first cortex a smell reaches in mammals, and its input comes straight from the olfactory bulb.

options.text: Mushroom body.
options.why: The mushroom body is where smell inputs are spread across many more cells in an insect brain. The three-layered sheet in mammals is the piriform cortex.

options.text: Ventral stream.
options.why: The ventral stream is a series of visual areas running from the primary visual cortex to the inferior temporal cortex. It has nothing to do with the olfactory bulb.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: The pyramidal neuron is the cell the piriform cortex is built around, not the sheet itself. The sheet is the piriform cortex.

items.stem: Signals from the eyes, the ears, and the skin each reach the cortex through a relay in the thalamus. How do signals from the nose reach the cortex in a mammal?

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output straight to the piriform cortex, so smell reaches the cortex with no relay in the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. Smell is the exception among the senses. The olfactory bulb, the first stop for signals from the nose, sends its output directly to the piriform cortex, the first cortex a smell reaches.

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output to a smell relay in the thalamus, which passes it on to the piriform cortex as it would for any other sense.
options.why: That is the route the other senses take. What makes the piriform cortex unusual is that its input arrives from the olfactory bulb with no relay in the thalamus.

options.text: The nose sends its signals straight to the piriform cortex, and the olfactory bulb receives them only after the piriform cortex has worked on them.
options.why: That reverses the order. The olfactory bulb is the first stop for signals from the nose, and the piriform cortex receives the bulb’s output.

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output to layer 4 of the neocortex, the layer that receives the input the thalamus relays to the sensory areas.
options.why: Layer 4 is where the neocortex receives input relayed by the thalamus. A smell’s first cortex is the three-layered piriform cortex, reached without that relay.

items.stem: What is a pyramidal neuron?

options.text: The main excitatory cell of the cortex, with a roughly triangular cell body, a long apical dendrite reaching toward the surface, and shorter dendrites near the cell body.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex and the neocortex are both built around the pyramidal neuron. The olfactory bulb’s input lands on the far ends of its apical dendrites.

options.text: A smaller cell that sits among the excitatory cells of the cortex and damps their activity down, acting on the cell bodies of the excitatory cells on either side of it.
options.why: That describes the inhibitory cells that sit among the pyramidal neurons. The pyramidal neuron is the excitatory cell whose activity they damp.

options.text: A cell in the insect mushroom body that receives input from a few of about 50 kinds of smell input, wired at random, and responds sparsely to each odor.
options.why: That is a Kenyon cell, in a fly. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the mammalian cortex, recognized by its shape.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of a particular orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: That is a complex cell, defined by what it responds to. A pyramidal neuron is defined by its shape and by its place as the cortex’s main excitatory cell.

items.stem: What is the name for the main excitatory cell of the cortex, with a roughly triangular cell body, a long apical dendrite reaching toward the surface, and shorter dendrites near the cell body?

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: Correct. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the piriform cortex and of the neocortex alike.

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: A simple cell is defined by its receptive field, divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it, not by its shape.

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: A complex cell is defined by what it responds to, an edge of one orientation anywhere in a fairly large receptive field, not by its shape.

options.text: Piriform cortex.
options.why: The piriform cortex is the three-layered sheet built around this cell. The cell itself is the pyramidal neuron.

items.stem: Researchers record from the main excitatory cells in a rat’s piriform cortex, and then from the main excitatory cells in its neocortex. What kind of cell are they most likely recording from in each?

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in both, since the pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the piriform cortex and of the neocortex alike.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex is built around the pyramidal neuron, which is also the main excitatory cell of the neocortex.

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in the neocortex only, since the older, three-layered piriform cortex is built around a simpler and older kind of cell.
options.why: Being older in form does not mean the piriform cortex lacks pyramidal neurons; it is built around them. It is the lamprey’s pallium whose cells lack part of the pyramidal neuron.

options.text: A different kind of cell in each, since the main excitatory cell of a cortical sheet depends on which sense supplies the sheet’s input.
options.why: Input does shape what a cortical area does. But the pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of both the piriform cortex and the neocortex, though different senses feed them.

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in the piriform cortex only, since the neocortex’s six layers are built around simple cells and complex cells instead.
options.why: Simple and complex cells are kinds of cell in the primary visual cortex, defined by how they respond rather than by their shape, so they are not an alternative to the pyramidal neuron. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the neocortex, as it is of the piriform cortex.

items.stem: In the piriform cortex, each pyramidal neuron’s axon leaves the area, but on the way it sends side branches to other pyramidal neurons nearby. In the terms of Module 4, what are those side branches, and what can they let a circuit do?

options.text: Recurrent connections, through which the cells excite one another, of the kind that let a circuit hold a state.
options.why: Correct. The side branches let pyramidal neurons excite their neighbors. Connections of this kind let a Module 4 circuit hold a state, and they are what the proposal that the piriform cortex completes smells relies on.

options.text: Mutual inhibition, through which the cells silence one another, of the kind that lets one unit win in a winner-take-all circuit.
options.why: The side branches excite their neighbors rather than silencing them. Damping is done by separate inhibitory cells that sit among the pyramidal neurons.

options.text: A labeled line, through which each cell’s output is routed straight to the machinery that responds to one particular smell.
options.why: A labeled line runs from one kind of sensory neuron to the machinery that acts on it, like the worm’s copper neuron. These side branches end on neighboring pyramidal neurons.

options.text: A relay, through which each cell passes the olfactory bulb’s signals on to the thalamus to be sorted before they reach the neocortex.
options.why: Smell reaches the piriform cortex without any relay in the thalamus. The side branches stay local, ending on nearby pyramidal neurons.

items.stem: Two kinds of connection inside the piriform cortex act on its pyramidal neurons. How does the effect of the side branches of the pyramidal neurons’ axons differ from the effect of the inhibitory cells?

options.text: The side branches excite neighboring pyramidal neurons, while the inhibitory cells damp the pyramidal neurons’ activity down.
options.why: Correct. Through the side branches the pyramidal neurons excite one another, and the inhibitory cells sitting among them damp that activity down.

options.text: The side branches damp neighboring pyramidal neurons down, while the inhibitory cells excite the pyramidal neurons around them.
options.why: That swaps the two. The side branches are excitatory recurrent connections, and the inhibitory cells are the ones that damp activity.

options.text: The side branches carry the olfactory bulb’s input into the piriform cortex, while the inhibitory cells carry its output away.
options.why: The olfactory bulb’s input arrives on the tips of the apical dendrites, and the output leaves along the main axon. The side branches link neighbors.

options.text: The side branches connect the piriform cortex to the thalamus, while the inhibitory cells connect it to the olfactory bulb.
options.why: No relay in the thalamus is involved. Both kinds of connection act within the piriform cortex, one exciting and one damping.

items.stem: In a topographic map, neighboring cells handle neighboring points in the world. A student expects the piriform cortex to be laid out in the same way, with neighboring cells responding to similar odors. What did the imaging study find?

options.text: The active cells were scattered with no clustering, and a cell’s neighbor was as likely to respond to a quite different odor as to the same one.
options.why: Correct. There was no map in the piriform cortex. Cells that responded to the same odor were not clustered together.

options.text: The active cells were clustered, so that the cells responding to the same odor sat together and their neighbors usually responded to that odor too.
options.why: Clustering is what the student expected, and it is not what was found. The cells responding to one odor were scattered.

options.text: The active cells were arranged by chemical structure, so that neighboring cells responded to odors whose molecules were alike in their structure.
options.why: An arrangement by structure would be a map, and the piriform cortex showed none. A neighbor was as likely to respond to a quite different odor.

options.text: The active cells were arranged by the odor’s strength, with cells near the surface responding to faint odors and deeper cells to strong ones.
options.why: The study reported no arrangement of this kind. The active cells were scattered, with no clustering and no map.

items.stem: Two odors with almost the same chemical structure are presented to a mouse. How does the overlap between the two odors at the olfactory bulb compare with their overlap in the piriform cortex?

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share more than 70 percent of their active inputs; in the piriform cortex they share only about a quarter of their active cells.
options.why: Correct. Two smells that look alike at the olfactory bulb look much less alike in the piriform cortex. That drop in overlap is pattern separation.

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share only about a quarter of their active inputs; in the piriform cortex they come to share more than 70 percent of their active cells.
options.why: That reverses the two stages. The overlap is high at the olfactory bulb and much lower in the piriform cortex.

options.text: At both stages they share more than 70 percent, since the piriform cortex passes the olfactory bulb’s pattern on to later stages unchanged.
options.why: The piriform cortex does not pass the pattern on unchanged. The two similar odors overlapped far less there than at the olfactory bulb.

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share more than 70 percent; in the piriform cortex they share no active cells, so similar odors are kept completely apart.
options.why: The overlap fell a long way but not to zero. The two similar odors still shared about a quarter of their active piriform cells.

items.stem: What is pattern separation?

options.text: Making inputs that overlap a great deal less alike than they were, so that a later stage can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. In the piriform cortex, two similar smells that overlap heavily at the olfactory bulb overlap much less, and that change is pattern separation.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a partial input gives the response the whole would.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which brings a partial input back to a whole pattern. Pattern separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units, so that a single straight boundary is more likely to separate the cases.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion. Pattern separation is defined by what happens to overlap, not by how many units carry the input.

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, the storing that makes pattern completion possible. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike.

items.stem: A deer browses two kinds of berry, one safe and one toxic, whose smells activate nearly the same inputs in its olfactory bulb. If its piriform cortex carries out pattern separation on those two smells, what happens, and why does it help the deer?

options.text: The two smells activate much less overlapping sets of piriform cells, so that the cells reading the piriform cortex’s output can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation is discrimination carried out by a circuit. Smells that overlap heavily at the olfactory bulb are made less alike, so a later stage can respond to them differently.

options.text: The two smells activate one shared set of piriform cells, so that the deer learns to treat both kinds of berry as a single kind of food to eat.
options.why: Drawing two inputs together is what generalization asks for, and it would be the wrong outcome here. Pattern separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: The olfactory bulb’s inputs for the two smells are made less alike, so that the piriform cortex receives patterns that are already separated.
options.why: In the piriform measurements, the overlap stayed high at the olfactory bulb. It was in the piriform cortex that similar smells came to overlap less.

options.text: Each smell activates its own single piriform cell, so that which cell fires is enough by itself to say which kind of berry is in front of the deer.
options.why: No single piriform cell stands for an odor. What identifies an odor is which set of cells is active.

items.stem: In the imaging study, one piriform cell responded to two odors whose chemical structures were unrelated. What does that finding imply about how the piriform cortex identifies an odor?

options.text: By which set of cells is active, since no single cell stands for any one odor.
options.why: Correct. A cell that responds to unrelated odors cannot stand for either one. The identity of an odor lies in the whole set of active cells.

options.text: By which single cell responds most strongly, since each odor has one cell that responds to it best.
options.why: That is a code with one cell per odor, and the finding rules it out. A cell responding to two unrelated odors stands for neither.

options.text: By how many cells are active, since odors with more complex structures activate larger sets of cells.
options.why: The study reported nothing linking set size to complexity. What identifies an odor is which cells are active, not how many.

options.text: By where the active cells lie, since each odor activates its own cluster of neighboring cells.
options.why: The active cells were scattered, with no clustering and no map, so location does not identify the odor.

items.stem: Suppose each piriform cell in a mouse receives input from a random handful of the olfactory bulb’s outputs. What follows about how the mouse comes to treat the smell of one particular kind of seed as meaning that food is near?

options.text: What the smell means cannot be built into the piriform cortex, so it has to come from the animal’s experience with that smell.
options.why: Correct. Random wiring carries no built-in meaning. If the wiring is random, the meaning of an odor has to come from experience.

options.text: What the smell means is built into the piriform cortex before birth, since connections that are wired at random do not change afterward.
options.why: Random wiring is exactly what rules out built-in meaning. Whether the random connections themselves change is beside the point; the meaning has to be learned.

options.text: What the smell means is fixed in the olfactory bulb, since the piriform cortex passes a random sample of the bulb’s signals on unchanged.
options.why: Nothing in the account places the meaning of a smell in the olfactory bulb. With random wiring into the piriform cortex, the meaning has to come from experience.

options.text: What the smell means cannot be learned, since connections wired at random leave nothing that experience could go on to adjust.
options.why: Random wiring with a trained output is a way of learning. The input wiring is random, and what an odor means is set by experience at the output.

items.stem: A classmate writes, “The imaging study showed that the piriform cortex is wired at random”. What is wrong with the sentence?

options.text: Random wiring is a model that fits the study’s data; the study observed which cells responded, not how they were connected.
options.why: Correct. The study measured responses. Random wiring was proposed to explain them, and it is a model that fits the data, not something the study observed.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since scattered responses with no map could only have come from wiring that is random.
options.why: Random wiring fits the data, but fitting is not observing, and the account never says no other wiring could produce the result.

options.text: The study showed the reverse, that each piriform cell receives its input from one family of related chemical structures.
options.why: The study did not show orderly wiring either. It measured responses, and random wiring was the proposed explanation.

options.text: Random wiring was observed in the study, but only for odors with unrelated structures, and not for the similar ones.
options.why: The study observed no wiring at all, for any odors. It imaged which cells responded.

items.stem: A student argues that the piriform cortex must work like the perceptron’s middle layer, spreading the olfactory bulb’s input across many more cells than it receives from. What does the imaging study say about that claim?

options.text: Nothing either way, since the study did not count cells and so cannot say whether any expansion happens in the piriform cortex.
options.why: Correct. Expansion is a question about numbers of cells, and the study did not count them. Whether the piriform cortex expands its input is untested by it.

options.text: It supports the claim, since each odor activated only 3 to 15 percent of the cells, which is what an expansion produces.
options.why: Sparse activity is not the same thing as expansion. A small active share says nothing about whether there are more cells than inputs.

options.text: It refutes the claim, since two similar odors still shared about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex.
options.why: A remaining overlap does not bear on how many cells there are. The study did not count cells, so it neither supports nor refutes expansion.

options.text: It supports the claim, since the study observed random wiring, and random wiring always comes together with an expansion.
options.why: The study did not observe the wiring, and random wiring is a model that fits its data. Expansion was not tested.

items.stem: Pattern separation and dimensionality expansion are easy to run together. How do they differ, as far as the piriform cortex is concerned?

options.text: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike and was measured there; expansion spreads input across more cells and was not tested by the imaging study.
options.why: Correct. The imaging study measured a drop in overlap, which is pattern separation. It did not count cells, so it says nothing about expansion.

options.text: Pattern separation spreads input across more cells and was not tested by the imaging study; expansion makes overlapping inputs less alike and was measured there.
options.why: That swaps the two definitions. Pattern separation is about overlap and was measured; expansion is about the number of cells, which the study did not count.

options.text: They are one operation under two names, so the imaging study that measured pattern separation also measured expansion there.
options.why: They are different operations. One is defined by overlap and the other by the number of cells, and the study measured only overlap.

options.text: Pattern separation needs a teacher to set its weights, while expansion needs no training, so only expansion fits random wiring.
options.why: The proposed random wiring is offered as an explanation of the measured pattern separation. Neither operation is defined by needing a teacher.

items.stem: What is auto-association?

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: Correct. The patterns are stored in the connections among the very cells that carry them, which is what makes later completion from part possible.

options.text: Pairing two different things, such as a tone and food, by strengthening the connections that link their separate representations.
options.why: That is learning to pair two different things, as in Module 5. Auto-association stores a pattern in the connections among its own cells.

options.text: Learning in which units that receive the same input inhibit one another until one wins, and only the winner moves its weights.
options.why: That is competitive learning, which needs no teacher and finds clusters of inputs. Auto-association stores whole patterns in a circuit’s own connections.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern when only part of it arrives, as when a faint trace of a smell gives the whole smell’s response.
options.why: That is pattern completion, the recovery that auto-association makes possible. Auto-association names the storing.

items.stem: What is the name for storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest?

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Correct. Auto-association is the storing; pattern completion is the recovery it makes possible.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. The storing that makes it possible is auto-association.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning has units inhibit one another until one wins and moves its weights. It does not store whole patterns among a circuit’s own cells.

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation is a code in which each thing is a pattern across many units. Storing such patterns in a circuit’s own connections is auto-association.

items.stem: What is pattern completion?

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a partial input produces the response the whole would.
options.why: Correct. A faint or partial version of a familiar smell can produce the response the whole smell would, if the pattern has been stored.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike than they were, so that a later stage can tell those inputs apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which pulls overlapping inputs apart. Pattern completion brings a partial input back to a whole.

options.text: Adding an input, such as the product of two smells, so that a single straight line can separate the cases that matter.
options.why: Adding a feature can make a hard problem easy for one straight line, but that is not completion. Completion recovers a stored pattern from part of it.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, through wiring that is random and is never trained.
options.why: That is random expansion, as in the mushroom body. Pattern completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it.

items.stem: What is the name for recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it?

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Correct. Pattern completion is generalization, one of the two demands of recognition, carried out by a circuit.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike. Recovering a whole pattern from part runs the other way, and is pattern completion.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association is the storing of patterns in a circuit’s own connections. The recovery that storing makes possible is pattern completion.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units. It stores nothing and recovers nothing.

items.stem: Recognizing a smell makes two demands: telling apart inputs that call for different responses, and treating alike inputs that call for the same one. How do the two circuit operations studied in the piriform cortex line up with those demands?

options.text: Pattern separation carries out the telling apart, and pattern completion carries out the treating alike.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation is discrimination carried out by a circuit, and pattern completion is generalization carried out by a circuit.

options.text: Pattern completion carries out the telling apart, and pattern separation carries out the treating alike.
options.why: That swaps the two. Completion brings a partial input back to a whole, which treats it alike; separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: Pattern separation carries out both, since making smells less alike also lets a faint trace match the whole smell.
options.why: Making smells less alike works against matching a faint trace to the whole. Treating alike is the job of pattern completion.

options.text: Pattern completion carries out both, since recovering whole patterns also keeps two similar smells from being confused.
options.why: Recovering a whole from part draws inputs together, which does nothing to keep similar smells apart. That is the job of pattern separation.

items.stem: How does the evidence for pattern separation in the piriform cortex compare with the evidence for pattern completion there?

options.text: Pattern separation has been measured directly in mice, while pattern completion there comes mostly from models, with few direct tests in animals.
options.why: Correct. The lecture sets the two side by side as a difference in the grade of evidence: separation was measured, and completion in the piriform cortex is mostly a model result.

options.text: Pattern completion has been measured directly in mice, while pattern separation there comes mostly from models, with few direct tests in living animals.
options.why: That swaps the two. The imaging study measured separation; completion is supported mainly by network models of the piriform circuit.

options.text: Both have been measured directly in mice, in the same imaging study that presented one odor after another to many cells at once.
options.why: The imaging study measured the overlap between odors, which is separation. It did not test completion from part of a smell.

options.text: Both come only from network models, since neither operation could be measured in the piriform cortex of a living animal.
options.why: Separation was measured directly in anesthetized mice. Only completion rests mostly on models.

items.stem: A news story reports that “scientists have proved that the piriform cortex of a mouse completes smells from fragments”. How does the chapter’s account of the evidence differ?

options.text: Models built on the piriform circuit complete patterns from part, but direct tests in animals are few, so the support comes mostly from models.
options.why: Correct. Network models of the piriform circuit do store and complete patterns. In animals the direct tests are few, so the claim is a proposal with mostly model support.

options.text: The account agrees with the story, since the imaging study that measured pattern separation in mice measured pattern completion in the same animals.
options.why: The imaging study measured how much odors overlap, which is separation. It did not test completion, which rests mostly on models.

options.text: The account reverses the story, since a circuit shown to pull similar smells apart has been shown to be unable to complete them as well.
options.why: Nothing shows the piriform cortex cannot complete smells. The hippocampus, for example, is proposed to do both separation and completion.

options.text: The account limits the story to the hippocampus, since pattern completion has been tested in the piriform cortex of mice and ruled out.
options.why: Completion has not been ruled out in the piriform cortex. Direct tests there are few, and the hippocampus is named as another proposed site.

items.stem: Claims about the piriform cortex rest on evidence of different strengths. In a short paragraph, sort these four claims by what supports each, and say why the difference matters: similar smells are pulled apart there; its wiring is random; it spreads its input across more cells than it receives from; it completes a familiar smell from part of it.
items.answer: That similar smells are pulled apart was measured directly: in the imaging study, two similar odors that shared more than 70 percent of their active inputs at the olfactory bulb shared only about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex, though how much they overlap depends on how strongly a cell must respond to be counted as active. That the wiring is random is a model that fits those data; the study did not observe the wiring. Whether the input is spread across more cells was not tested by the study, because it did not count cells. And completion from part comes mostly from network models, with few direct tests in animals. The difference matters because a model that fits the data, or a possibility the study did not test, should not be reported as if it had been observed.
rubric: Identifies pattern separation as measured directly.
Identifies random wiring as a model that fits the data, not something observed.
Identifies expansion as not tested by the study, because it did not count cells.
Identifies pattern completion as supported mostly by models, with few direct tests in animals.
Says why the grades matter, for example that a model or an untested possibility should not be reported as an observation.

pools.title: Other Brains, and One Plan Across Many Areas
pools.covers: reading §7.3.4, §7.3.5 · lecture 7.3 slides a_fly_a_bird_a_fish, one_plan_many_areas, rewired_ferrets

items.stem: What is the mushroom body?

options.text: An insect brain structure that spreads smell inputs across many more cells through connections that appear random, with learning at the connections to its output neurons.
options.why: Correct. In the fruit fly, about 50 kinds of smell input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells through combinations that look random, and the learning happens downstream, at the connections to the output neurons.

options.text: A structure in the mammalian brain, a sheet of three layers, where the olfactory bulb’s output arrives directly, without passing through a relay in the thalamus on the way.
options.why: That describes the piriform cortex of mammals. The mushroom body is in insects, and what defines it is the random spread of smell input across many Kenyon cells.

options.text: A structure in the insect brain where each kind of smell input has a dedicated cell of its own, laid out so that neighboring cells handle smells that are chemically similar.
options.why: That would be a localist code arranged as a topographic map. In the mushroom body each Kenyon cell combines a few inputs, the combinations look random, and there is no map.

options.text: A structure in the insect brain where the connections from the smell inputs are trained by passing an error back from the output neurons after each wrong response.
options.why: Passing errors back is backpropagation. The connections into the mushroom body’s Kenyon cells are never trained; learning happens only at the connections to the output neurons.

items.stem: Random wiring has been proposed both for the mouse’s piriform cortex and for the fruit fly’s mushroom body. Why does the fly give the clearer evidence?

options.text: In the fly, the connections of Kenyon cells were traced and looked random; in the mouse, random wiring is only a model that fits the measured activity.
options.why: Correct. In the piriform cortex, pattern separation was measured and random wiring is a model that fits it. In the fly, the wiring itself was traced, which is why an insect gives the clearest evidence.

options.text: In the fly, every odor activates nearly all of the Kenyon cells at once; in the mouse, only a few piriform cells respond to each odor, which hides the wiring.
options.why: Kenyon cells respond sparsely, so each odor activates only a few of them, much as in the piriform cortex. The difference in the evidence is that the fly’s wiring was traced.

options.text: In the fly, the random combinations are identical in every animal, so they can be mapped once and for all; in the mouse, they differ from one animal to the next.
options.why: That reverses the tracing result. The fly’s combinations differed from fly to fly. What makes the fly the clearer case is that its connections were traced at all.

options.text: In the fly, learning happens at the Kenyon cells’ input connections, where it can be watched directly; in the mouse, it happens only at the output connections.
options.why: The fly’s input connections are never trained; its learning happens downstream, at the connections to the output neurons. The fly is clearer because its wiring was traced.

items.stem: In the fruit fly’s mushroom body, how does the number of kinds of smell input compare with the number of Kenyon cells, and how many of those inputs does each Kenyon cell receive?

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives a few of the 50 kinds.
options.why: Correct. A few dozen kinds of input are spread across tens of times as many cells, each combining a few of them. That spreading is the expansion the mushroom body is known for.

options.text: About 2,000 kinds of input converge on about 50 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives hundreds of them.
options.why: That runs the arrangement backward, compressing many inputs into few cells. The mushroom body expands about 50 kinds of input into about 2,000 cells.

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 50 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives exactly one kind of input.
options.why: A one-to-one relay would add no new combinations at all. Each Kenyon cell combines a few of the 50 inputs, and there are about 2,000 Kenyon cells.

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives all 50, weighted differently.
options.why: The counts are right, but each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the 50 kinds. Combining a random few is what gives each cell a different combination to respond to.

items.stem: Researchers traced which kinds of smell input reach each of 200 Kenyon cells in fruit flies. What did the tracing find?

options.text: The combinations looked random, and they were not the same from one fly to the next.
options.why: Correct. No structure appeared in which Kenyon cell received which inputs, and the combinations differed between flies. That is the clearest evidence for random wiring.

options.text: The combinations looked random, but every fly had exactly the same set of combinations.
options.why: The combinations did look random, but they were not shared between flies. Each fly’s combinations were different.

options.text: The combinations were orderly, with neighboring Kenyon cells receiving the same few inputs.
options.why: That would be a map, with neighbors alike. The tracing found no structure of that kind; the combinations looked random.

options.text: The combinations were orderly, with each Kenyon cell receiving every kind of input.
options.why: Each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the roughly 50 kinds of input, and which few looked random.

items.stem: An engineer builds a smell sensor for a robot. Thirty kinds of chemical detector feed 3,000 middle units, each connected to a random four of the detectors, and those connections are never adjusted. Only the connections from the middle units to the output are trained. Which way of setting a hidden layer’s weights does the design use, and which animal structure shows it most plainly?

options.text: Fixed random wiring with a trained output, the arrangement found in the fruit fly’s mushroom body.
options.why: Correct. A large middle layer wired at random and never trained, with learning only at the output, is the mushroom body’s arrangement: about 50 inputs spread across about 2,000 cells.

options.text: Error-driven learning, in which the error at the output trains every layer, as in the digit-reading network.
options.why: Passing the error back trains every weight in the network. The robot’s middle connections are never adjusted, which is the mark of fixed random wiring.

options.text: Competitive learning, with the middle units’ starting weights set at random, as in a topographic map formed by experience.
options.why: Competition moves the winning unit’s weights toward the input. The robot’s middle connections never move, and only the output is trained.

options.text: Auto-association, with the middle units trained so that part of a pattern brings back the rest, as proposed for the piriform cortex.
options.why: Auto-association stores patterns in a circuit’s connections among its own cells. The robot has no such connections, and its middle layer is never trained.

items.stem: The connections into the fruit fly’s Kenyon cells are never trained, and learning happens only at the connections to the output neurons. Why can that arrangement still let the fly learn from its experience with odors?

options.text: With about 2,000 cells each combining a random few of about 50 inputs, some cells are likely to respond to the combinations that matter, and only the output connections need to learn to read them.
options.why: Correct. Spreading a few inputs across many randomly combining cells makes useful combinations likely without anyone arranging them, so a single trained layer at the output can do the rest.

options.text: With each Kenyon cell receiving all of the roughly 50 inputs, every cell already carries every combination the fly could need, and the output only has to read any one of the cells.
options.why: Each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the inputs. The arrangement works because many cells combine a random few, which makes the needed combinations likely, not certain.

options.text: With the output neurons passing their errors back to the Kenyon cells, the input connections are corrected after each mistake, even though they start out wired at random in every fly.
options.why: That is backpropagation, and it would train the input connections. In the mushroom body those connections are never trained.

options.text: With the Kenyon cells competing until one wins for each odor, each odor ends up with a cell of its own, and the output connections only have to learn which cell goes with which odor.
options.why: That is competitive learning, which moves the winner’s weights. The mushroom body’s input connections are never trained, and no Kenyon cell is dedicated to one odor.

items.stem: A fruit fly is trained so that one odor comes with sugar, and afterward it approaches that odor. On the chapter’s account of the mushroom body, where does the change that stores this happen, and what settles which connections change?

options.text: At the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, where a signal carried by dopamine settles which of those connections change.
options.why: Correct. Learning happens downstream of the randomly wired Kenyon cells, and a dopamine signal settles which output connections change. That is Module 5’s three-factor rule.

options.text: At the connections from the smell inputs to the Kenyon cells, where a signal carried by dopamine settles which of them change, so that one cell comes to stand for the odor.
options.why: Dopamine is the right signal, but the connections into the Kenyon cells are never trained, and no single cell comes to stand for an odor. The change is at the output connections.

options.text: Among the Kenyon cells themselves, where connections between cells active together are strengthened so that part of the odor brings back the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, the proposal for the piriform cortex’s recurrent connections. In the mushroom body the change is at the output connections, under a dopamine signal.

options.text: At the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, where a connection strengthens whenever its two cells are active together, with no third signal.
options.why: The place is right, but activity at the two ends of a connection alone is Hebb’s rule. In the mushroom body a dopamine signal also settles which output connections change, which makes it the three-factor rule.

items.stem: The fly’s mushroom body and the mouse’s piriform cortex both spread smell input across many cells through connections that look random. Why is the resemblance read as convergent evolution rather than as a structure both animals inherited from a common ancestor?

options.text: The fly and mouse lineages have been separate for more than half a billion years, and the ancestor they share had nothing like either structure.
options.why: Correct. A structure the common ancestor lacked cannot have been inherited from it. So the two lineages arrived separately at a similar arrangement for a similar problem, which is convergent evolution in Module 2’s terms.

options.text: The fly’s wiring was traced while the mouse’s wiring is a model that fits the data, so the two cannot be counted as one and the same structure.
options.why: That difference is real, but it is a difference in the evidence, not in ancestry. The convergence reading rests on the common ancestor having had neither structure.

options.text: The two structures solve the same problem, and any two structures that solve the same problem count as convergent, whatever their ancestry.
options.why: Convergence is a claim about ancestry: the similar arrangement arose separately in each lineage. Doing the same job does not settle that; the family tree does.

options.text: The two structures differ in size and in the number of cells they hold, so they cannot have descended from a single structure in a shared ancestor.
options.why: Structures descended from one ancestral structure can still differ in size. The reading rests on the ancestor having had nothing like either structure.

items.stem: Fish have no neocortex. What does the chapter conclude about whether a fish can recognize objects?

options.text: A fish can recognize objects with no neocortex at all, though the study offered as evidence has a gap that keeps it from being clean.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says a fish can recognize objects without a neocortex, though the evidence is less clean than it sounds: in the goldfish study, the fish may have used color alone.

options.text: A fish cannot recognize objects without a neocortex, so the fish in recognition studies must have been using simpler cues.
options.why: The chapter does not tie object recognition to the neocortex. It says a fish can recognize objects without one, while noting that the evidence is less clean than it sounds.

options.text: A fish recognizes objects with a neocortex of its own, smaller than a mammal’s and with fewer layers.
options.why: A fish has no neocortex. It has a pallium, and it meets the recognition problem with other circuits.

options.text: A fish recognizes objects across rotation as cleanly as a mammal does, and the goldfish study settles it.
options.why: The chapter holds the goldfish result at arm’s length, since the two toys in that study always differed in color.

items.stem: Module 6 described the neocortex as a nearly uniform sheet. What correction does the chapter make to that description?

options.text: The neocortex is not one circuit copied identically from area to area, but one circuit plan repeated with variations.
options.why: Correct. The uniform-sheet description survives with that one correction. The areas share a plan, and they vary within it.

options.text: The neocortex is far from uniform, since each area is built from its own classes of cells, each suited to the area’s job.
options.why: That overcorrects. Every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way. What varies is how many cells of each class there are and how strongly they connect.

options.text: The neocortex is uniform across the sensory areas, while the motor cortex follows a separate plan of its own.
options.why: The motor cortex differs mainly in having little layer 4. It follows the same plan as the other areas, with variations.

options.text: No correction is needed, since the areas are copies of one identical circuit and differ in nothing but what connects to them.
options.why: That is the picture the chapter corrects. Areas are not identical copies; they differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly those cells connect.

items.stem: A town has many houses. Which way of building them best matches the chapter’s picture of how neocortical areas relate to one another?

options.text: All built from one blueprint, with rooms of different sizes in each house and wider or narrower doorways.
options.why: Correct. One plan repeated with variations: the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way, with areas differing in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly they connect.

options.text: All stamped from one mold, identical in every room, so that what goes on in each depends only on who moves in.
options.why: Identical copies whose use depends only on what arrives is the uniform-sheet picture the chapter corrects. Areas vary in cell counts and in connection strengths.

options.text: Each built to its own blueprint by a different architect, so that they share nothing but the street they stand on.
options.why: Areas do not each have their own plan. They share the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way.

options.text: Each built to a different blueprint, yet alike from the street because every one was built for the same weather.
options.why: That is resemblance from meeting similar demands with different plans, the pattern of convergence. Neocortical areas share one plan and vary within it.

items.stem: Neocortical areas share one circuit plan. Where are the biggest differences between them found?

options.text: In layer 4, the layer that receives the input arriving from the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. Layer 4 is where areas differ most, and it is the layer where input from the thalamus arrives.

options.text: In the classes of cells, since each area has some classes of its own.
options.why: Every area has the same classes of cells. The biggest differences are in layer 4.

options.text: In the number of layers, since some areas have six and others three.
options.why: Every neocortical area follows the same six-layered plan, though layer 4 is thin in some; the three-layered sheet is the piriform cortex. The biggest differences are in layer 4.

options.text: In the direction of signals, since sensory areas only send them forward.
options.why: The cortex sends feedback from each area to the one before it, as well as signals forward. The biggest differences are in layer 4, which receives the thalamus’s input.

items.stem: Layer 4 of the visual cortex is the layer that receives input from the thalamus. How do the excitatory synapses there that arrive from the thalamus compare in number with those that come from other cortical cells?

options.text: Those from the thalamus are fewer than a tenth of the total, and most of the rest come from other cortical cells.
options.why: Correct. Most of a cortical cell’s input comes from other cortical cells, not from outside. Even in the input layer of the visual cortex, the thalamus supplies less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses.

options.text: Those from other cortical cells are fewer than a tenth of the total, and most of the rest come from the thalamus.
options.why: That reverses the proportions. Even in the layer that receives the thalamus’s input, most excitatory synapses come from other cortical cells.

options.text: Those from the thalamus and those from other cortical cells are about equal in number, as in every other cortical area.
options.why: The shares are far from equal. Connections from the thalamus make up less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses, and the rest come mostly from cortical cells.

options.text: Those from the thalamus are most of the total in this layer, though other cortical cells supply most of the input to the layers above and below.
options.why: Layer 4 is where the thalamus’s input arrives, which makes this seem likely. But even there, connections from the thalamus make up less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses.

items.stem: As the rewired ferrets grew up, what kind of cells developed in their auditory cortex, which was now receiving signals from the eyes?

options.text: Cells that responded to edges at particular orientations, like the cells in the visual cortex.
options.why: Correct. The auditory cortex, fed by the eyes, developed cells tuned to oriented edges, the kind of cell the visual cortex normally has.

options.text: Cells that responded to particular pitches of sound, like the cells in a normal auditory cortex.
options.why: The area had stopped receiving signals from the ears. Fed by the eyes, it developed cells tuned to oriented edges.

options.text: Cells that responded to nothing, since the area could make no use of signals from the eyes.
options.why: The area did use them. It developed cells that responded to edges at particular orientations.

options.text: Cells that responded to whole objects, like the cells at the far end of the ventral stream.
options.why: Responses to whole objects belong to the inferior temporal cortex. The rewired cells responded to oriented edges, like cells in the primary visual cortex.

items.stem: Recordings had shown that the rewired auditory cortex contained cells tuned to oriented edges. Another study then trained rewired ferrets to go to one spout for a sound and to another for a light. What could the trained ferrets reveal that the recordings could not?

options.text: Whether the animals themselves treated signals arriving through the rewired cortex as light or as sound.
options.why: Correct. The lecture puts the question this way: did the animals treat those signals as light or as sound? Cells tuned like visual cells do not say how the animal takes the signal; its choice of spout does.

options.text: Whether the rewired cells were arranged in an orientation map like the one found in the visual cortex.
options.why: The map was found by recording from the cortex. The trained ferrets answered a question about the animal, not about how its cells were arranged.

options.text: Whether axons from the eyes had in fact grown into the auditory part of the thalamus after rewiring.
options.why: Where the axons grew is a question about anatomy, answered from the tissue. The behavioral study asked how the animals treated the signals.

options.text: Whether the rewired auditory cortex still responded to sound as well as to light reaching it from the eyes.
options.why: Responses to sound could be recorded from the cells themselves. The trained ferrets showed something recordings cannot: how the animal treated what reached it.

items.stem: Rewired ferrets had learned to go to one spout for a sound and to another for a light. When lights could reach the cortex only through the rewired route, what did the three fully tested animals do?

options.text: They treated those lights as lights, going to the spout they had been trained to use for lights.
options.why: Correct. All three animals that were fully tested treated those lights as lights, not as sounds, even though the signals reached them through the auditory cortex.

options.text: They treated those lights as sounds, going to the spout they had learned to go to for a sound.
options.why: That is what we might expect if the area kept its usual job whatever reached it. The animals treated the lights as lights.

options.text: They responded at about chance, as if the lights reaching the rewired route went unnoticed.
options.why: Responses fell to about chance only later, after the auditory cortex was removed. Before that, the animals treated the lights as lights.

options.text: They ignored those lights until their auditory cortex was removed, and then treated them as lights.
options.why: The order runs the other way. They treated the lights as lights first, and removing the auditory cortex brought their responses down to about chance.

items.stem: A headline about the rewired ferrets reads “Any brain area can do any job”. How does the chapter’s reading of the results compare with the headline?

options.text: The results show that input shapes what a cortical area does, not that cortical areas are interchangeable.
options.why: Correct. An area that would have handled sound came to treat light as light. But the map was less orderly and sight less sharp, so the areas are not interchangeable.

options.text: The results support the headline, since the auditory cortex came to do the visual cortex’s job as well as the visual cortex does.
options.why: The rewired area did less well: its map was less orderly, and the animals saw less sharply through it. The headline claims more than the results show.

options.text: The results show nothing either way, since only three animals were fully tested in the behavioral study.
options.why: Three is a small number, and the chapter keeps that qualifier. But it still reads the results as showing that input shapes what an area does.

options.text: The results show the reverse, that each area’s job is fixed by its circuit, and that the input made no difference.
options.why: The input made a large difference: the auditory cortex developed visual-like cells and came to treat light as light.

items.stem: How did the rewired ferrets’ vision through the rewired route compare with vision through the normal visual pathway?

options.text: It was less sharp, which is part of why the area is described as becoming more visual-like, not visual.
options.why: Correct. The animals saw less sharply through the rewired route, and its map was less orderly. The area became visual-like without becoming a visual cortex.

options.text: It was just as sharp, since the rewired cells were tuned to orientation like the cells in the visual cortex.
options.why: Orientation tuning was there, but the animals saw less sharply through the rewired route. The results do not show that the ferrets saw normally.

options.text: It was absent altogether, since the ferrets treated lights reaching the rewired route as sounds.
options.why: The fully tested animals treated those lights as lights. They could see through the rewired route, though less sharply.

options.text: It was sharper, since the rewired cortex had no ear signals left to blur what came from the eyes.
options.why: Sight through the rewired route was less sharp, not sharper, and the rewired map was less orderly than the visual cortex’s.

items.stem: The fly’s mushroom body is often set beside the mouse’s piriform cortex. Which property has actually been observed in both, as the chapter describes them?

options.text: Each odor activates only a small share of the cells, so the response is sparse in both structures.
options.why: Correct. Kenyon cells respond sparsely, and in the piriform cortex each odor activated only a small set of the imaged cells. Sparse responding was observed in both.

options.text: The connections were traced in both, and in each they turned out to combine their inputs at random.
options.why: Only the fly’s connections were traced. In the piriform cortex, random wiring is a model that fits the measured activity.

options.text: Each spreads its input across many more cells than it receives from, as counted in both animals.
options.why: The fly’s expansion from about 50 inputs to about 2,000 cells is known, but the piriform study did not count cells, so expansion there was not measured.

options.text: Both descend from one structure that was present in the last common ancestor of flies and mice.
options.why: That ancestor had nothing like either structure. The resemblance is read as convergent evolution, an inference from the family tree.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the resemblance between the fly’s mushroom body and the mouse’s piriform cortex is read as convergent evolution, and say what kind of claim that reading is.
items.answer: The fly and the mouse are separated by more than half a billion years of evolution, and their last common ancestor had nothing like either the mushroom body or the piriform cortex. So the similar arrangement cannot have been inherited from that ancestor. The two lineages arrived at it separately, for a similar problem, which is convergent evolution in Module 2’s terms. That reading is an inference from the family tree of animals. Neither the fly study nor the mouse study tested it.
rubric: Says the fly and mouse lineages have been separate for more than half a billion years.
Says their last common ancestor had nothing like either structure.
Concludes that the two lineages arrived separately at a similar arrangement for a similar problem.
Labels the reading an inference from the family tree, not something either study tested.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what the rewired ferrets show about the neocortex and where the limits of that conclusion lie, giving the evidence for each.
items.answer: The rewired ferrets show that input shapes what a cortical area does. When signals from the eyes were routed through the auditory part of the thalamus to the auditory cortex, it developed cells tuned to edges at particular orientations, arranged in an orientation map. Animals trained to tell sounds from lights treated lights that reached the cortex only through the rewired route as lights, and their responses fell to about chance when the auditory cortex was removed. An area that would normally have handled sound came to treat light as light, because light was what reached it. But the results do not show that areas are interchangeable, or that the ferrets saw normally. The rewired map was less orderly, the animals saw less sharply through the rewired route, and the area is described as becoming more visual-like, not visual. The behavioral result also comes from the three animals that were fully tested.
rubric: States the positive conclusion: input shapes what a cortical area does.
Gives evidence for it: orientation-tuned cells or an orientation map in the auditory cortex, or lights treated as lights with a drop to chance after removal.
States that the results do not show that areas are interchangeable or that the ferrets saw normally.
Gives evidence for the limit: a less orderly map, less sharp sight, or the area becoming “more visual-like, not visual”.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the correction the chapter makes to Module 6’s picture of the neocortex as a nearly uniform sheet. Say what stays the same from one area to the next, what varies, and where the variation is greatest.
items.answer: The neocortex is not one circuit copied identically across the sheet. It is one circuit plan, repeated with variations. Every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way, so areas resemble one another the way hands resemble feet. What varies is how many cells of each class an area has and how strongly they connect. The biggest differences are in layer 4, the layer that receives input from the thalamus. Layer 4 is prominent in the areas that receive signals from the senses and nearly absent in the motor cortex.
rubric: States the correction: one circuit plan repeated with variations, not one circuit copied identically.
Says the classes of cells and the way they connect are shared across areas.
Says areas differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly they connect.
Places the biggest differences in layer 4, which receives input from the thalamus.
Says layer 4 is prominent in areas that receive signals from the senses and nearly absent in the motor cortex.

pools.title: The Visual Cortex Beside a Network
pools.covers: reading §7.3.6, §7.3.7 · lecture 7.3 slides visual_cortex_beside_a_network, two_homes, could_cortex_pass_errors_back

items.stem: What is a cell’s receptive field?

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes the cell’s activity, together with the kind of stimulus that does it.
options.why: Correct. A receptive field names both where a stimulus has to fall and what kind of stimulus it has to be, such as an edge at a particular orientation.

options.text: The set of other cells whose axons end on the cell, together with the strength of each of those connections to it.
options.why: That describes a cell’s inputs and their weights, which is wiring. A receptive field is defined by the stimulus in the world that changes the cell’s activity, not by which cells connect to it.

options.text: The patch of cortex around the cell, within which neighboring cells respond to stimuli similar to the ones the cell responds to.
options.why: Neighboring cells handling neighboring or similar stimuli is a topographic map, an arrangement of many cells in tissue. A receptive field belongs to one cell and is a region of the sensory world.

options.text: The range of changes to a stimulus, such as shifts in position or size, over which the cell keeps its preferred response.
options.why: That is tolerance, a cell’s keeping its response over a limited range of changes. A receptive field is where a stimulus has to fall, and what kind it has to be, to change the cell’s activity at all.

items.stem: What is a simple cell?

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: Correct. Because its field is a map of excitatory and inhibitory regions, a simple cell’s response to any pattern of light can be predicted from that map.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: That is a complex cell. Its response depends on the orientation of an edge and hardly on where in its field the edge falls, so no map of regions predicts it.

options.text: A cell in the inferior temporal cortex that responds to a whole object and keeps that response over a limited range of changes.
options.why: That describes cells at the far end of the ventral stream, which have tolerance. A simple cell sits at the start, in the primary visual cortex, with a small field mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: A unit in a network’s hidden layer, driven directly by neither the world nor the response, that comes to stand for a combination of inputs.
options.why: That is a hidden unit in an artificial neural network. A simple cell is a neuron in the primary visual cortex, defined by a receptive field split into regions where light excites and inhibits it.

items.stem: What is the name for a cell in the primary visual cortex whose response to any pattern of light can be predicted from a map of the regions of its receptive field where light excites it and where light inhibits it?

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: Correct. The excitatory and inhibitory regions of a simple cell’s receptive field form a map, and the map predicts the cell’s response to any pattern of light.

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: A complex cell responds to an edge of the right orientation anywhere within a larger field, so its response cannot be read off a map of excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the cortex, named for its triangular cell body and long apical dendrite. It is defined by its shape, not by a map of its receptive field.

options.text: Receptive field.
options.why: Every visual cell has a receptive field, the region and kind of stimulus that changes its activity. The cell whose field is mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions is the simple cell.

items.stem: What is a complex cell?

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of a particular orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: Correct. Orientation matters to a complex cell, and exact position within its field hardly does, which is why it is compared with pooling in a network.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: That is a simple cell. Its response can be predicted from a map of those regions, while a complex cell responds to the right orientation wherever in its larger field the edge falls.

options.text: A cell in the inferior temporal cortex whose activity, summed with that of a few hundred others, reports which object is in view.
options.why: A weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons can report the object, but those cells sit at the far end of the ventral stream. A complex cell is in the primary visual cortex and responds to oriented edges.

options.text: A cell in the piriform cortex whose axon sends side branches that excite neighboring cells, so that a circuit of them can store patterns.
options.why: That describes the pyramidal neurons of the piriform cortex and their recurrent connections. A complex cell is a visual cell, defined by its response to an oriented edge anywhere within a larger field.

items.stem: What is the name for a cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field?

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: Correct. A complex cell keeps its preference for an orientation across positions within its field, unlike a simple cell, whose response depends on exactly where the light falls.

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: A simple cell is also tuned to orientation, but its field is split into regions where light excites and inhibits it, so where the edge falls matters a great deal.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: Pyramidal neurons are the main excitatory cells of the cortex, named for their shape. The cell defined by responding to an oriented edge anywhere in a larger field is the complex cell.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling is the network operation a complex cell is compared with, combining detections over a small neighborhood. It is an operation in an artificial neural network, not a cell in the visual cortex.

items.stem: What is a visual cell’s tolerance?

options.text: Its keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size.
options.why: Correct. Tolerance is limited by definition. Cells up the ventral stream have more of it, but no single cell becomes fully invariant.

options.text: Its recognizing a thing across every change that alters its input a great deal, such as changes of distance or viewpoint.
