options.why: That describes invariance, and in its strongest form. No single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant; what a cell has is tolerance over a limited range.

options.text: How close its resting state sits to firing, which sets how much input it needs before it begins to respond at all.
options.why: That is excitability, the neuron’s counterpart of the criterion, which neuromodulators change. Tolerance is about how far a stimulus can change before the cell’s preferred response is lost.

options.text: The region of the visual field where a stimulus changes its activity, together with the kind of stimulus that does it.
options.why: That is the cell’s receptive field. Tolerance is the range of changes, such as shifts in position or size, over which the cell keeps its preferred response.

items.stem: Mapping a cell in the primary visual cortex, researchers find a narrow vertical strip of its receptive field where a spot of light excites the cell, with strips on either side where a spot of light inhibits it. What kind of cell is it, and what does the map make possible?

options.text: A simple cell, whose response to a new pattern of light, such as a tilted bar, can be predicted from the map of its regions.
options.why: Correct. A receptive field split into regions where light excites and regions where light inhibits is what makes a cell simple, and the map predicts its response to any pattern.

options.text: A complex cell, whose response to a vertical bar would be the same wherever in its large receptive field the bar happened to fall.
options.why: A complex cell responds to an oriented edge anywhere within a larger field, so where the light falls hardly matters. Separate excitatory and inhibitory strips mark a simple cell.

options.text: A simple cell, whose response to a new pattern cannot be predicted, because only single spots of light were used to make its map.
options.why: The point of a simple cell is the reverse: its response to any pattern can be predicted from the map of where light excites it and where light inhibits it.

options.text: A complex cell, built from simple cells, whose map shows which of the simple cells feed it and at which positions in the field.
options.why: Building complex cells from simple cells is a tentative proposal, and a map of where light excites and inhibits says nothing about wiring. Such a map describes a simple cell.

items.stem: A cell in the primary visual cortex fires to a bar of light tilted at 45 degrees whether the bar falls toward one side, in the middle, or toward the other side of its fairly large receptive field. It barely fires to a vertical bar in any of those places. What kind of cell is it?

options.text: A complex cell, which responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a larger receptive field.
options.why: Correct. Orientation matters to this cell and exact position within its field does not, which is what defines a complex cell.

options.text: A simple cell, whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites the cell and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: A simple cell is tuned to orientation too, but its response depends on exactly where the light falls relative to its excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: A cell in IT, which responds to a whole object and keeps its response over wider changes in the object’s position and size.
options.why: IT cells respond to whole objects, not single bars, and they lie at the far end of the ventral stream. The cell described is in V1 and tuned to an orientation.

options.text: A fully invariant cell, which keeps its response to a stimulus across every change of position, size, and orientation.
options.why: This cell stops responding when the orientation changes, so it does not keep its response across every change. And no single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant.

items.stem: Suppose complex cells are built as proposed, from simple cells that prefer the same orientation at slightly different positions. Which network operations would the two kinds of cell correspond to?

options.text: Simple cells to convolution, detecting a feature at each position, and complex cells to pooling, which ignores exactly where.
options.why: Correct. Each simple cell detects an oriented edge at one position, as one copy of a convolution detector does, and the complex cell combines them so the exact position no longer matters.

options.text: Simple cells to pooling, combining detections over a neighborhood, and complex cells to convolution, applying one detector everywhere.
options.why: The pairing is reversed. The cells that detect a feature at each position are the simple cells, and the cell that combines them and ignores where is the complex cell.

options.text: Simple cells to the input layer, which receives the image, and complex cells to the output, a weighted sum that reports the object.
options.why: In the comparison, the weighted sum that reports the object sits at the top of the ventral stream, over IT, not in V1. Simple and complex cells correspond to convolution and pooling.

options.text: Simple cells to a randomly wired middle layer that is never trained, and complex cells to the output connections that are trained.
options.why: Random wiring with a trained output is the mushroom body’s arrangement. The proposal for V1 pairs simple cells with convolution and complex cells with pooling.

items.stem: What is the difference between saying that a cell in IT is tolerant of changes in an object’s position and saying that the cell is invariant to them?

options.text: A tolerant cell keeps its response over a limited range of changes; an invariant one would keep it across all of them.
options.why: Correct. Tolerance is limited by definition. Cells up the ventral stream gain more of it, but no single cell becomes fully invariant.

options.text: A tolerant cell keeps its response across every change of position; an invariant cell keeps it over only a limited range of such changes.
options.why: The two terms are swapped. Tolerance is the limited range, and invariance would be keeping the response across all of the changes.

options.text: A tolerant cell responds to many different objects; an invariant cell responds to one single object and to nothing else at all.
options.why: That confuses tolerance with broad selectivity. Tolerance is about how far one stimulus can change before the cell’s response is lost.

options.text: A tolerant cell’s response is learned from experience; an invariant cell’s response is built into its wiring before learning begins.
options.why: Learned against built in is a different distinction. Tolerance and invariance differ in how wide a range of changes a cell’s response survives.

items.stem: A cell in IT responds strongly to a toy car at the center of view. It keeps responding when the car is moved a little or shown somewhat smaller, but stops when the car is moved far to one side or shrunk to a speck. Which description fits the cell?

options.text: It is tolerant: it keeps its preferred response over a limited range of changes, as cells in IT do.
options.why: Correct. Keeping a response over some changes but not all is tolerance. No single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant.

options.text: It is invariant: it keeps its preferred response across changes of position and size, as cells in IT do.
options.why: The cell loses its response once the change is large, so it is not invariant. No single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant; cells have tolerance.

options.text: It is a complex cell: it responds to an edge of the right orientation anywhere in a large receptive field.
options.why: Complex cells are in V1 and respond to oriented edges, not to whole objects. This cell is in IT, and the property described is tolerance.

options.text: It is a simple cell: its response to the car can be predicted from a map of where light excites and inhibits it.
options.why: Simple cells are in V1, with small fields mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions. A cell in IT that responds to a whole car over a range of changes is showing tolerance.

items.stem: Cells in IT respond to whole objects. According to the chapter, what is enough to report which object is in view?

options.text: A weighted sum of the activity of a few hundred neurons in IT.
options.why: Correct. No one cell has to carry the answer. A weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons is enough to report which object is in view.

options.text: The activity of a single neuron in IT that stands for the object.
options.why: A code like this would need a cell devoted to each object, and no single IT cell is fully invariant. What reports the object is a weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons.

options.text: Several further hidden layers stacked above every neuron in IT.
options.why: Further layers are not needed. The input has already been re-represented by the time it reaches IT, so a single weighted sum, a straight line, will do.

options.text: A match of IT’s activity against stored copies of every past view.
options.why: Matching stored copies is how an exemplar model works, not what reads out IT. A weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons is enough.

items.stem: In a unit, the criterion is set by the threshold or the baseline. What is the counterpart of the criterion in a neuron?

options.text: How excitable the cell is, meaning how close its resting state sits to firing, which neuromodulators change.
options.why: Correct. Excitability plays the part of the criterion: a more excitable neuron needs less input before it fires, and neuromodulators are what change it.

options.text: How well the input the cell receives separates the things that matter, which the stages upstream build up.
options.why: That is the physical home of sensitivity, not of the criterion. The two quantities live in different places: criterion in excitability, sensitivity in the representation upstream.

options.text: How large the cell’s receptive field is, which grows at each successive stage up the ventral stream toward IT.
options.why: Receptive fields do grow up the ventral stream, but field size is about where a stimulus must fall. The criterion’s counterpart is how close the cell’s resting state sits to firing.

options.text: How many side branches the cell’s axon sends to its neighbors, which lets a circuit of cells hold a stored pattern.
options.why: Recurrent side branches belong to the account of pattern completion. The criterion’s counterpart is excitability, which neuromodulators change.

items.stem: Suppose that when an owl is hungry, a neuromodulator makes the neurons that read out “mouse” more excitable, and nothing else changes. In signal detection terms, what would we expect?

options.text: The criterion moves: the owl strikes at weaker evidence, with more hits and more false alarms, and sensitivity unchanged.
options.why: Correct. Excitability is the neuron’s counterpart of the criterion, and a neuromodulator is one way to move it. The evidence for “mouse” and for “no mouse” is as well separated as before.

options.text: Sensitivity rises: more excitable neurons separate mice from rustling leaves more sharply, so the owl makes fewer errors.
options.why: This conflates the two quantities. Sensitivity depends on how well the input separates the things that matter, and that lives upstream. Excitability moves the criterion.

options.text: Both change together: the owl strikes at weaker evidence, and its evidence for mice and for leaves becomes better separated.
options.why: Raising excitability lowers the criterion, so the owl does strike at weaker evidence. But nothing upstream changed, so the separation of the evidence, the sensitivity, stays the same.

options.text: Nothing changes: a neuromodulator alters only the chemistry around a circuit, so what the circuit does stays the same.
options.why: The hungry and fed worm of Module 4 show the opposite: the same circuit with different chemistry behaved differently. A change in excitability moves the criterion.

items.stem: The criterion and sensitivity of signal detection theory have different physical homes in a nervous system. Where does sensitivity live?

options.text: In the representation built upstream, since it depends on how well the input a neuron receives separates what matters.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation in the piriform cortex, expansion in the mushroom body, and the stages of the ventral stream are all places where sensitivity is built.

options.text: In how excitable the reading-out neuron is, since sensitivity depends on how close that neuron’s resting state sits to firing.
options.why: Excitability is the home of the criterion, and neuromodulators change it. Sensitivity lives upstream, in how well the neuron’s input separates what matters.

options.text: In the recurrent connections of the reading-out area, since sensitivity depends on completing a stored pattern from part of it.
options.why: Completing a pattern from part of it is the generalization proposed for circuits like the piriform cortex, not sensitivity. Sensitivity depends on how well the input separates what matters.

options.text: In the energy budget of the cortex, since sensitivity depends on how many neurons can be strongly active at any one moment.
options.why: The energy budget limits how many neurons can be active at once, which is the story of sparse coding. Sensitivity depends on how well the input separates the things that matter.

items.stem: A speech recognizer often confuses “b” and “p”. One engineer lowers the threshold of the output unit for “p”. Another retrains the layers below so that the patterns of activity for “b” and “p” overlap less. What does each change do?

options.text: The first moves only the criterion; the second can raise sensitivity, by improving what the readout receives.
options.why: Correct. A threshold is a criterion, and moving it trades misses for false alarms. Pulling the two patterns apart upstream is what separates the evidence better.

options.text: The first raises sensitivity, since the unit now catches more of the “p” sounds; the second moves the criterion only.
options.why: Catching more “p” sounds by lowering a threshold also brings more false alarms, so it is a criterion change. Separating the patterns upstream is what changes sensitivity.

options.text: Both raise sensitivity, since each one makes the recognizer say “p” correctly more often than it did before the change.
options.why: Saying “p” correctly more often is more hits, which a lower criterion gives along with more false alarms. Only the retraining changes sensitivity.

options.text: Both move the criterion only, since retraining the layers below also changes how readily the output unit fires to the sounds.
options.why: Retraining below can change how often the unit fires, but it does so by changing how well the input to the readout separates “b” from “p”, and that is sensitivity. The criterion is set by the threshold.

items.stem: The lecture on the cortex says that pattern separation in the piriform cortex, expansion in the mushroom body, and the stages of the ventral stream have all been about building the same one of signal detection’s two quantities. Which quantity, and why?

options.text: Sensitivity, because each builds a better representation of the input, and sensitivity improves only through a better representation.
options.why: Correct. The criterion lives in excitability and can move with no change in the representation. All three structures improve the input a readout receives, which is where sensitivity lives.

options.text: Criterion, because each changes how excitable the neurons downstream are, and excitability is the neuron’s counterpart of the criterion.
options.why: Excitability is the criterion’s home, but none of the three structures is described as changing it; neuromodulators do. All three improve the input a readout receives, which is sensitivity.

options.text: Criterion, because each sets how much evidence a later readout needs before it responds to one of its inputs.
options.why: Setting how much evidence a readout needs is the criterion, and it is set at the readout, by its threshold or its excitability. The three structures build what the readout receives, which is sensitivity.

options.text: Sensitivity, because each makes the neurons downstream more excitable, and excitability is what sensitivity measures.
options.why: Sensitivity is the right quantity, but for the wrong reason: excitability is the counterpart of the criterion. The three structures build sensitivity by improving the representation.

items.stem: Three convolutional networks are tested on the same photographs of objects: one categorizes them poorly, one fairly well, and one very well. If they follow the pattern found in comparisons with IT, which network’s internal responses should best predict how neurons in IT respond?

options.text: The network that categorizes the photographs best, since better categorizers are also better at predicting IT responses.
options.why: Correct. Among convolutional networks, the ones better at categorizing objects are also better at predicting how IT neurons respond. That is part of why the comparison holds.

options.text: The network that categorizes the photographs worst, since a network that makes mistakes as a brain does should resemble IT more.
options.why: Matching a brain’s errors is a reasonable idea in general, but the pattern found runs the other way: better categorizers predict IT better.

options.text: All three about equally, since every convolutional network shares the ventral stream’s receptive fields that grow at each stage.
options.why: Growing receptive fields are shared, but networks differ in how well they predict IT, and the better categorizers do better.

options.text: None of the three, since networks have no feedback and so cannot predict the responses of any neuron in the cortex.
options.why: The lack of feedback is a real limit, but networks do predict IT responses in part, about half of what could be predicted at all for the best one.

items.stem: A student reasons: “The pallium learns with no teaching signal, so it cannot be learning from errors of any kind”. How does prediction learning qualify that reasoning?

options.text: The pallium may lack an external teacher without lacking an error, since its next input can serve as a target.
options.why: Correct. With the next input as the target, a prediction can be compared with what arrives. What the pallium lacks is an external teacher, not necessarily an error.

options.text: The pallium must have a dedicated teaching pathway after all, carrying the error from a teacher elsewhere.
options.why: Prediction learning fits the absence of a teaching pathway rather than overturning it. The target arrives as ordinary input.

options.text: The pallium learns without any target at all, so the reasoning is right and its learning involves no error.
options.why: Prediction learning does have a target, the next input, so the pallium may still learn from an error. Only an external teacher is missing.

options.text: The pallium receives the correct answer from the thalamus, which serves as the teacher the reasoning overlooks.
options.why: No external teacher is proposed. The point is that the next input itself can serve as a target, so an error need not come from a teacher.

items.stem: If the cortex learned by backpropagation taken literally, what property would its error signals need, although no one has found such signals there?

options.text: They would have to be positive or negative, over a huge range of values.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation’s errors carry a sign and a size, and the size can vary enormously. No one has found error signals like that in the cortex.

options.text: They would have to be positive only, carried by one neuromodulator to every synapse.
options.why: A single positive signal spread everywhere is closer to a reward signal. Literal backpropagation needs signed errors, positive or negative, over a huge range.

options.text: They would have to be carried forward by neurons dedicated to what a prediction missed.
options.why: Neurons dedicated to carrying the error are predictive coding’s central prediction, and it lacks clear support. Literal backpropagation needs signed errors over a huge range.

options.text: They would have to be the same size at every synapse, so that every weight changed equally.
options.why: In backpropagation each connection changes in proportion to the error at its receiving unit and the activity of its sending unit, so changes differ across synapses.

items.stem: One of the things backpropagation, taken literally, would need in the cortex concerns what the feedback does to the neurons along its path. What would it need?

options.text: The feedback would have to change synapses without changing the activity of the neurons it passes through.
options.why: Correct. In literal backpropagation the error travels back without disturbing the forward activity. No one has found feedback like that in the cortex.

options.text: The feedback would have to change the neurons’ activity, so that they could learn from their activity before and after.
options.why: That is the alternative family of proposals, which turns the change in activity into the learning signal. Literal backpropagation needs feedback that leaves activity unchanged.

options.text: The feedback would have to carry predictions, so that the neurons pass forward only what those predictions missed.
options.why: That is predictive coding, a related proposal whose error neurons lack clear support. Literal backpropagation needs feedback that changes synapses without changing activity.

options.text: The feedback would have to make the neurons more excitable, so that they fire to weaker input than they did before.
options.why: A change in excitability moves a criterion, and neuromodulators make it. Literal backpropagation needs feedback that changes synapses and leaves activity alone.

items.stem: Backpropagation was made widely known in 1986, as a way of training networks rather than as a model of learning in brains. Taken literally, which three things would it need in the cortex that no one has found there?

options.text: Feedback weights that match the forward ones, error signals that are positive or negative over a huge range, and feedback that changes synapses without changing activity.
options.why: Correct. All three are things literal backpropagation needs and no one has found in the cortex. Not finding them is not the same as ruling out something like backpropagation, which the evidence does not do.

options.text: Feedback from each area to the area before it, error signals that are positive or negative over a huge range, and synapses whose strengths change with experience.
options.why: Signed errors over a huge range are one real requirement. But the cortex does send feedback from each area to the one before it, and its synapses do change; what has not been found is feedback with matching weights that leaves activity unchanged.

options.text: Feedback weights that match the forward ones, neurons dedicated to carrying the error forward, and feedback that changes a neuron’s activity so that it learns from before and after.
options.why: Matching weights is a real requirement. But error neurons belong to predictive coding, and feedback that changes activity is what the before-and-after proposals use; literal backpropagation needs feedback that leaves activity unchanged.

options.text: Feedback weights that match the forward ones, a dopamine signal that reaches every synapse, and neuromodulators that change how excitable each neuron is.
options.why: Matching weights is a real requirement. But a dopamine signal is the third factor of the mushroom body’s learning, and neuromodulators changing excitability move a criterion; literal backpropagation needs signed errors over a huge range and feedback that leaves activity unchanged.

items.stem: As the evidence stands, what can be said about whether the cortex learns by anything like backpropagation?

options.text: There is no direct evidence for anything like it in the cortex, and no evidence that rules it out either.
options.why: Correct. The question is open in both directions. Its literal requirements have not been found, but not finding them is not the same as ruling it out.

options.text: It has been ruled out, since the three things literal backpropagation needs were looked for in the cortex and shown to be absent.
options.why: The three requirements are things no one has found, not things shown impossible. Nothing rules out something like backpropagation in the cortex.

options.text: It has been confirmed, since networks trained by backpropagation predict how IT neurons respond better than anything else.
options.why: The best network in the 2014 comparison was not trained by backpropagation, and a match in responses is not direct evidence about a learning rule.

options.text: There is evidence for something like it in the ventral stream, where errors pass back, but none in the piriform cortex.
options.why: No such split has been found. For the cortex as a whole, there is no direct evidence for anything like backpropagation and none against it.

items.stem: Suppose a study searched a patch of visual cortex and found no feedback connections whose weights match the forward ones. A classmate concludes that the cortex therefore cannot learn by anything like backpropagation. Why does that conclusion go too far?

options.text: Learning from the change feedback makes to a neuron’s activity could approximate backpropagation, with signals a neuron could have.
options.why: Correct. Failing to find literal backpropagation’s requirements leaves that family of proposals untouched, which is why nothing rules out something like backpropagation in the cortex.

options.text: The study looked in the wrong place, since feedback with matching weights is known to be found in the inferior temporal cortex.
options.why: No one has found matching weights anywhere in the cortex. The conclusion goes too far because other mechanisms could approximate backpropagation.

options.text: Matching weights are not needed by literal backpropagation, which passes errors back along new connections of any weight.
options.why: Literal backpropagation does need them: errors pass back through the same weights the activity passed forward through. It is the alternatives that drop the requirement.

options.text: The cortex has been shown to use predictive coding, which is backpropagation under a different name, so the search was beside the point.
options.why: Predictive coding is an open hypothesis whose central prediction lacks clear support, and it is a different proposal from backpropagation.

items.stem: In one family of proposals for learning in the cortex, feedback is allowed to change the activity of the neurons it reaches. What do those neurons learn from?

options.text: The difference between a neuron’s activity before the feedback arrived and its activity after.
options.why: Correct. The change that feedback makes to activity, which literal backpropagation would have to avoid, becomes the learning signal itself.

options.text: A signed error passed back through feedback weights that exactly match the forward weights.
options.why: That is backpropagation taken literally, with requirements no one has found in the cortex. This family of proposals drops them.

options.text: A reward signal carried by a neuromodulator, at synapses where both neurons were recently active.
options.why: That is the three-factor rule of Module 5, which the mushroom body uses at its output connections. This family learns from the change feedback makes to activity.

options.text: The co-activity of neurons that fire together, strengthening their links whatever the feedback carries.
options.why: That is Hebb’s rule, used in the account of pattern completion in the piriform cortex. This family learns from activity before and after feedback.

items.stem: What does predictive coding hold about the signals running up and down the cortical hierarchy?

options.text: Feedback carries predictions back down, and the forward connections carry what the predictions missed.
options.why: Correct. On this proposal, what travels forward is the part of the input that the predictions did not capture.

options.text: Feedback carries errors back down, and the forward connections carry the predictions those errors corrected.
options.why: The directions are reversed. Predictions travel down as feedback, and what they missed travels forward.

options.text: Feedback carries errors back down through the same weights as the forward connections, leaving activity alone.
options.why: That is backpropagation taken literally, which needs matching weights and feedback that no one has found in the cortex.

options.text: Feedback changes a neuron’s activity, and the neuron learns from its activity before and after the feedback.
options.why: That is the before-and-after family of proposals, which differs from predictive coding, though both are open hypotheses.

items.stem: What is the standing of predictive coding as an account of how the cortex works?

options.text: An open hypothesis, since its central prediction, neurons dedicated to carrying the error, lacks clear support.
options.why: Correct. Its originator says that much of it remains to be tested. Predictive coding is a proposal, not an established account of the cortex.

options.text: An established account, since neurons dedicated to carrying the error have been recorded throughout the visual cortex.
options.why: Neurons dedicated to carrying the error are exactly what has not been clearly found. That is why the proposal remains open.

options.text: A rejected idea, since the cortex has no feedback connections that could carry predictions back down the hierarchy.
options.why: The cortex does send feedback from each area to the one before it. Predictive coding is not rejected; it is an open hypothesis.

options.text: A rejected idea, since the cortex was shown to learn by backpropagation instead, which leaves no part for predictions.
options.why: Nothing has shown that the cortex learns by backpropagation; there is no direct evidence for or against it. Predictive coding remains an open hypothesis.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how complex cells might be built from simple cells, how that arrangement corresponds to convolution followed by pooling in a network, and how firmly the visual-cortex half of the comparison is established.
items.answer: A complex cell might be built by combining the outputs of several simple cells that prefer the same orientation at slightly different positions. Each simple cell then detects an oriented edge at one position, as each copy of a convolution detector does, and the complex cell responds if any of them does, ignoring exactly where, as pooling does. The same arrangement was built into the neocognitron and is what a network does with convolution followed by pooling. But in the visual cortex the wiring is a proposal, put forward as “obviously tentative”, not an established fact.
rubric: Says a complex cell would combine simple cells that prefer the same orientation at slightly different positions.
Matches simple cells to convolution, detecting a feature at each position.
Matches complex cells to pooling, keeping the detection and ignoring exactly where.
Says the complex-from-simple wiring is a tentative proposal, not an established fact.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, assess how far the ventral stream resembles a convolutional network. Give one way the comparison holds and two of its stated limits.
items.answer: The comparison holds in part. Among convolutional networks, the ones that are better at categorizing objects are also better at predicting how neurons in IT respond, and in 2014 the best of them predicted about half of the variation in IT responses that could be predicted at all. But there are limits. The cortex sends feedback from each area to the one before it, and the networks in these comparisons have none, and whether fast recognition of a familiar object needs that feedback is debated. Some of the resemblance may also rest on a shared sensitivity to texture rather than on recognizing shapes the same way.
rubric: Says the comparison holds in part, not fully.
Gives the positive evidence: better categorizers predict IT better, or the best network predicted about half of what could be predicted.
Names the networks’ lack of the feedback the cortex has as a limit.
Names a second limit: possible shared texture sensitivity, or that the role of feedback in fast recognition is debated.

items.stem: Backpropagation, taken literally, would need feedback in the cortex that changes synapses without changing the activity of the neurons it passes through, and no one has found that. In a few sentences, describe how one family of proposals uses feedback instead, what learning of that kind can achieve, and how firmly it is established.
items.answer: In this family of proposals, feedback is allowed to change a neuron’s activity, and that change becomes the learning signal: the neuron learns from the difference between its activity before the feedback arrived and after. Learning of that kind can approximate what backpropagation computes, using only signals a neuron could have, so it keeps the idea of passing errors back while changing the mechanism. It is an open hypothesis, not an established account of how the cortex learns.
rubric: Says that in the proposal feedback changes a neuron’s activity, instead of leaving it unchanged.
Says the neuron learns from the difference between its activity before and after the feedback.
Says this can approximate what backpropagation computes, with signals a neuron could have.
Says the proposal is an open hypothesis.

items.stem: The question of whether the cortex could pass errors back splits into two: whether there is an error to learn from at all, and how an error would be delivered. In a short paragraph, say what the chapter concludes about each part.
items.answer: On the first part, prediction learning helps. The pallium has no dedicated teaching pathway, but in prediction learning the target is the next input, which arrives anyway, so the pallium lacks an external teacher, not necessarily an error. Delivery is the harder part. Backpropagation taken literally needs things no one has found in the cortex, such as feedback weights that match the forward ones, and as the evidence stands there is no direct evidence for anything like backpropagation there, and none that rules it out. The alternatives, learning from the difference in a neuron’s activity before and after feedback, and predictive coding, whose dedicated error neurons lack clear support, are both open hypotheses.
rubric: Says the next input can serve as the target, so no separate pathway is needed to deliver it.
Concludes that the pallium lacks an external teacher, not necessarily an error.
Says delivery is the harder, open question, with no direct evidence for or against anything like backpropagation in the cortex.
Names at least one alternative proposal, before-and-after learning or predictive coding, as an open hypothesis.

pools.title: Sparse Codes, and What Recognition Does and Does Not Explain

items.stem: A classmate writes, “The brain uses sparse codes to save energy, and as a bonus they help with recognition”. The lecture stresses that the direction of this argument matters. Which statement has the direction right?

options.text: The energy budget limits how many neurons can be strongly active at once, and a code that sparse also suits recognition.
options.why: Correct. Energy is a limit on activity, not a saving the brain is pursuing. Sparseness follows from the limit, and its fit with recognition is a separate fact about what such a code can do.

options.text: Recognition is the reason cortical codes are sparse, and the energy that sparseness leaves unspent is a side effect of that.
options.why: This reverses the dependence. The chapter starts from the energy budget, which limits how many neurons can be active, and only then asks what a code that sparse does for recognition.

options.text: Sparse codes waste energy, since the few active neurons must fire much harder, and their help with recognition makes up for it.
options.why: Sparse coding is a consequence of the energy budget, not an inefficiency that something else has to pay back. Nothing in the chapter says the active neurons fire harder to compensate.

options.text: Energy and recognition pull in opposite directions, so cortical codes settle at a measured middle level of sparseness.
options.why: The two do not pull against each other: a code as sparse as the budget allows also suits recognition. And how sparse cortical codes actually are is still argued, so no settled level has been measured.

items.stem: A learning rule with no teacher, whose goals were to describe small patches of natural-scene photographs accurately with as few active units as possible, developed receptive fields like those of V1’s simple cells. A news story about it runs under the headline “Scientists discover how the visual cortex learns”. What does the result actually support?

options.text: Only that a rule of that kind could produce what V1 has, which falls short of showing that V1 learns that way.
options.why: Correct. The two goals alone were enough to produce the main properties of simple cells. That shows a rule of this kind could produce them, not that V1 uses it.

options.text: That V1 learns by this rule, since the units came to match simple cells in all of their main properties.
options.why: A match between a rule’s output and V1 shows what the rule can produce. Other rules might produce the same receptive fields, so the match does not show how V1 actually learns.

options.text: That edge-tuned cells must be built into V1 from birth, since the rule found edges without anything teaching it about them.
options.why: Finding edges with no teacher is still learning, from the patches themselves; nothing about edges was built into the rule. And the result says what a rule of this kind could produce, not how V1 actually comes by its cells.

options.text: That nothing about V1 follows from it at all, since the rule ran on a computer rather than on cells in a brain.
options.why: That is too skeptical. Running on a computer does not empty the result. It shows that a rule of this kind could produce what V1 has, which is a real if limited conclusion.

items.stem: A learning rule with no teacher was given small patches of natural-scene photographs, and its units came to resemble the simple cells of V1. Nothing in the rule said anything about edges or orientations. Why does that make the result striking?

options.text: Two goals alone, accurate description and few active units, were enough to produce the main properties of simple cells.
options.why: Correct. Accurate description with few active units, and nothing else, produced small, elongated, oriented receptive fields. Edge detectors did not have to be built in or taught.

options.text: Edges were the only structure the natural photographs contained, so any rule at all would have ended up with edge detectors.
options.why: Natural scenes contain far more than edges. What produced the oriented fields was the pair of goals, accurate description with as few active units as possible.

options.text: Units that learn with no teacher always come to be tuned to orientation, whatever goals their rule is given.
options.why: Rules with no teacher differ in what they find. Competitive learning, for example, finds clusters of overlapping inputs. Here it was these two goals that produced simple-cell properties.

options.text: It shows that the simple cells of V1 acquire their orientations in exactly this way as an animal develops.
options.why: That is the conclusion the result cannot carry. It shows that a rule of this kind could produce what V1 has, not that V1 learns this way.

items.stem: A layer codes each input with only a few of its many units active. What does that make easier for a single trained layer reading from it?

options.text: Many more divisions of the inputs can be drawn with one straight line, so one trained layer can do what would otherwise take several.
options.why: Correct. With few of many units active, far more divisions of the inputs become linearly separable, so a single trained layer is often enough.

options.text: The layer can have fewer units than it receives inputs from, so the single trained layer reading it has fewer weights to set.
options.why: The benefit runs the other way. The code uses many units with few active, and what it gives the reader is more divisions it can draw with one straight line.

options.text: Each active unit stands for one whole category, so the single layer reading it can name the category with no trained weights.
options.why: That is a localist code, in which which unit is active is itself the information. A sparse code is not the same thing, and its reader still needs trained weights.

options.text: Similar inputs share most of their active units, so the single trained layer generalizes from one example to every similar one.
options.why: Similar things sharing active units is a strength of distributed codes in general, and it does not carry a reader from one example to every similar one. The advantage named for a code with few of many units active is that many more divisions become linearly separable.

items.stem: How sparse are the codes in the cortex, by the chapter’s account?

options.text: Still argued: the energy budget limits activity, but how sparse cortical codes actually are has not been settled.
options.why: Correct. The chapter keeps this open. The energy budget allows only a small share of neurons to be strongly active, but how sparse cortical codes actually are is still argued.

options.text: Sparser in the areas that receive signals from the senses than in the motor cortex, as recordings across the sheet have shown.
options.why: Areas do differ, most of all in layer 4, which is prominent in sensory areas and nearly absent in the motor cortex. But no such comparison of sparseness is reported, and how sparse cortical codes actually are is still argued.

options.text: Sparse in insects but dense in mammals, since the clearest case of sparse coding was traced in the fly’s mushroom body.
options.why: The fly’s Kenyon cells do respond sparsely, but so does the mouse’s piriform cortex, where each odor activated only a small set of cells. What is unsettled is how sparse cortical codes are, not whether mammals have any.

options.text: As sparse as the budget allows and no sparser, a level that has been measured to be the same in every area.
options.why: No single level has been measured across the cortex. The budget sets a limit, but how sparse cortical codes actually are is still argued.

items.stem: A classmate says, “The brain uses sparse codes to save energy”. In a few sentences, explain what is wrong with the direction of that claim, and say what a code with few active neurons does for recognition.
items.answer: The claim treats sparseness as a strategy chosen to save energy. In the chapter the energy budget comes first, as a limit: a spike is expensive, so only a small share of cortical neurons can be strongly active at any moment. Sparse coding is a consequence of that limit. Separately, a code that sparse also suits recognition. When only a few of many units are active for each input, many more ways of dividing the inputs can be drawn with a single straight line, so one trained layer can do what would otherwise take several. How sparse cortical codes actually are is still argued.
rubric: States that the energy budget limits how many neurons can be strongly active, because spikes are expensive.
Treats sparseness as a consequence of that limit, not as a purpose or strategy for saving energy.
Says that with few of many units active, many more divisions of the inputs can be drawn with a single straight line.
Says that this lets a single trained layer do what would otherwise take several.

items.stem: One study trained a learning rule on small patches cut from photographs of natural scenes. In a short paragraph, say what goals the rule had and whether anything supplied it with labels or targets, what its units came to look like, and how far the result goes as evidence about how V1 learns.
items.answer: Researchers gave a learning rule with no teacher many small patches cut from photographs of natural scenes. The rule had two goals: describe each patch accurately, and use as few active units as possible. The units came to have receptive fields like the simple cells of V1, small, elongated, and tuned to edges at particular orientations. So the two goals alone were enough to produce the main properties of simple cells. That shows that a rule of this kind could produce what V1 has. It does not show that V1 actually learns this way.
rubric: Says the rule had no teacher: no labels or target outputs were supplied.
Names both goals: accurate description, and as few active units as possible.
Describes the outcome as receptive fields like V1 simple cells: small, elongated, tuned to oriented edges.
Concludes that a rule of this kind could produce what V1 has.
States that the result does not show that V1 learns this way.

items.stem: Is a structure that does the same thing to every kind of input doing something very general, or nothing in particular? What answer does the chapter build?

options.text: Something very general: it re-represents whatever input reaches it.
options.why: Correct. The one operation is re-representation. Whatever arrives, the structure recodes it so that later stages can sort it.

options.text: Nothing in particular: what each area does comes entirely from what is connected to it.
options.why: Input does shape what an area does, as the rewired ferrets showed. But the chapter’s answer is that the shared operation is very general, not empty: it re-represents whatever arrives.

options.text: Something very general: it stores each input so that a part can later recall the whole.
options.why: Storing patterns and completing them from part is auto-association, proposed for the piriform cortex mostly on the strength of models. The general operation in the answer is re-representation.

options.text: Something very general: it detects edges at particular orientations in whatever arrives.
options.why: Edge detection is what simple cells in V1 do with visual input, and rewired auditory cortex developed such cells because visual input reached it. The general operation is re-representing whatever arrives.

items.stem: By the chapter’s account, what does a structure accomplish by re-representing whatever input reaches it?

options.text: It pulls apart inputs that call for different responses and brings together inputs from the same thing, until one straight line can do the rest.
options.why: Correct. Both demands, discrimination and generalization, are met by recoding, and the recoding goes on until one straight line, a single unit’s boundary, can finish the sorting.

options.text: It spreads every input across many more cells, so that no two inputs ever share an active cell and no boundary of any kind has to be drawn at all.
options.why: Spreading an input across more cells is dimensionality expansion, one way to recode. But the aim is to make a single straight line enough, not to do away with the line.

options.text: It averages the members of each category into a single prototype, so that each new input can be sorted by the nearest prototype.
options.why: That is a prototype model, one of the psychologists’ algorithms, and with one prototype per category it can only sort linearly separable categories. Re-representation pulls apart and brings together.

options.text: It passes each input on unchanged to a final stage, where one curved boundary does all of the sorting at once, with no recoding.
options.why: Passing the input on unchanged is the opposite of re-representing it. The point of the recoding is that the final step can be a single straight line.

items.stem: A penguin parent returning to a crowded colony has to pick out its own chick’s call. The chick’s call varies from one call to the next, and some neighbors’ chicks sound much like it. In the chapter’s terms, what must the stages between the parent’s ears and its response do with these calls?

options.text: Bring its own chick’s varied calls together and pull the neighbors’ similar calls apart, until one straight line separates them.
options.why: Correct. That is re-representation: different-sounding calls from one chick are brought together, and similar calls from other chicks are pulled apart, until one line will do.

options.text: Pull every call apart from every other one, so that no two calls, not even two calls from its own chick, are ever treated alike.
options.why: That meets only the demand to tell apart. A parent that did only this would treat each of its own chick’s calls as a new thing.

options.text: Bring similar-sounding calls together, so that its own chick and the neighbors’ chicks that sound like it are treated as one.
options.why: That meets only the demand to treat alike, and it would lump the neighbors’ chicks in with its own. Both demands have to be met at once.

options.text: Pass the raw sounds unchanged to a single unit, and lower that unit’s criterion until every call from its own chick is caught.
options.why: Lowering the criterion catches more of the chick’s calls but also more of the neighbors’, since it trades misses for false alarms. Only a better representation pulls the calls apart.

items.stem: In the chapter’s terms, the computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt beneath it. Which observation from the chapter best illustrates that?

options.text: A fly’s mushroom body and a mouse’s piriform cortex both handle similar smells, in structures their last common ancestor had nothing like.
options.why: Correct. The problem of sorting smells is the same, and the tissue that handles it arose separately in two lineages. Reading the resemblance as convergent evolution is an inference from the family tree, not something either study tested.

options.text: The neocortex is one circuit plan repeated with variations, so every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way.
options.why: That is roughly the reverse pattern: one implementation repeated across areas that receive different inputs. Whether one plan means one computation everywhere is still open.

options.text: A hungry worm and a fed worm run the same circuit with different chemistry, so the same input can lead to different responses.
options.why: That is a criterion moved by neuromodulators, with the same wiring in both worms. The implementation stays put; it is not rebuilt beneath a steady problem.

options.text: Two odors that share more than 70 percent of their active inputs at the bulb share only about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex.
options.why: That is pattern separation, measured in one structure. It shows what one implementation does with its input, and sets no second, different implementation against the same problem.

items.stem: Suppose researchers find that an octopus tells a crab from a rock by the pattern of activity across many receptors on its arms, from inputs that are never twice the same. Using the chapter’s lesson about levels, what can be said in advance about how the octopus does it?

options.text: It faces the same computational problem as a fish, a fly, or a mouse, though its machinery may turn out quite unlike any of theirs.
options.why: Correct. The problem does not fix the tissue. A fish, a fly, a mouse, and a network share the problem and differ in machinery, so an octopus could too.

options.text: It will turn out to have a pallium or something descended from one, since fish and mice both recognize with structures of that kind.
options.why: A fly recognizes smells with a mushroom body and no pallium at all. The computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt.

options.text: It will turn out to have a layered cortex like the mouse’s, since only a sheet of repeated circuits can re-represent its input.
options.why: The fly’s mushroom body re-represents smells with no cortex at all. Knowing the problem does not tell us which machinery handles it.

options.text: It is not recognizing patterns in the chapter’s sense, since an animal with no cortex has no means of telling inputs apart.
options.why: A fish and a fly recognize patterns with no neocortex. Lacking a cortex does not rule out handling the problem with other machinery.

items.stem: A fox recognizes a shape in the long grass as a hare. Which question does that recognition, by itself, leave unanswered?

options.text: What would happen if the fox pounced on the hare from where it now stands.
options.why: Correct. Recognizing a pattern tells an animal what a thing is. It does not, by itself, say what would happen if the animal acted on it, or why the thing is there.

options.text: Whether the shape in the grass is a hare at all, rather than a clump of earth.
options.why: Telling a hare from a clump of earth is exactly what recognition supplies: what the thing is.

options.text: Whether this hare, seen from the side, is the same kind of thing as hares seen from the front.
options.why: Treating one thing alike across viewpoints is invariance, part of the recognition problem itself. Recognition does answer it, imperfectly.

options.text: Whether the smell drifting from the grass belongs with hare smells the fox has smelled before.
options.why: Treating a new smell like familiar ones is generalization, one of the two demands of recognition. It is not among what recognition leaves out.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what it means to say that the computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt beneath it. Use two of the chapter’s cases.
items.answer: The computational level is the problem being solved. In this chapter it is the same for every case: tell apart what calls for different responses, and treat alike what comes from the same thing, from inputs that are never twice the same. The implementation is the physical machinery, and it differs from case to case. A mouse’s piriform cortex pulls similar smells apart with sparsely active cells in a three-layered cortex. A fly faces the same problem with a mushroom body, in a different nervous system altogether, built by an expansion onto randomly wired cells. The problem holds steady across the two while the tissue that handles it is rebuilt, so knowing the problem does not tell us which machinery will handle it.
rubric: Identifies the computational level as the problem: telling apart and treating alike from inputs never twice the same.
Identifies the implementation as the physical machinery that handles the problem.
Describes two of the chapter’s cases correctly (for example the fish’s pallium, the fly’s mushroom body, the mouse’s piriform cortex, the ventral stream, or a network).
States that the two cases share the problem but differ in machinery.
Draws the consequence that the problem does not fix which machinery handles it.

items.stem: When the lab’s first scenario loads, its fish has no hidden units and no weights set yet. Over the first ten encounters, watched live, which of the four outcomes did it produce?

options.text: Only hits and false alarms, because it darted to cover at every encounter, whether an eel was there or a sucker.
options.why: Correct. With every weight at zero the evidence is 0 against a criterion of 0, and the fish darts when the evidence is at or above the criterion. So every eel was a hit and every sucker a false alarm, and a miss or a correct rejection never occurred.

options.text: Only misses and correct rejections, because it stayed to feed at every encounter, whether an eel was there or a sucker.
options.why: Staying at every encounter is what would happen if the evidence fell below the criterion. Here the two were equal, and the fish darts at equality, so it fled every time.

options.text: All four outcomes in roughly equal numbers, because a fish with no weights responds to each smell more or less at random.
options.why: Nothing in the fish is random: zero evidence against a zero criterion gives the same verdict every time. The fish fled at every encounter, so only two outcomes occurred.

options.text: Mostly hits and correct rejections, because an eel’s smell and a sucker’s smell differ enough to be sorted from the start.
options.why: The smells do differ, but a fish whose weights are all zero gives both the same evidence, 0 against a criterion of 0, so the difference never reaches the verdict. It fled every time.

items.stem: In the Jumpy or blind? scenario, under The fish’s stakes (a miss costs 20, a correct rejection earns 1, and the other outcomes earn nothing), the healthy fish’s criterion is moved from 0 down to the liberal setting that earns the most energy. How do percent correct and Energy per 100 encounters at that setting compare with their values at 0?

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy goes from a clear loss at 0 to a small gain.
options.why: Correct. At 0 the healthy fish is right about 86 percent of the time and still loses energy, because each miss costs 20. Lowered to about −0.6 or −0.7 it is right noticeably less often, but it almost never misses, so it earns a little. Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts.

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy goes from a small gain at 0 to a much larger gain.
options.why: Percent correct does fall, but at 0 the healthy fish was not gaining energy. It misses enough eels at 0, at 20 apiece, to run at a clear loss, and the best setting only just turns that into a small gain.

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy rises from a heavy loss at 0 to a smaller loss that is still below zero.
options.why: Percent correct does fall and energy does rise, but at the best setting energy crosses into a small gain. With misses nearly gone, the correct rejections that remain earn more than the few misses cost.

options.text: Percent correct is higher than at 0, and energy goes from a clear loss at 0 to a small gain.
options.why: Energy does go from a loss to a small gain, but percent correct falls. Lowering the criterion trades misses for false alarms, and here the false alarms grew far faster than the misses fell.

items.stem: In the Jumpy or blind? scenario, keeping The fish’s stakes, How often an eel is upstream is set to 20 percent, so eels are now rare. Where did the criterion that earns the most energy end up, compared with where it sat when eels were half the stream?

options.text: Closer to zero than before, but still below it, so the best criterion stayed liberal.
options.why: Correct. Rarer eels pulled the best criterion toward zero, from about −0.6 or −0.7 to somewhere around −0.3 to −0.5, but a miss still costs twenty times what a correct rejection earns, so the best setting stayed liberal. A conservative best criterion needs rare targets and costly false alarms together.

options.text: Above zero, so the best criterion became conservative once eels were rare.
options.why: Rare targets push toward a conservative criterion only when false alarms are also costly. Under these stakes a false alarm costs only a missed meal, and the best criterion stayed below zero.

options.text: Further below zero than before, so the best criterion became more liberal as eels grew rare.
options.why: That is the direction the best criterion moved when eels became common, at 80 percent. With eels rare it moved toward zero.

options.text: At about zero, so the best criterion became neutral once eels were rare.
options.why: The best criterion did move toward zero, but it stopped short. A miss still costs twenty times what a correct rejection earns, so the best setting stayed below zero, on the liberal side.

items.stem: On the lab’s Fish tab, two diagnosed fish gave nearly the same counts, with almost no misses and many false alarms, and Reveal said one of them was “not broken”. That fish comes with a switch for its own stream, where eels make up 80 percent of encounters. In a few sentences, say whether that fish’s Energy per 100 encounters in its own stream came out as a clear gain, about break-even, or a loss, how that compared with the healthy fish’s at the same base rate, and what that says about calling an animal “too jumpy” from its behavior alone.
items.answer: In the stream with 80 percent eels, the low-criterion fish came out near break-even, a little below zero rather than a clear gain, while the healthy fish, with its criterion at 0, lost heavily, about two hundred per hundred encounters. So the low criterion was not a fault: which criterion is best depends on the stakes and on how common targets are, and with eels this common a liberal criterion pays. Its counts looked just like those of the fish whose chemistry was at fault, so behavior alone cannot say whether a criterion is wrong. That depends on the world the animal lives in, which has to be measured too.
rubric: Reports that the low-criterion fish came out near break-even (slightly below zero, not a clear gain) in its own stream.
Reports that the healthy fish, at the same 80 percent base rate, lost heavily, so the low-criterion fish did far better.
Says the best criterion depends on how common targets are (and on the stakes), so a liberal criterion suits a stream with many eels.
Says the two fish with the same counts had different causes (one a fault in chemistry, one suited to its stream).
Concludes that counts alone cannot show a criterion is a fault without knowing the animal’s world.

items.stem: In the lab’s fruit scenario, either of two smells alone marks ripe fruit, and both together mark rotting fruit. A fish with no hidden units learns whether to eat over two runs of 1,000 encounters, with the feature space checked after each run. What did the white line and the test set’s percent wrong do, and why?

options.text: The white line kept swinging from place to place and never came to rest, and percent wrong stayed high, because each smell comes with nourishing fruit half the time.
options.why: Correct. Neither smell says anything about food by itself: each is present in half the cases that nourish and half the cases that do not. With no hidden units, each run of encounters pushes the weights one way and then another, and nothing the fish learns from one smell at a time makes the errors go away.

options.text: The white line came to rest across the middle after the first run and stayed put, with about half the fruit wrong, because one line can do no better than chance here.
options.why: It is true that no single line sorts this fruit. But the line did not settle anywhere; it kept moving from run to run, and percent wrong did not hold steady at one value.

options.text: The white line settled between the ripe and the rotting fruit after a slow start, and percent wrong fell close to zero, because the evidence from the two smells was added together.
options.why: More encounters did not help. Added up, the two smells give rotting fruit the most evidence of all, so adding the evidence from each smell cannot single out the rotting fruit.

options.text: The white line came to rest pointing the wrong way, and the fish ate only the rotting fruit and the twigs, because the rule pushed each weight backward.
options.why: The fish did not learn the problem backward; it could not learn it at all. Its errors come from the fact that neither smell alone carries any information about food.

items.stem: A fish with no hidden units learns only from eels and suckers that pass close by, so every smell it learns from is strong. Then it is taken downstream, where every smell arrives diluted to three tenths of its strength, and learning is switched off. Over a dozen encounters there, what did it do, and which demand does that show it failing?

options.text: It stayed to feed at every encounter and was struck by every eel, failing invariance, which asks it to treat faint and strong eel smells as one thing.
options.why: Correct. Far off, every smell is weak, and the fish treated every far smell the way it had treated a near sucker, so it stayed. Recognizing one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as distance, is invariance.

options.text: It fled at every encounter and never fed, failing discrimination: it treated every faint smell, a sucker’s as well as an eel’s, as an eel.
options.why: A fish that fled every faint smell would at least survive, and its failure would be one of discrimination. The downstream fish did the opposite: it stayed for everything, eels included.

options.text: It told the far eels from the far suckers about as well as near ones, showing that what it learned from strong smells carries over to faint ones.
options.why: The far smells were not told apart at all. Every one reached the fish weak, the fish stayed for every one, and every eel struck it.

options.text: It stayed for every sucker and fled from every eel, but late, failing the demand to reach a verdict while there is still time to get away.
options.why: The fish never fled a far eel at all, early or late. The failure lies in treating a faint eel smell as an eel, not in timing.

items.stem: In the lab’s new-predator scenario, a fish with six hidden units learns eels and suckers for 1,000 encounters, then spends 1,000 encounters with a pike and a chub alone. Then an eel comes back. What happened at that encounter, and what does it show?

options.text: The fish stayed and was struck, showing that learning the pike and the chub overwrote what it had learned about eels instead of adding to it.
options.why: Correct. After learning the pike and the chub alone, the fish stayed for the returning eel and the eel lunged: a miss. New learning has to add to old learning without overwriting it, and here it did not.

options.text: The fish darted to cover in time, showing that learning the pike and the chub added to what it had learned about eels without overwriting it.
options.why: That is what the requirement asks for, but not what happened. The fish stayed for the eel and was struck: learning the new pair alone cost it what it knew about eels.

options.text: The fish darted to cover in time, since the pike’s and the chub’s smells differ from the eel’s, so learning about them left the old learning alone.
options.why: Different smells are still carried by the same two receptors, so learning about one thing bears on what was learned about others. The fish stayed for the eel and was struck.

options.text: The fish stayed and was struck, showing that it had never learned eels well in its first 1,000 encounters, before the pike and the chub arrived.
options.why: The fish did stay and was struck, but not for that reason. After its first 1,000 encounters it was nearly always right about eels and suckers; what it knew was lost while it learned the pike and the chub alone.

items.stem: In the lab’s One line will do scenario, where smells vary only a little, the encounters land on the feature space, receptor A across and receptor B up, in two clouds. How do the two clouds sit relative to each other?

options.text: The eel cloud lies further along receptor A and lower on receptor B than the sucker cloud, with a clear gap between them.
options.why: Correct. An eel’s smell is around A 0.75 and B 0.45, and a sucker’s around A 0.45 and B 0.60. Each sniff is one point, and at this small spread the two clouds do not overlap.

options.text: The eel cloud lies higher on both receptors than the sucker cloud, since an eel’s smell is stronger at every receptor than a sucker’s.
options.why: An eel’s smell has more A than a sucker’s, but less B. The eel cloud sits to the right of the sucker cloud and lower, not higher on both.

options.text: The two clouds lie on top of each other in the middle, since eels and suckers smell alike and only the outcome tells them apart.
options.why: Two averages landing on top of each other in the middle happens in the fruit problem, not here. Eels and suckers smell different, and their clouds are apart.

options.text: The eel cloud lies lower on receptor A and higher on receptor B than the sucker cloud, overlapping it heavily at its edge.
options.why: That reverses the two kinds. And at this small spread the clouds do not overlap; overlap comes when smells are made to vary more.

items.stem: In the lab’s One line will do scenario, How much smells vary is raised from 0.06 to 0.20, and the fish learns for 1,000 encounters, with the rule working exactly as before. What did the test set show, and why?

options.text: Most answers were right, but a sizeable share stayed wrong, because the clouds now overlap and no straight line puts every eel on one side and every sucker on the other.
options.why: Correct. At 0.06 the test set ends almost perfect; at 0.20 something like a fifth to two fifths stay wrong, so the fish still does far better than guessing. Overlapping clouds are no longer linearly separable, and more training cannot remove errors that no line can avoid.

options.text: About half stayed wrong, no better than guessing, because once the two clouds overlap a single straight line carries no information about which fish is there.
options.why: Overlap leaves errors only where the clouds meet. Most eel sniffs and most sucker sniffs still lie on their own sides of the line, so the fish ends well short of half wrong, though well above none.

options.text: Nearly every answer came out right, because the rule kept moving the line until it found one that put every eel on its own side of the space.
options.why: No such line exists once the clouds overlap. However the rule moves the line, some eels and some suckers sit on the wrong side.

options.text: A sizeable share stayed wrong, because 1,000 encounters were too few, and a few thousand more would bring the test set back to nearly perfect.
options.why: More training would not help. The errors come from the overlap of the two clouds, not from the rule running out of time.

items.stem: In the lab’s Ripe or rotting scenario, with no hidden units, the fish was given the built-in receptor Both together, which responds to the product of the two smells, and then learned for a few hundred encounters. In a few sentences, say what happened, and explain in terms of the feature space why.
items.answer: The fish solved the fruit within a few hundred encounters, with no hidden layer at all. The product is large only when both smells are present, so it adds a third axis along which the rotting corner moves away from the other three. In that three-axis space a single flat plane separates the two ripe corners from the twig and the rotting fruit, so one unit can now draw a boundary that sorts them. With only the two smells, the ripe cases sat at opposite corners, and no single line could put both on one side.
rubric: Reports that the fish solved the problem (nearly every test answer right) within a few hundred encounters.
Says the product is active only when both smells are present.
Says the new input moves the rotting corner away from the other three, along a third axis.
Says a single flat plane (one boundary) now separates ripe from not ripe, which no line could do with the two smells alone.

items.stem: In the lab’s island scenario, fruit nourishes only when both receptors respond at about the right strength, so the nourishing smells form a disk in the middle of the feature space. A fish with no hidden units is given the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength. Once it succeeds, what does its decision boundary look like on the feature space?

options.text: A circle around the disk, since one threshold on the new input marks off every smell within a fixed reach of the center.
options.why: Correct. The receptor reports how far each smell is from the ideal, so one threshold on that one input marks off the island. Drawn on the two original axes, the smells at that threshold form a circle, and the fish reached 5 percent wrong within a few hundred encounters.

options.text: A single straight line across the disk, since one unit can only ever draw one straight boundary, whatever distance its inputs report.
options.why: On the two original axes the boundary here is not straight. A straight cut can take off one side of the island but cannot wrap around it, and this fish succeeded.

options.text: Two parallel lines with a band between them through the middle, since a band is the shape a single unit draws when it combines two smells.
options.why: A band is what two hidden units and an output draw for exclusive or. This fish has no hidden units, and its boundary wraps all the way round.

options.text: A rounded triangle around the disk, since one built-in receptor gives the unit three straight sides to work with.
options.why: A rounded triangle is what three learned hidden units draw. The distance receptor gives one threshold on distance, which wraps the disk in a circle.

items.stem: One of the four fish on the Fish tab turned out, after Reveal, to have low sensitivity, although its weights were about as large as the healthy fish’s. What was different about its weights, and what did that do?

options.text: Nearly all its weight sat on receptor B, which separates eels from suckers less well than receptor A does, so its white line lay nearly flat and its two histograms overlapped far more.
options.why: Correct. With weights near 0.3 on A and −3.3 on B, this fish leaned on the receptor whose responses differ less between eel and sucker. In the chapter’s terms, the dimension that separates eel from sucker had not been stretched, so its evidence separated the two poorly, and its d′ came out at about half the healthy fish’s.

options.text: Nearly all its weight sat on receptor A, which separates eels from suckers less well than receptor B does, so its white line stood nearly upright and its two histograms overlapped far more.
options.why: This has the right kind of fault, weight piled on one receptor, but the wrong receptor. In this stream receptor A is the one whose responses differ more between eel and sucker, and the healthy fish leans on it. The low-sensitivity fish leaned on receptor B, and its line lay nearly flat.

options.text: Its weights pointed the same way as the healthy fish’s, but its criterion sat well below zero, so it fled from nearly every smell and its false alarms piled up.
options.why: That describes a fish with a moved criterion, whose histograms are the same as the healthy fish’s. This fish’s histograms overlapped more, which no move of the criterion can do.

options.text: Its weights were reversed in sign from the healthy fish’s, so its white line stayed in the same place, but it fled from suckers and stayed for eels.
options.why: Reversed weights would make it wrong far more often than right. This fish was still right about seven times in ten; its weights sat on the wrong receptor rather than pointing the wrong way.

items.stem: Show each kind’s average (its prototype) marks one cross for each category. In the One line will do scenario the two crosses sat well apart, one in each cloud. Where did they sit in the Ripe or rotting scenario, and what follows for a model that keeps one prototype per category?

options.text: On top of each other near the middle, so a model that sorts by the nearest single prototype cannot tell nourishing fruit from the rest.
options.why: Correct. The two nourishing corners average to the center of the square, and so do the other two. Two categories with the same prototype cannot be told apart by their prototypes, however the comparison is made.

options.text: In the two ripe corners, one cross in each, so a model that sorts by the nearest single prototype handles the fruit easily once it has learned.
options.why: Each category gets one cross, its average. The ripe category’s two corners are opposite each other, so its average falls in the middle, not in a corner.

options.text: Well apart on the diagonal through the two ripe corners, so a model that sorts by the nearest single prototype draws a band holding both ripe corners.
options.why: A nearest-prototype model draws a straight boundary halfway between its two prototypes, never a band. And here the prototypes did not sit apart at all.

options.text: On top of each other near the middle, so a model that sorts by the nearest single prototype simply needs more training to pull the two apart.
options.why: Training cannot move an average: the prototypes coincide because of where the cases lie. A model with one prototype per category is limited to linearly separable categories.

items.stem: A hand-built hidden layer using the threshold function (a hard step) is handed to Pass the error back, and the fish learns for 1,000 encounters, with the hidden units’ sliders on the Network tab and the lines under The arithmetic on the Learning tab in view. What did the scene show?

options.text: No hidden slider moved at all, and the hidden unit’s printed slope, f′(net), and its printed Φ both read 0.000 on the encounters watched.
options.why: Correct. In backpropagation each unit’s share of the error is scaled by how much its output would change if its input changed, and a hard step’s output does not change with a small change of input. A slope of zero made the hidden unit’s Φ zero, so nothing in the hidden layer moved. Switched to the sigmoid, the hidden unit’s Φ was no longer zero and the hidden sliders began to move.

options.text: The hidden sliders crept slowly, since the slope read 0.000 but the hidden unit’s Φ still carried a small share of the output’s error.
options.why: The slope did read 0.000, but a hidden unit’s Φ is its slope times its weight to the output times the output’s Φ, so the hidden Φ read 0.000 too. Nothing reached the hidden weights.

options.text: The hidden sliders swung widely, since the step’s slope read large on every encounter, so each hidden unit took a large share of the error.
options.why: A step jumps at one point and is flat everywhere else, so its slope read 0.000, not large. With a zero slope the hidden unit’s share of the error was zero, and the sliders stayed still.

options.text: The hidden sliders moved only on the encounters the fish got wrong, when the output’s error was large enough to be passed back to them.
options.why: A large output error does not help when the slope is zero: the hidden unit’s Φ is the slope times the weight times the output’s Φ, and it read 0.000. No hidden slider moved.

items.stem: With Pass the error back and the sigmoid, the fruit is run with a single hidden unit, over three seeds. How often did the test set reach 5 percent wrong, and why?

options.text: Never, because one hidden unit draws one straight line, and no one straight line puts both ripe corners on one side.
options.why: Correct. A single hidden unit hands the output one line’s worth of information, so the network can do no better than one line. Separating the ripe corners from the other two takes at least two hidden units, each drawing its own line.
