options.text: In every seed, because any hidden layer at all lets passing the error back find the combination the fruit needs.
options.why: A hidden layer helps only if it has enough units for the combination. With one unit the network is limited to a single line, which cannot hold both ripe corners.

options.text: In about two seeds in three, because whether a run succeeds depends on where its random starting weights happen to fall.
options.why: That describes two hidden units, which sometimes stick and sometimes succeed. With one, no starting point could succeed.

options.text: Never, because passing the error back cannot train a hidden layer of any size on a problem of the exclusive-or kind.
options.why: With two or more hidden units, passing the error back did solve the fruit. The trouble here was the single unit, not the rule.

items.stem: On the island, under Fixed at random, the hidden weights are drawn once and never change, and only the output unit learns. With 200 hidden units and Sparse on, after 1,000 encounters, what did the decision boundary on the feature space look like?

options.text: A ragged, roughly circular boundary around the disk of nourishing fruit, although only the output unit’s weights had changed.
options.why: Correct. No hidden weight was learned. The output unit draws one straight boundary, but in the space of the 200 random units’ activity, not in the space of the two smells. Spreading the smells across many units is dimensionality expansion, and a straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions. Drawn back onto receptors A and B, that one boundary came out as a ragged curve around the disk.

options.text: A single straight line across the feature space, since only the output unit’s weights change, and a single unit can draw only one straight line.
options.why: The output unit’s boundary is straight in the space of the random units’ activity, not in the space of the two smells. Drawn back onto receptors A and B, it bent around the disk.

options.text: A smooth, perfect circle around the disk, the same boundary that the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength drew there.
options.why: The built-in receptor did draw a clean circle. The random units supply only whatever combinations they happened to compute, and the boundary they gave was ragged.

options.text: A rounded triangle around the disk, since the output unit can combine only a few of the random units’ lines into the boundary it draws.
options.why: A rounded triangle is what three hidden units trained by passing the error back drew. With 200 random units the boundary was a ragged curve, not three sides.

items.stem: On the Learning tab, the arithmetic for the output unit prints Φ = a − p, with a line under it saying where the target comes from. On one encounter the fish darts to cover, and an eel lunges at the empty water where it was. On that encounter, what are a and p?

options.text: a is the outcome a moment later, an eel there, although the fish was not struck, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: Correct. The line under Φ says the target is the outcome, a moment later, and that nothing inside the fish is a teacher. The outcome arrives on every encounter whatever the fish did, so an eel lunging at empty water still counts as an eel there. The world supplies the target, which is why it needs no teacher.

options.text: a is no eel, since the fish darted away and was not struck, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: Not being struck is what darting bought the fish, not what the world sent. The target is whether an eel was there, and here one lunged, whatever the fish did.

options.text: a is the correct answer that the experimenter supplies, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: The experimenter keeps the test sets but supplies no answers to the fish. The line under Φ says the target is the outcome, and that nothing inside the fish is a teacher.

options.text: a is the outcome a moment later, an eel there, and p is the criterion that the fish’s chemistry set when the smell arrived.
options.why: The criterion is never read by the prediction or written by learning. p is the prediction itself, the sigmoid of the evidence when the smell arrived.

items.stem: On the island, with Pass the error back, a network with three hidden units was run for up to 5,000 encounters. In a few sentences, say how close it came to 5 percent wrong, describe the boundary it drew around the disk, and explain why that is the best three hidden units can do.
items.answer: Three units usually fell short, leaving something like a fifth of the fruit wrong. The boundary was a rounded triangle around the disk. Each hidden unit draws its own straight line through the feature space, and the output combines those lines, so three units can at most cut out a three-sided region. A triangle cannot fit a disk, so some fruit near its corners or along its sides always lands on the wrong side. More units give more sides, which is why six units nearly always reached the mark, though only after thousands of encounters.
rubric: Reports how close the run came; most runs stopped short of 5 percent wrong, and a run that reached it, reported as such, also earns this element.
Describes the boundary as a (rounded) triangle around the disk.
Says each hidden unit contributes one straight line, which the output combines.
Says three lines can at most make a three-sided region, which cannot match a disk.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, a fish trained on eels and suckers in phase 1 is scored on the pike and chub test set before it has encountered either animal. The pike lunges and the chub is harmless. How did the fish do on that test set, and why?

options.text: Wrong on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on receptor B, like a sucker’s, and a chub’s is heavy on receptor A, like an eel’s, so it stayed for pikes and fled from chubs.
options.why: Correct. On the World tab a pike’s typical smell is heavy on B, as a sucker’s is, and a chub’s is heavy on A, as an eel’s is, and the pike and chub test set came out wrong on nearly every item. Shared weights give similar inputs similar outputs without any extra work, which is generalization, and here it carried the fish the wrong way.

options.text: Wrong on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on receptor A, like a sucker’s, and a chub’s is heavy on receptor B, like an eel’s, so it stayed for pikes and fled from chubs.
options.why: The fish was wrong for this reason, resemblance to the old animal of the other kind, but the receptors are swapped. An eel’s smell is heavier on A and a sucker’s on B, while a pike’s is heavy on B and a chub’s on A.

options.text: Wrong on about half: a pike’s and a chub’s smells each fall about midway between an eel’s and a sucker’s, so the fish’s answers to them were close to guesses.
options.why: A network gives some answer to every smell, and similar inputs get similar outputs. The pike and chub smells lie far out on the old animals’ sides, and the test set came out wrong on nearly every item, not on half.

options.text: Right on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on the same receptor as an eel’s, and a chub’s on the same receptor as a sucker’s, so it fled from pikes and stayed for chubs.
options.why: That would be true if each new animal resembled the old animal of its own kind. In the scene the pike smells like a sucker and the chub like an eel, so the fish got both backward.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, a fish trained on eels and suckers in phase 1, and nearly all right on them, moves to phase 2, where only the pike and the chub arrive, with learning on. How did its eel and sucker test set change over the next 1,000 encounters?

options.text: It was already far worse within the first 100 encounters, and by 1,000 it was wrong on nearly every item.
options.why: Correct. The old test set collapsed fast and went past chance to nearly all wrong. Learning the pike and chub moved the shared weights to treat a smell heavy on A as harmless and one heavy on B as dangerous, the reverse of what eels and suckers need. Like the network that answered ones problems as if they were twos problems, the fish answered the old animals by the new pair’s rule.

options.text: It barely changed in the first 100 encounters, then worsened steadily, and by 1,000 it was wrong on nearly every item.
options.why: The end point is right, but the loss was not slow to start. Within the first 100 encounters the old test set was already far worse; in a network trained by backpropagation, the disturbance can be extreme.

options.text: It was already far worse within the first 100 encounters, and then it recovered to about half wrong by 1,000 as the weights settled.
options.why: The weights did not settle at a blank state. They moved to suit the new pair, which reverses the old one, so the old test set ended wrong on nearly every item, not on half.

options.text: It barely changed over the whole 1,000 encounters, since the eel and sucker learning was carried by hidden units the new pair did not use.
options.why: Every weight takes part in many input–output pairs. The new learning moved the same weights the old pair depended on, and the old test set collapsed within the first 100 encounters.

items.stem: In the downstream scenario, a fish that learns only from near eels and suckers gets the far test set about half wrong. The run is repeated with Learn from every distance switched on, so that half its encounters are far. What happened to the near and far test sets?

options.text: The far test set came out nearly all right, and the near test set stayed nearly all right as well, with no new receptor added to the fish.
options.why: Correct. Trained with near and far encounters mixed, the fish ended nearly all right on both test sets. That is how artificial networks mostly get across changes of size: by training on examples that already include those changes. Whether training of that kind is enough to explain how animals do it is a live dispute.

options.text: The far test set came out nearly all right, but the near test set lost much of its accuracy, since only half the encounters were now near.
options.why: That trade-off is what many expect, but the near test set stayed nearly all right. Half the encounters near was plenty for the near smells.

options.text: The far test set improved only to about three in four right, since faint eel and sucker smells overlap too much for any line to separate them well.
options.why: The far test set came out nearly all right. Faint smells keep the eel’s larger share of A, so a line can separate them once the fish has learned from them.

options.text: Neither test set changed much, since a fish with no hidden units draws only one line, and no single line serves near and far smells alike.
options.why: One line did serve both. With far encounters in its training, the fish’s single line came to sort faint smells as well as strong ones, and both test sets ended nearly all right.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, the run is repeated from the same starting weights, but with Eels and suckers stay around switched on during phase 2, so the old animals keep arriving among the pike and the chub. In a few sentences, say what happened to both test sets, including how the eel and sucker test set behaved early in phase 2, and explain why mixing the animals was enough, using what the chapter names as the trigger for catastrophic interference.
items.answer: Both test sets ended nearly all right, within a few percent of perfect. On the way, the eel and sucker line jumped up and down for the first few hundred encounters of phase 2 before it settled. The fish, the network and the rule were the same as before; only the mix of encounters changed. The trigger for catastrophic interference is learning in sequence: trained on one set and then another, the weights move to wherever suits the newest set. With both sets arriving together, a change that suited the new animals but hurt the old ones was pulled back by the old animals’ errors, so the weights settled where both were right.
rubric: Reports that both test sets ended nearly all right.
Reports that the eel and sucker line jumped up and down for the first few hundred encounters before settling.
Says nothing about the fish, the network or the rule changed, only the mix of encounters.
Names learning in sequence as the trigger.
Explains that with both sets present the weights move to a setting that suits both, not to wherever suits the newest set.

items.stem: To close the gap between training and test in the small pool, three changes were tried one at a time: two hidden units instead of eight, a pool of 24 or 60 individuals, and a stream in which every encounter is a new individual. What did they show about where the trouble came from?

options.text: The smaller network left the gap about where it was, but larger pools shrank it and a stream closed it, so the small pool was the trouble.
options.why: Correct. Two hidden units, or none at all, still left a gap of about 16 or 17 points, because even one line can fit the accidents of six individuals. With 24 individuals the gap fell to about 6, at 60 to about 3, and in a stream training and test stayed within a few points.

options.text: The smaller network closed the gap while the larger pools made little difference, so having too many hidden units for so small a pool was the trouble.
options.why: A smaller network is the common remedy, which is why the lab tries it, but here it barely changed the gap. What was small was the pool.

options.text: All three closed the gap about equally well, the stream included, so any change that makes the six individuals harder to memorize removes overfitting.
options.why: The three did not work equally: the smaller network left the gap almost untouched. Only more individuals, or a new one every encounter, closed it.

options.text: None of the three closed the gap, so the trouble came from the learning rule itself, which fits whatever examples it is given.
options.why: The larger pools and the stream did close it. The rule fits its examples, but with enough different individuals the accidents of any one stop mattering.

items.stem: A fish with no hidden units learns only from eels and suckers close by, where every smell is strong. Its learning curve tracks a near test set and a far test set, whose smells are diluted to three tenths of their strength. What did the two lines show after the first 300 encounters, and after 2,000 more?

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set about half wrong, and 2,000 more encounters left the far set where it was.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in training near the fish was as faint as the far test set, so more of the same training did not reach it. A classifier is reliable near the region its training examples occupy and much less reliable far from it, which is the weakness of out-of-distribution generalization.

options.text: Both sets were still about half wrong at 300, and 2,000 more encounters made the near set almost error-free while the far set stayed about half wrong.
options.why: The near set did not need thousands of encounters: a single line sorts strong eel and sucker smells within a few hundred. The far set’s failure was there from the start and did not move.

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set about half wrong, and 2,000 more encounters slowly brought the far set close to the near set.
options.why: The far set did not improve at all. Training on strong smells taught the fish about strong smells, and the far smells lie well outside them.

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set nearly all wrong, because the fish took every faint smell for an eel and fled.
options.why: The fish stayed for every faint smell, not fled. About half the far set is suckers, and staying was right for those, which leaves the far set about half wrong.

items.stem: A fish that learns only from nearby eels and suckers was given Proportion of A, a built-in receptor that responds to the share of a smell that is A, whatever its strength. In a few sentences, say what happened to the far test set with receptors A and B still connected beside it, and with them disconnected, and explain why the fish did not rely on the proportion when it had A and B as well.
items.answer: With A and B still connected, the far test set was not rescued: it stayed far worse than the near set, with many far eels taken for suckers. With A and B disconnected, the far test set came out nearly all right, though the fish had never been downstream. Near the fish, raw strength and proportion both sorted every eel from every sucker perfectly, so the rule, which only reduces errors on the encounters the fish has, had no reason to prefer the proportion. Only when A and B were removed did the proportion become the fish’s whole input space, and the one difference it could register survives dilution. A built-in feature helps only if the learner comes to depend on it.
rubric: Reports that the proportion beside A and B left the far test set poor, and that the proportion alone fixed it.
Says that near the fish, raw strength (A and B) worked just as well as the proportion on every training encounter.
Says the rule reduces error only on the encounters it gets, so nothing pushed it toward the proportion.
Says removing A and B left the proportion as the only input, which is unchanged by dilution.

items.stem: The island was solved three ways: with the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength, with 50 hidden units fixed at random under Sparse, and with hidden units trained by Pass the error back. Which route needed the fewest encounters and the fewest units, and what did it need in place before learning began?

options.text: The built-in receptor, which needed no hidden units and a few hundred encounters, but needed the right feature for this problem chosen in advance.
options.why: Correct. With the distance receptor the fish reached 5 percent wrong within a few hundred encounters and no hidden layer. The price is that someone had to know, before learning began, that distance from the middle is what matters.

options.text: The random hidden units, which needed few units and encounters, since unlike a built-in receptor a layer wired at random needs nothing in place before learning.
options.why: The random route needed dozens of units, and its assumption that useful combinations will turn up among many random ones is itself built in before learning.

options.text: The trained hidden units, which needed the fewest units and encounters, since passing the error back finds exactly the combinations the task needs.
options.why: Passing the error back did find the combinations, but slowly: it needed several units and thousands of encounters on the island.

options.text: All three needed about the same number of encounters and units, since the island is equally hard whichever way its features are supplied.
options.why: The routes differed a great deal. The built-in receptor was fastest by far, and the learned hidden layer was the slowest.

items.stem: A fish that learns only from nearby eels and suckers is given the built-in receptor Proportion of A alone, with receptors A and B disconnected. On the feature space, receptor A across and receptor B up, what does its decision boundary look like, and why does it also work far downstream?

options.text: A straight line running out from the lower-left corner, so a smell stays on its side however far it is diluted toward that corner.
options.why: Correct. Every smell with the same share of A lies on one straight line out from the corner where both receptors are zero, and diluting a smell slides it along that line toward the corner without changing its share. So the boundary sorts far smells as it sorts near ones, and the far test set came out nearly all right.

options.text: A circle around the near eels, so any smell far from where the eels were learned, a diluted one included, falls outside the circle.
options.why: A circle is what the distance receptor drew on the island. Far eels would fall outside a circle around near eels, and the fish would stay for them.

options.text: A straight line across the middle, parallel to the receptor B axis, so that the amount of A alone decides which side a smell falls on.
options.why: A boundary set by the amount of A is the kind that fails downstream, since dilution cuts the amount of A. The share of A is what survives dilution.

options.text: A straight line in the same place as the near-trained fish’s line, so that the boundary is unchanged and only the criterion has moved.
options.why: The near-trained fish’s line passed to one side of the far smells and missed every far eel. This fish’s boundary runs through the corner the far smells crowd toward.

items.stem: On the island, under Fixed at random, the hidden weights are drawn once and never change, and only the connections to the output learn. The card for that setting names an animal whose brain is wired this way, and adds a sentence about fish. What do the card and the runs, taken together, license about real fish?

options.text: No conclusion on their wiring: the card names the fruit fly’s mushroom body as wired like this, and leaves open whether a fish’s pallium is.
options.why: Correct. In the fly, about 50 kinds of smell input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells through connections that look random, and learning happens at the connections to the output neurons. The lab shows the arrangement can work, not that a fish has it.

options.text: No conclusion on their wiring: the card names the mouse’s piriform cortex as wired like this, and leaves open whether a fish’s pallium is.
options.why: The fish half is right, but the card names the fruit fly’s mushroom body, where the connections were traced and look random. In the mouse’s piriform cortex, random wiring is a model the data fit, not something seen.

options.text: That a fish’s pallium must be wired at random, since the lab’s fish solved the island with a hidden layer wired in just this way.
options.why: A model that works shows what an arrangement can do, not what a fish has. The card says outright that whether a fish’s pallium is wired like this is not known.

options.text: That a fish’s pallium is wired like the mouse’s piriform cortex, since random wiring was measured there and fish and mice are both vertebrates.
options.why: Random wiring in the piriform cortex is a model the data fit, not a measurement. And neither result says how a fish’s pallium is wired.

items.stem: The healthy fish is run twice: once with the criterion slider at −0.50, and once with the slider at 0 and arousal and vigilance raised to 3. How did the two scorecards compare?

options.text: They were the same, count for count, since raising arousal moved the effective criterion to −0.50 and changed nothing else.
options.why: Correct. Arousal moved the criterion by exactly the amount the slider did, so the four counts matched. In a unit the criterion is the threshold, and in a neuron its counterpart is excitability, which is what neuromodulators change.

options.text: They differed in d′, since arousal sharpened how well the fish’s evidence separates eels from suckers, while the slider moved only the criterion.
options.why: Arousal did not change d′; the histograms did not move. Like the slider, it moved only the criterion.

options.text: They differed in every count, since arousal changes the fish’s weights, while the slider changes the criterion and nothing else.
options.why: Arousal changed no weight; the weights on the Network tab stayed at their locked values. Its only effect was on the effective criterion.

options.text: They differed in the size of the shift: hits and false alarms rose together both times, but arousal moved the effective criterion less far than the slider did.
options.why: Arousal did move the criterion in the same direction as the slider, with d′ unchanged. But at 3 it moved the effective criterion to −0.50, exactly as far as the slider, so the four counts matched.

items.stem: A fish that learned only from strong, nearby smells is taken downstream, where every smell is diluted to three tenths of its strength. Going downstream switches learning off, so the fish’s weights, criterion and chemistry stay as they were. Its scorecard there shows only misses and correct rejections, with no hits and no false alarms. Which account of that scorecard is right?

options.text: It stayed for every smell and was struck by every eel, although its criterion had not moved: every diluted smell gave evidence below that criterion.
options.why: Correct. All misses and no false alarms looks like a high criterion, but the criterion and the chemistry were untouched. What changed was what the world sent: far eels and far suckers sit in one small knot on the no-eel side of the fish’s line, so they gave it weak and far less different evidence.

options.text: It stayed for every smell and was struck by every eel, because diluted smells raised its criterion, as lowering satiety and tone did to the healthy fish.
options.why: The behavior is right, but the reason confuses the two quantities. The criterion lives in the chemistry, and the chemistry was unchanged; the faint smells gave evidence that fell below the same criterion as before.

options.text: It stayed for every smell and was struck by every eel, because going downstream lowered the fish’s sensitivity by changing its weights toward the sucker’s receptor.
options.why: Sensitivity did fall in effect, but not through the weights, which stayed exactly as they were. What changed was the input: diluted smells gave weak, crowded evidence that fell below the unchanged criterion.

options.text: It stayed for every smell and was struck by every eel, because with learning switched off the fish could no longer turn evidence into a decision to flee.
options.why: Switching learning off freezes the weights; it does not stop the fish from comparing evidence with its criterion. The fish still decided on every encounter, and every diluted smell simply gave evidence below the criterion.

items.stem: On the island, with 200 hidden units fixed at random, Sparse is switched on and the run repeated. A line under the network’s drawing reports, for the smell now, how many of the 200 hidden units are active. What did Sparse change?

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set held or improved, since few of many units active lets one line draw many more divisions.
options.why: Correct. Without Sparse about half the units were active; with it, far fewer. The test set came out nearly all right. When only a few of many units are active for each input, many more ways of dividing the inputs can be drawn with a single straight line, so one trained layer can do the work.

options.text: More of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set improved, because more active units give the output unit more evidence to add up for each smell.
options.why: That reverses the count: Sparse cut the number of active units well below the hundred or so active without it. The gain comes from few units being active, not many.

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set got worse, because silencing most of the units throws away information the output unit needed.
options.why: The count did fall, but fewer active units did not cost accuracy here; the test set held or improved. A code with few of many units active makes more divisions drawable with one straight line.

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the hidden weights began to change, because under Sparse the active units’ weights are trained.
options.why: Under Fixed at random the hidden weights are drawn once and never move, with Sparse on or off; only the output unit learns. What changed was how many units each smell made active.
